1.full:
[font_size=26][b]Start here[/b][/font_size]

picosim runs programs written in [b]assembly language[/b] — the instructions the Raspberry Pi Pico's processor understands — and lets you watch them run one step at a time. Try anything: nothing can break, and [color=#e5c07b][code]Reload[/code][/color] always starts your program over.

[color=#61afef][b]Your first five minutes[/b][/color]
[ol type=1]Click [color=#e5c07b][code]Examples[/code][/color] in the toolbar and pick [b]Say hello[/b]. Your program appears in the Disassembly list on the left; the row marked ▶ is the instruction that runs next. The [b]Source[/b] column shows the line of your file that each row came from.
▶ is on [code]main[/code], the first line of your program. Press [color=#e5c07b][code]Step instruction[/code][/color] ([color=#e5c07b][code]S[/code][/color]) once: [code]push {r7, lr}[/code] runs and SP changes.
Step once more and look at the [url=registers][color=#61afef][u]Registers[/u][/color][/url]: the one that just changed turns [color=#f2cc60]yellow[/color]. After [code]movs r0, #'H'[/code], R0 holds [code]0x00000048[/code], the [url=numbers][color=#61afef][u]ASCII code[/u][/color][/url] for the letter H.
Step again. [code]bl putchar[/code] calls the function that prints the character in R0, and an [b]H[/b] appears in the [url=serial][color=#61afef][u]serial console[/u][/color][/url] on the right.
Press [color=#e5c07b][code]Run[/code][/color] ([color=#e5c07b][code]Space[/code][/color]) to let the rest go by itself. When the status text at the top says [b]halted[/b], the program has finished; press [color=#e5c07b][code]Reload[/code][/color] to watch it again.[/ol]
Each time you step, the [url=explain][color=#61afef][u]Explain this step[/u][/color][/url] panel at the top right says what that instruction did and what the next one will do, so you can follow along without guessing.

[table=1][cell bg=#2a2a2a border=#61afef padding=14,9,14,9 expand=1][color=#61afef][b]Stuck?[/b][/color]   Nothing you do here can break anything, and [color=#e5c07b][code]Reload[/code][/color] always starts the program over. [url=running][color=#61afef][u]How a program runs[/u][/color][/url] explains each of the steps above.[/cell][/table]

[color=#61afef][b]Words you will meet[/b][/color]
[ul]​[b]Register[/b] — a small storage box inside the processor that holds one number. R0–R12 are for your values; SP, LR and PC have special jobs.
​[b]PC[/b] (program counter) — the address of the next instruction. Watch it move as you step.
​[b]Hex[/b] — numbers written in base 16 with a [code]0x[/code] in front: [code]0x2A[/code] = 42. Hover a register to see it in decimal, or switch the Registers panel's [color=#e5c07b][code]Hex[/code][/color] menu to [color=#e5c07b][code]Decimal[/code][/color].
​[b]Flags[/b] N Z C V — four yes/no facts about the last result (negative? zero? …) that branches like [code]BNE[/code] use to decide where to go.[/ul]
More words are in the [url=glossary][color=#61afef][u]Glossary[/u][/color][/url].

[color=#61afef][b]What to read next[/b][/color]
If you missed the first class, read these in order. Each takes a few minutes:
[ol type=1]​[url=tour][color=#61afef][u]The screen at a glance[/u][/color][/url] — every button and panel you can see.
​[url=running][color=#61afef][u]How a program runs[/u][/color][/url] — what happens when you press Step and Run.
​[url=numbers][color=#61afef][u]Hex, binary and ASCII[/u][/color][/url] — how to read the numbers on screen.
​[url=instructions][color=#61afef][u]Instructions[/u][/color][/url] and [url=branches][color=#61afef][u]Flags and branches[/u][/color][/url] — what each line of a program does.
​[url=examples][color=#61afef][u]Level 1 examples[/u][/color][/url] — step through them with a guide beside you.
​[url=programs][color=#61afef][u]Writing programs[/u][/color][/url] — write, save and run your own.[/ol]

[color=#61afef][b]Levels: see more when you are ready[/b][/color]
The [color=#e5c07b][code]Level[/code][/color] menu (top right) decides how much of picosim is shown. Each level adds to the one before:
[ul]​[b]1 · Basics[/b] — Run programs one instruction at a time and watch the registers and the serial console   [color=#f2cc60]← you are here[/color]
​[b]2 · Memory & I/O[/b] — Adds the Memory tab, the stack and the Raspberry Pi Pico board with its pins
​[b]3 · Inside the CPU[/b] — Adds the CPU diagram: step through every clock cycle on the datapath
​[b]4 · Pipeline & performance[/b] — Adds the Pico's 2-stage pipeline and the Performance window[/ul]
Your teacher will tell you when to change level. Changing it never changes your program. When you raise it, picosim switches on what is new (the Memory tab, the CPU diagram, the pipeline), says what appeared in a strip under the toolbar, and outlines each new button and panel with a [color=#f2cc60][b]NEW[/b][/color] tag for a few seconds.

[table=1][cell bg=#2a2a2a border=#61afef padding=14,9,14,9 expand=1][color=#61afef][b]Tip[/b][/color]   The list on the left gets longer at each level. Click a section's heading (such as [b]▾ GETTING STARTED[/b]) to fold its topics away, and click it again to bring them back. picosim remembers which sections you folded.[/cell][/table]

1.sum:
picosim runs programs written in [b]assembly language[/b], the instructions the Raspberry Pi Pico's processor understands, and lets you watch them one step at a time. To begin, click [color=#e5c07b][code]Examples[/code][/color] and pick [b]Say hello[/b]. Press [color=#e5c07b][code]Step instruction[/code][/color] ([color=#e5c07b][code]S[/code][/color]) to run one instruction: whatever changed turns [color=#f2cc60]yellow[/color] in the Registers, the [url=explain][color=#61afef][u]Explain this step[/u][/color][/url] panel says what happened and what comes next, and anything printed appears in the serial console. [color=#e5c07b][code]Run[/code][/color] ([color=#e5c07b][code]Space[/code][/color]) lets the program go by itself, [color=#e5c07b][code]◀ Step back[/code][/color] ([color=#e5c07b][code]B[/code][/color]) undoes a step and [color=#e5c07b][code]Reload[/code][/color] starts over. Nothing you do can break anything.

The [color=#e5c07b][code]Level[/code][/color] menu (top right) decides how much of picosim you see: start at Level 1 and move up when your class does. Then read [url=tour][color=#61afef][u]The screen at a glance[/u][/color][/url] and [url=running][color=#61afef][u]How a program runs[/u][/color][/url]; the [url=glossary][color=#61afef][u]Glossary[/u][/color][/url] explains any word you do not know.

1.full:
[font_size=26][b]The screen at a glance[/b][/font_size]

Before a program is loaded, picosim shows a welcome page with the examples; click one to open it. After that the window has a toolbar across the top and these panels:

[table=2][cell bg=#2a2a2a border=#474747 padding=16,12,16,12 expand=1][b]Registers[/b]
[color=#8c8c8c]the CPU's 16 registers and flags[/color]

[b]Disassembly[/b]
[color=#8c8c8c]your program, one instruction per row[/color][/cell][cell bg=#2a2a2a border=#474747 padding=16,12,16,12 expand=1][b]Explain this step[/b]
[color=#8c8c8c]what the last step did, and what happens next[/color]

[b]Serial console[/b]
[color=#8c8c8c]what your program prints, and the keys you type[/color][/cell][/table]

Click a panel's name to read about it: [url=registers][color=#61afef][u]Registers[/u][/color][/url], [url=memory][color=#61afef][u]Disassembly[/u][/color][/url], [url=explain][color=#61afef][u]Explain this step[/u][/color][/url], [url=serial][color=#61afef][u]Serial console[/u][/color][/url]. Drag the bars between panels to resize them.

[color=#61afef][b]The toolbar, left to right[/b][/color]
[table=2][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Control[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]What it does[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#e5c07b][code]Open…[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Open a [code].s[/code] file of your own ([color=#e5c07b][code]Ctrl/Cmd+O[/code][/color]).[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#e5c07b][code]Examples[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Open one of the example programs. One marked [i](Level 2)[/i] or higher is meant for later, but opens all the same.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#e5c07b][code]Reload[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Read the file again and start the program from the beginning ([color=#e5c07b][code]Ctrl/Cmd+R[/code][/color]). Use it after you save a change, or to watch again.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#e5c07b][code]◀ Step back[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Undo the last step ([color=#e5c07b][code]B[/code][/color]; hold it to keep going back). Registers, flags, memory and the console go back to what they were.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#e5c07b][code]Step instruction[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Run exactly one instruction, then stop ([color=#e5c07b][code]S[/code][/color] or [color=#e5c07b][code]F10[/code][/color]; hold it to keep stepping). On a call into the built-in OS ([code]bl putchar[/code]) it runs the whole call.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#e5c07b][code]Run[/code][/color] / [color=#e5c07b][code]Pause[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Let the program run by itself; press again to pause ([color=#e5c07b][code]Space[/code][/color] or [color=#e5c07b][code]F5[/code][/color]). It stops at the end, at a breakpoint, or on a CPU fault.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#e5c07b][code]Speed[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]How fast Run goes, in clock cycles per second ([code]cyc/s[/code]). An instruction takes several clock cycles (about 6 or 7 on average in the Level 1 examples), so the starting speed of 8 cyc/s runs about one instruction a second. [b]Max[/b] runs as fast as possible.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Status text[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]How many instructions have run, and why the program stopped: [b]halted[/b] (finished), [b]waiting for input[/b] (type a key in the console) or [b]stopped by a CPU fault[/b] (read the console).[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#e5c07b][code]−[/code][/color] [color=#e5c07b][code]100%[/code][/color] [color=#e5c07b][code]+[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Zoom the whole window. Click the percentage to fit it to the window again.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#e5c07b][code]View[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The colour scheme: [b]System[/b] (follows your computer's light or dark setting), [b]Blue[/b], [b]Dark[/b] or [b]Light[/b]; and [b]Show the tour again[/b].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#e5c07b][code]Level[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]How much of picosim to show (you are on 1 · Basics). See [url=start][color=#61afef][u]Start here[/u][/color][/url].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#e5c07b][code]Guide[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]This guide ([color=#e5c07b][code]F1[/code][/color]). [color=#e5c07b][code]Esc[/code][/color] closes it.[/cell][/table]

Buttons that cannot be used right now are greyed out: for example Step and Run after the program has halted, until you press [color=#e5c07b][code]Reload[/code][/color].

[color=#61afef][b]The tour[/b][/color]
The first time you load a program, a short tour points out Step, Explain this step, the Registers, the Disassembly, the console and this guide, one at a time. [color=#e5c07b][code]Next ▶[/code][/color] moves on and [color=#e5c07b][code]Skip tour[/code][/color] (or [color=#e5c07b][code]Esc[/code][/color]) ends it. To see it again, choose [color=#e5c07b][code]View[/code][/color] ▸ [b]Show the tour again[/b].
1.name: The screen at a glance
1.sum:
Across the top is the toolbar: [color=#e5c07b][code]Open…[/code][/color] and [color=#e5c07b][code]Examples[/code][/color] load a program, [color=#e5c07b][code]Reload[/code][/color] starts it over, [color=#e5c07b][code]◀ Step back[/code][/color], [color=#e5c07b][code]Step instruction[/code][/color] and [color=#e5c07b][code]Run[/code][/color] move through it, and [color=#e5c07b][code]Speed[/code][/color] sets how fast Run goes. Below it, the [b]Registers[/b] (top left) show the numbers the CPU is working on, the [b]Disassembly[/b] under them lists your program with ▶ on the next instruction, [b]Explain this step[/b] (top right) describes each step, and the [b]serial console[/b] (bottom right) shows what the program prints.

Hover any button for a reminder of what it does. A greyed-out button cannot be used right now: for example Step after the program has finished, until you press [color=#e5c07b][code]Reload[/code][/color]. [color=#e5c07b][code]View[/code][/color] ▸ [b]Show the tour again[/b] replays the short first-run tour.

1.full:
[font_size=26][b]How a program runs[/b][/font_size]

Every program runs the same way: picosim's small [b]built-in OS[/b] starts it, it runs one instruction at a time, it calls functions such as [code]putchar[/code] to print, and it ends by returning to the OS. At Level 1 the OS's own instructions are hidden, so you only step through [i]your[/i] lines. Here is the [b]Say hello[/b] example, exactly as [color=#e5c07b][code]Step instruction[/code][/color] shows it. Open it from [color=#e5c07b][code]Examples[/code][/color] and step along.

[color=#61afef][b]Before you press anything[/b][/color]
When the program loads, the OS has already run its three start-up instructions and called your [code]main[/code]. That is why ▶ starts on [code]main[/code] at [code]3000[/code], and why R0 already holds [code]0x00003001[/code] (the address of main, plus 1) and LR holds [code]0x00000007[/code] (where main returns to, in the OS). At Level 2 you will step through those instructions too.

[table=4][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Press[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Address[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Instruction[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]What happens[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]1[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]3000[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]push {r7, lr}[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Saves R7 and LR on the stack, so SP goes down by 8 to [code]0x0000FFF8[/code].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]2[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]3002[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]movs r0, #'H'[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]R0 = [code]0x00000048[/code], the character H. The Z flag is cleared.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]3[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]3004[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]bl putchar[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Calls putchar, which prints the character in R0: [b]H[/b] appears in the console. LR = [code]0x00003009[/code] (the next line, plus 1): that is how putchar knew where to come back to.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]4–9[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The same two steps print [code]i[/code], [code]![/code] and a new line.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]10[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]301A[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]movs r0, #0[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]R0 = 0, which means "finished without errors". The result is zero, so the Z flag turns on.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]11[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]301C[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]pop {r7, pc}[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Takes R7 and the saved LR back off the stack, putting the LR value into PC: main returns to the OS, which stops the processor. SP is back to [code]0x00010000[/code] and the status text says [color=#f2cc60][b]halted[/b][/color].[/cell][/table]

[color=#61afef][b]Step, Run and breakpoints[/b][/color]
[ul]​[color=#e5c07b][code]Step instruction[/code][/color] ([color=#e5c07b][code]S[/code][/color]) runs one line of your program. On [code]bl putchar[/code] it runs the whole call, so the character is printed in one step.
​[color=#e5c07b][code]Run[/code][/color] ([color=#e5c07b][code]Space[/code][/color]) keeps going at the [url=tour][color=#61afef][u]Speed[/u][/color][/url] you chose, until the program halts, reaches a breakpoint, or you press [color=#e5c07b][code]Pause[/code][/color]. If the program is waiting for a key ([code]getchar[/code]), Run waits too and carries on once you type one in the console.
A [b]breakpoint[/b] (click the first column of a Disassembly row) makes Run stop just before that instruction. Then you can Step from there.
​[color=#e5c07b][code]◀ Step back[/code][/color] ([color=#e5c07b][code]B[/code][/color]) undoes the last step, so you can go back and watch a line again. Everything goes back with it, the console's text too. A key you typed for [code]getchar[/code] is handed to the program again when it gets there.
You can mix them: Run to a breakpoint, Step a few lines, Run again.[/ul]

[color=#61afef][b]Starting again[/b][/color]
When the program has halted, Step and Run are greyed out. [color=#e5c07b][code]Reload[/code][/color] reads the file again and starts it from the beginning, with every register and flag reset. When you save your file, picosim reloads it by itself. The console keeps what was printed before, under a grey [code][lb]loaded …][/code] line that marks the new start; [color=#e5c07b][code]Clear[/code][/color] empties it.

[color=#61afef][b]Where the numbers come from[/b][/color]
The addresses are always the same: the OS is at [code]0000[/code]–[code]2FFF[/code] and your program starts at [code]3000[/code]. The stack is at the top of memory, just below [code]0x00010000[/code], and you will look inside it at Level 2.
1.name: How a program runs
1.sum:
Every program runs the same way: picosim's small [b]built-in OS[/b] calls your [code]main[/code], the CPU runs one instruction at a time from top to bottom (unless a branch jumps somewhere else), the program calls functions such as [code]putchar[/code] to print, and [code]main[/code] ends with [code]pop {…, pc}[/code], which returns to the OS. The OS then stops the processor and the status text says [b]halted[/b]. At Level 1 the OS's own instructions are hidden, so ▶ starts on [code]main[/code] and each [code]bl putchar[/code] is one step.

[color=#e5c07b][code]Step instruction[/code][/color] runs one instruction. [color=#e5c07b][code]Run[/code][/color] keeps going until the program ends, reaches a [b]breakpoint[/b] (click a row's first column in the Disassembly) or you press [color=#e5c07b][code]Pause[/code][/color]. [color=#e5c07b][code]◀ Step back[/code][/color] undoes a step, and [color=#e5c07b][code]Reload[/code][/color] starts again. The full details walk through Say hello line by line, with the real values.

1.full:
[font_size=26][b]Writing programs[/b][/font_size]

A program is a plain text file whose name ends in [code].s[/code], written in ARM [b]Thumb[/b] assembly language for the GNU assembler. Here is a complete one:

[table=1][cell bg=#0e0e0e border=#474747 padding=14,10,14,10 expand=1][code]        .syntax unified
        .cpu cortex-m0plus
        .thumb

main:
        push    {r7, lr}        @ save the return address
        movs    r0, #'H'        @ R0 = the letter H
        bl      putchar         @ print the letter in R0
        movs    r0, #0
        pop     {r7, pc}        @ return: the program halts[/code][/cell][/table]

[color=#61afef][b]The parts of a program[/b][/color]
[table=3][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Part[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Example[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]What it is[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Directive[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code].thumb[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]An order to the assembler, not an instruction for the CPU. Start every program with the same three lines shown above: they choose the Pico's instruction set.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Label[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]main:[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]A name for the address of the next instruction, written at the start of a line and ending in a colon. Branches and calls jump to labels.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Instruction[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]movs r0, #'H'[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]One step for the CPU: the [b]mnemonic[/b] ([code]movs[/code]) says what to do, the [b]operands[/b] ([code]r0[/code], [code]#'H'[/code]) say what to do it to. One per line.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Immediate[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]#72[/code][/color]  [color=#56b6c2][code]#0x48[/code][/color]  [color=#56b6c2][code]#'H'[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]A constant written into the instruction, after a #. Decimal, hex and a character in quotes all mean the same number here.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Comment[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]@ print it[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Everything after @ is ignored by the assembler. Use comments to explain your code.[/cell][/table]

Indentation and capital letters do not matter ([code]MOVS R0, #5[/code] is fine), but commas between operands do. [url=instructions][color=#61afef][u]Instructions[/u][/color][/url] lists what each instruction does.

[color=#61afef][b]Edit and save[/b][/color]
picosim runs your file but does not edit it. Use any plain-text code editor (VS Code, for example).
[ol type=1]Start from an example: open it from the [code]examples[/code] folder in your editor and use [i]Save As[/i] to save a copy in your own folder, with a name ending in [code].s[/code].
In picosim, click [color=#e5c07b][code]Open…[/code][/color] ([color=#e5c07b][code]Ctrl/Cmd+O[/code][/color]) and pick your file.
Change the file in your editor and save it. picosim notices and loads it again by itself, from the beginning (the console says [code][lb]… changed on disk: reloading][/code]). [color=#e5c07b][code]Reload[/code][/color] ([color=#e5c07b][code]Ctrl/Cmd+R[/code][/color]) does the same by hand.[/ol]
If the assembler finds a mistake, a [b]Could not load program[/b] box lists each one: the line number, that line of your file, what is wrong and what usually causes it. Fix the line and save; picosim tries again as soon as you save. [url=trouble][color=#61afef][u]Troubleshooting[/u][/color][/url] explains the common messages.

[color=#61afef][b]Entry point and ending[/b][/color]
Execution starts at [code]main:[/code] (the label [code]asm_main:[/code] also works, and is what the Pico build uses). The built-in OS calls [code]main[/code] like a function, so it should begin with [code]push {…, lr}[/code] and end with [code]pop {…, pc}[/code]. When it returns, the OS runs [code]BKPT[/code] and the simulator halts. Press [color=#e5c07b][code]Reload[/code][/color] to run it again. See [url=running][color=#61afef][u]How a program runs[/u][/color][/url].

[color=#61afef][b]Input and output[/b][/color]
[ul]​[code]bl putchar[/code] — prints the character in [code]r0[/code] to the [url=serial][color=#61afef][u]serial console[/u][/color][/url].
​[code]bl getchar[/code] — waits for one key typed in the console and returns it in [code]r0[/code].[/ul]
They behave the same on a real Pico, so the same file runs on both. Both may change R0–R3, so keep values you need afterwards in R4–R7 (and add those registers to [code]push[/code] and [code]pop[/code], as the [url=examples][color=#61afef][u]Count with a loop[/u][/color][/url] example does).

[color=#61afef][b]Like the real chip[/b][/color]
picosim runs only the instructions the Pico's Cortex-M0+ processor has, and stops with a [b]CPU fault[/b] message in the console wherever a real Pico would crash. See [url=trouble][color=#61afef][u]Troubleshooting[/u][/color][/url].
1.name: Writing programs
1.sum:
A program is a plain text file whose name ends in [code].s[/code]. It starts with three lines ([code].syntax unified[/code], [code].cpu cortex-m0plus[/code], [code].thumb[/code]), then the label [code]main:[/code] and one instruction per line; anything after [code]@[/code] is a comment. [code]main[/code] begins with [code]push {r7, lr}[/code] and ends with [code]pop {r7, pc}[/code], and [code]bl putchar[/code] prints the character in R0.

Write and save the file in any text editor (VS Code, for example); picosim reloads it by itself when you save. [color=#e5c07b][code]Open…[/code][/color] ([color=#e5c07b][code]Ctrl/Cmd+O[/code][/color]) loads a file. If the assembler finds a mistake, a box lists each wrong line and what usually fixes it. The easiest start is a copy of an example.

1.full:
[font_size=26][b]Challenges[/b][/font_size]

Some examples end their opening comment with a [b]challenge[/b]: a small change to make, which picosim checks for you. The task is shown in a strip under the toolbar. When the program finishes, the strip turns [color=#98c379]green[/color] if you did it. If not, it lists each check: what was wanted and what your program did instead. Change your file, save it (picosim reloads it) and run it again. A stock example fails its own challenge, because you have not changed it yet.
Not every example has one: the LED and button programs never finish, so there is nothing to check at the end. [color=#e5c07b][code]About challenges[/code][/color] opens this page and [color=#e5c07b][code]✕[/code][/color] hides the strip until you load another program.

[color=#61afef][b]Writing your own (for teachers)[/b][/color]
Put the lines in the comment at the top of the file, before the first instruction:
[code]@ Challenge: Change the two numbers so it prints 9, and R3 is still 1.
@ Expect: output "9\n"
@ Expect: R3 = 1[/code]
[table=2][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Line[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]What it checks[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]@ Challenge: …[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The task the strip shows. Optional; without it, the strip lists the checks.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]@ Expect: output "…"[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Everything the program printed, from start to finish, must be exactly this text. Write it in quotes; [code]\n[/code] is a new line (what [code]movs r0, #10[/code] + [code]bl putchar[/code] prints).[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]@ Expect: R2 = 7[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The register's value when the program finishes. R0–R12, SP and LR; the value may be decimal, hex ([code]0x64[/code]), negative ([code]-1[/code]) or a character ([code]'H'[/code]).[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]@ Hint: …[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Your own hint for [url=ask][color=#61afef][u]Ask picosim[/u][/color][/url]. When a student asks for help with the challenge, it gives these first, one per request, in order, before its own hints. Optional.[/cell][/table]

Use as many Expect lines as you like; all must pass. Checks run only in the simulator, and not when the program stops with a CPU fault. A line picosim cannot read is reported in the console when the file loads, and the rest of the program still runs.
1.name: Challenges
1.sum: Some examples set a [b]challenge[/b]: a small change for you to make, shown in a strip under the toolbar. Change the file, save it and run the program to the end: the strip turns [color=#98c379]green[/color] if your program did it, or lists what is still wrong. Teachers can add their own with [code]@ Challenge:[/code] and [code]@ Expect:[/code] comment lines (see the details).

1.full:
[font_size=26][b]Hex, binary and ASCII[/b][/font_size]

Inside the computer every value is a pattern of bits (0s and 1s). A register holds 32 of them. picosim shows them in [b]hexadecimal[/b] (hex), base 16, because each hex digit stands for exactly 4 bits, so 32 bits are always 8 hex digits.

[color=#61afef][b]The 16 hex digits[/b][/color]
[table=6][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Hex[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Decimal[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Binary[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Hex[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Decimal[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Binary[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]0[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]0[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0000[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]8[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]8[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]1000[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]1[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]1[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0001[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]9[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]9[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]1001[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]2[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]2[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0010[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]A[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]10[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]1010[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]3[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]3[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0011[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]B[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]11[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]1011[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]4[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]4[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0100[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]C[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]12[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]1100[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]5[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]5[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0101[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]D[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]13[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]1101[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]6[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]6[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0110[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]E[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]14[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]1110[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]7[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]7[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0111[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]F[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]15[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]1111[/code][/cell][/table]

[color=#61afef][b]Reading a hex number[/b][/color]
Hex numbers start with [code]0x[/code] so you can tell them apart from decimal. Each place is worth 16 times the one to its right (1, 16, 256, 4096, …):
[ul]​[code]0x48[/code] = 4 × 16 + 8 = [b]72[/b]
​[code]0x2A[/code] = 2 × 16 + 10 = [b]42[/b]
​[code]0x3000[/code] = 3 × 4096 = [b]12288[/b][/ul]
Leading zeros change nothing: the Registers panel's [code]0x00000048[/code] is just [code]0x48[/code]. And to turn hex into binary, write each digit as its 4 bits: [code]0x48[/code] = [code]0100 1000[/code].

[table=1][cell bg=#2a2a2a border=#61afef padding=14,9,14,9 expand=1][color=#61afef][b]Shortcut[/b][/color]   Hover any register to see its value in hex, decimal, signed decimal and binary at once, or switch the Registers panel's menu from [color=#e5c07b][code]Hex[/code][/color] to [color=#e5c07b][code]Decimal[/code][/color].[/cell][/table]

[color=#61afef][b]Negative numbers[/b][/color]
The same 32 bits can be read two ways. As [b]unsigned[/b], [code]0xFFFFFFFF[/code] is 4 294 967 295. As [b]signed[/b] (two's complement), every value from [code]0x80000000[/code] up is negative, and [code]0xFFFFFFFF[/code] is −1, [code]0xFFFFFFFE[/code] is −2, and so on. The top bit (bit 31) is 1 for a negative number; that is what the N flag reports. Choose [color=#e5c07b][code]Signed[/code][/color] in the Registers panel's menu to see registers this way.

[color=#61afef][b]Characters are numbers too (ASCII)[/b][/color]
A character is stored as its [b]ASCII code[/b]. [code]putchar[/code] prints the character whose code is in R0. The ones you will use most:

[table=3][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Characters[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Hex[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Decimal[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0[/code] [code]1[/code] … [code]9[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0x30[/code] – [code]0x39[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]48 – 57[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]A[/code] [code]B[/code] … [code]Z[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0x41[/code] – [code]0x5A[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]65 – 90[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]a[/code] [code]b[/code] … [code]z[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0x61[/code] – [code]0x7A[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]97 – 122[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]space[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0x20[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]32[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]![/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0x21[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]33[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]new line[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0x0A[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]10[/cell][/table]

In your program you can write the character in quotes and let the assembler look up its code: [code]movs r0, #'H'[/code] is the same as [code]movs r0, #0x48[/code] and [code]movs r0, #72[/code]. (The Disassembly always shows the hex.)

[color=#61afef][b]Printing a number[/b][/color]
To print the [i]number[/i] 7 you must print the [i]character[/i] '7', whose code is 7 + [code]0x30[/code] = [code]0x37[/code]. So add [code]'0'[/code] (that is, [code]0x30[/code]) before calling putchar:

[table=1][cell bg=#0e0e0e border=#474747 padding=14,10,14,10 expand=1][code]        movs    r0, #7
        adds    r0, #'0'        @ R0 = 0x37, the character '7'
        bl      putchar[/code][/cell][/table]

This works only for 0–9. For 10 it gives [code]0x3A[/code], which is the character [b]:[/b] — to print bigger numbers you must print one digit at a time.
1.name: Hex, binary and ASCII
1.sum:
The CPU stores everything as bits (0s and 1s), and picosim shows them in [b]hexadecimal[/b]: base 16, with the digits 0–9 and A–F and [code]0x[/code] in front. One hex digit is exactly 4 bits, so a 32-bit register is 8 hex digits. For example [code]0x2A[/code] = 2 × 16 + 10 = 42. Hover a register to see its value in decimal and binary too.

Characters are numbers as well ([b]ASCII[/b]): 'H' is 72 ([code]0x48[/code]) and the digits '0' to '9' are 48 to 57. That is why printing the number 7 needs the character '7': add [code]'0'[/code] (48) before calling putchar.

1.full:
[font_size=26][b]Instructions[/b][/font_size]

Every instruction in the Level 1 examples. In the forms, [b]Rd[/b] is the register that gets the result, [b]Rn[/b] and [b]Rm[/b] are registers it reads, and [b]#imm[/b] is a constant.

[table=1][cell bg=#2a2a2a border=#f2cc60 padding=14,9,14,9 expand=1][color=#f2cc60][b]Two rules[/b][/color]   1. Write [code]movs[/code], [code]adds[/code] and [code]subs[/code] with the [b]S[/b] on the end (it means "set the flags").   2. Use registers [b]R0 to R7[/b]. Break either rule and the assembler says [i]cannot honor width suffix[/i].[/cell][/table]

The [b]Flags[/b] column lists the flags each instruction sets; the others keep their old values. [url=branches][color=#61afef][u]Flags and branches[/u][/color][/url] explains them.

[color=#61afef][b]Jumping[/b][/color]
[table=3][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Form[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Example[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]What it does[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]b label[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]b done[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Always jump to the label.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]b<cond> label[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]bne loop[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Jump only if a condition on the flags is true, otherwise go on to the next line. See [url=branches][color=#61afef][u]Flags and branches[/u][/color][/url].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]bl label[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]bl putchar[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Call a function: put the address of the next line in LR, then jump.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]bx lr[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]bx lr[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Jump to the address in LR: how a function returns.[/cell][/table]

[color=#61afef][b]Saving registers: push and pop[/b][/color]
[table=3][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Form[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Example[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]What it does[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]push {list}[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]push {r4, lr}[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Save the listed registers on the stack (SP goes down 4 bytes per register).[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]pop {list}[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]pop {r4, pc}[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Load them back (SP goes up again). Popping into PC jumps to the saved address.[/cell][/table]

Every example's [code]main[/code] begins with [code]push {r7, lr}[/code] (or [code]{r4, lr}[/code]) and ends with [code]pop {r7, pc}[/code]. The reason: [code]bl putchar[/code] overwrites LR, so the address [code]main[/code] must return to is saved first and popped straight into PC at the end.

[color=#61afef][b]Other instructions you may meet[/b][/color]
[table=2][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Form[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]What it does[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]ands Rd, Rm[/code][/color]  [color=#56b6c2][code]orrs Rd, Rm[/code][/color]  [color=#56b6c2][code]eors Rd, Rm[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Bitwise AND, OR and exclusive OR: Rd = Rd op Rm, bit by bit.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]lsls Rd, Rm, #n[/code][/color]  [color=#56b6c2][code]lsrs Rd, Rm, #n[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Shift Rm's bits left or right by n places into Rd (left by 1 doubles, right by 1 halves an unsigned number).[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]muls Rd, Rm, Rd[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Rd = Rm × Rd. The register that gets the result must also be the last one.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]mov Rd, Rm[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Copy without setting flags; this one also works with R8–R12.[/cell][/table]

Loads and stores ([code]ldr[/code], [code]str[/code]), which read and write memory, come at Level 2.
Mnemonics can be written in capitals or not. picosim runs only the instructions the Pico's Cortex-M0+ processor has; the ARMv6-M Architecture Reference Manual lists them all.
1.name: Instructions
1.sum:
Each line of a program is one [b]instruction[/b]: its name (the mnemonic, such as [code]movs[/code] or [code]adds[/code]) and what it works on (registers such as [code]r0[/code] and constants such as [code]#5[/code]). The Level 1 examples use [code]movs[/code] (put a value in a register), [code]adds[/code] and [code]subs[/code] (add and subtract), [code]cmp[/code] (compare), [code]b[/code] and the conditional branches (jump), [code]bl[/code] (call a function) and [code]push[/code] / [code]pop[/code] (save and restore registers).

Two rules avoid most mistakes: write [code]movs[/code], [code]adds[/code] and [code]subs[/code] with the [b]S[/b] on the end, and use registers [b]R0 to R7[/b]. A constant in [code]movs[/code], [code]cmp[/code] or two-register [code]adds[/code] / [code]subs[/code] must be 0 to 255; the three-register form ([code]adds r0, r1, #3[/code]) takes only 0 to 7.

1.full:
[font_size=26][b]Flags and branches[/b][/font_size]

A program decides what to do next in two steps: an instruction such as [code]cmp[/code] sets the [b]flags[/b], and then a conditional [b]branch[/b] reads them and either jumps or carries on.

[color=#61afef][b]The four flags[/b][/color]
[table=3][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Flag[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Name[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]It is 1 when the result…[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]N[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Negative[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]is negative: bit 31 of the result is 1.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]Z[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Zero[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]is zero. After [code]cmp a, b[/code] this means a = b.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]C[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Carry[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]carried out of bit 31 (adding), or did [i]not[/i] need to borrow (subtracting or [code]cmp[/code]). After [code]cmp a, b[/code], C = 1 means a ≥ b as unsigned numbers.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]V[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Overflow[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]was too big or too small to fit as a signed number, such as 0x7FFFFFFF + 1.[/cell][/table]

Instructions that end in [b]S[/b] ([code]movs[/code], [code]adds[/code], [code]subs[/code], …) and [code]cmp[/code] set the flags. Branches, [code]bl[/code], [code]push[/code] and [code]pop[/code] never change them, so a flag keeps its value until the next flag-setting instruction. The flags are the N Z C V boxes in the [url=registers][color=#61afef][u]Registers panel[/u][/color][/url].

[color=#61afef][b]What cmp does[/b][/color]
[code]cmp r4, #6[/code] works out R4 − 6, sets the flags from the answer, and throws the answer away. From the [b]Count with a loop[/b] example:

[table=6][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]R4[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]R4 − 6[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]N[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Z[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]C[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]bne loop[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]2[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]−4[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]1[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]0[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]0[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]jumps back (not equal)[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]5[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]−1[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]1[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]0[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]0[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]jumps back (not equal)[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]6[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]0[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]0[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#f2cc60][b]1[/b][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]1[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]goes on to the next line[/cell][/table]

[color=#61afef][b]Conditional branches[/b][/color]
Write the condition after [code]b[/code]. Each one reads like a question about the [code]cmp[/code] before it, [code]cmp a, b[/code]:
