instruction[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]N = 1[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]bpl[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]result positive or zero[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]after any S instruction[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]N = 0[/cell][/table]

[b]Signed or unsigned?[/b] If your values can be negative, use the signed branches. For character codes, addresses and counts that never go below 0, either kind works while the numbers are small; the unsigned ones are the safe choice.

[color=#61afef][b]Pattern: a loop[/b][/color]
[table=1][cell bg=#0e0e0e border=#474747 padding=14,10,14,10 expand=1][code]        movs    r4, #0          @ i = 0
loop:
        @ ... the loop body: what to repeat ...
        adds    r4, #1          @ i = i + 1
        cmp     r4, #10
        blt     loop            @ i < 10? go round again[/code][/cell][/table]

The body runs 10 times, with R4 = 0, 1, … 9. Keep the counter in R4–R7: [code]putchar[/code] may change R0–R3.

[color=#61afef][b]Pattern: if / else[/b][/color]
[table=1][cell bg=#0e0e0e border=#474747 padding=14,10,14,10 expand=1][code]        cmp     r0, r1
        bgt     bigger          @ R0 > R1?
        movs    r2, r1          @ no:  R2 = R1
        b       done
bigger:
        movs    r2, r0          @ yes: R2 = R0
done:                           @ R2 = the larger of R0 and R1[/code][/cell][/table]

The [code]b done[/code] matters: without it the "no" path would run on into the "yes" path.

[table=1][cell bg=#2a2a2a border=#61afef padding=14,9,14,9 expand=1][color=#61afef][b]Watch it happen[/b][/color]   Set a breakpoint on a branch, press Run, and look at the flags each time it stops. Then press Step instruction once to see whether it jumped.[/cell][/table]
1.name: Flags and branches
1.sum:
A program makes decisions in two steps. First an instruction such as [code]cmp r4, #6[/code] compares two numbers and sets the four [b]flags[/b]: N (negative), Z (zero), C (carry) and V (overflow). Then a conditional branch such as [code]bne loop[/code] reads the flags and either jumps to the label or carries on with the next line.

[code]beq[/code] jumps if the numbers were equal and [code]bne[/code] if they were not; [code]blt[/code], [code]bgt[/code], [code]ble[/code] and [code]bge[/code] compare signed numbers, and [code]blo[/code], [code]bhi[/code], [code]bls[/code] and [code]bhs[/code] unsigned ones. A loop works this way: change a counter, compare it, and branch back while the loop is not finished.

1.full:
[font_size=26][b]Level 1 examples[/b][/font_size]

Open each one from [color=#e5c07b][code]Examples[/code][/color] and keep this page beside it. Every example file also starts with a short [i]What to watch[/i] comment. At Level 1 each [code]bl putchar[/code] is one press of Step, although putchar's two instructions still run (the status text counts them); from Level 2 you also step through the [url=running][color=#61afef][u]built-in OS[/u][/color][/url]'s instructions (three at the start, two in each putchar).

[font_size=21][b]1 · Say hello[/b][/font_size]   [color=#8c8c8c]01_hello.s · 20 instructions, 11 presses of Step[/color]
Prints [code]Hi![/code] one letter at a time. Shows how [code]movs[/code] puts a character's code in R0 and how [code]bl putchar[/code] prints it.
[ul]Before each [code]bl putchar[/code], R0 holds the code: [code]0x48[/code] H, [code]0x69[/code] i, [code]0x21[/code] !, [code]0x0A[/code] new line.
Watch LR change on every [code]bl[/code] ([code]0x00003009[/code], [code]0x0000300F[/code], …): it is always the address of the next line, plus 1.
​[url=running][color=#61afef][u]How a program runs[/u][/color][/url] goes through this example line by line.[/ul]
[b]Try it:[/b] make it print your initials. Copy a [code]movs[/code] / [code]bl putchar[/code] pair for each letter, and use [code]#' '[/code] for a space.

[font_size=21][b]2 · Add two numbers[/b][/font_size]   [color=#8c8c8c]02_add.s · 17 instructions, 12 presses of Step[/color]
Puts 3 and 4 in registers, adds and subtracts them, and prints the sum.
[ul]R0 = 3, R1 = 4, then [code]adds r2, r0, r1[/code] makes R2 = 7 and [code]subs r3, r1, r0[/code] makes R3 = 1.
The [code]subs[/code] turns the C flag on: 4 − 3 did not need to borrow.
​[code]adds r0, #'0'[/code] turns 7 into [code]0x37[/code], the character '7', which is printed. See [url=numbers][color=#61afef][u]Printing a number[/u][/color][/url].[/ul]
[b]Try it:[/b] change 3 and 4 in the file (keep the sum under 10), save and press [color=#e5c07b][code]Reload[/code][/color]. Or, without editing: when ▶ reaches [code]movs r0, r2[/code], click R2 in the Registers panel, type 5, press Enter, then Run. It prints 5.

[font_size=21][b]3 · Count with a loop[/b][/font_size]   [color=#8c8c8c]03_count_loop.s · 49 instructions, 36 presses of Step[/color]
Prints [b]12345[/b] with a loop: the same five lines run once for each digit.
[ul]R4 is the counter. It is kept in R4, not R0–R3, because putchar may change those; that is why [code]main[/code] pushes R4.
In the Disassembly, the row labelled [code]loop[/code] is where [code]bne loop[/code] jumps back to; it shows as [code]bne #0x3004[/code].
After [code]cmp r4, #6[/code]: while R4 is less than 6, N = 1 and Z = 0, so [code]bne[/code] jumps back. When R4 reaches 6, Z = 1 and the loop ends. The table in [url=branches][color=#61afef][u]Flags and branches[/u][/color][/url] shows the values.[/ul]
[b]Try it:[/b] put a breakpoint on the [code]bne[/code] row and press Run several times to see the flags on each pass. Then make it count to 9 (change [code]#6[/code] to [code]#10[/code]).

[table=1][cell bg=#2a2a2a border=#61afef padding=14,9,14,9 expand=1][color=#61afef][b]Later[/b][/color]   Five more examples (memory, an LED, typing, functions, buttons) are marked [i](Level 2)[/i] in the Examples menu. They open at Level 1 too, but some of what they show only appears at Level 2.[/cell][/table]
1.name: Level 1 examples
1.sum:
Three examples for Level 1, opened from [color=#e5c07b][code]Examples[/code][/color]: [b]Say hello[/b] prints [code]Hi![/code] one letter at a time ([code]movs[/code] and [code]bl putchar[/code]), [b]Add two numbers[/b] adds 3 and 4 and prints 7, and [b]Count with a loop[/b] prints [code]12345[/code] with a loop ([code]cmp[/code] and [code]bne[/code]). Each file starts with a comment that says what to watch.

Step through each one with [url=explain][color=#61afef][u]Explain this step[/u][/color][/url] open, then try the change suggested in its [b]Try it[/b] line or its challenge.

1.full:
[font_size=26][b]Explain this step[/b][/font_size]


[color=#61afef][b]Where it is[/b][/color]
At the top of the right-hand column, above the serial console. Click its title ([b]▾ Explain this step[/b]) to fold it away, and again to bring it back. Drag the bar under it to give it more room: its text grows with it.

[color=#61afef][b]What just happened[/b][/color]
After each [color=#e5c07b][code]Step instruction[/code][/color] or [color=#e5c07b][code]◀ Step back[/code][/color], this part names the instruction (with its line number in your file) and says in plain words what it did, with the real values: [i]Worked out R2 = R0 + R1 = 3 + 4 = 7[/i], or [i]Checked the condition “not equal” (Z = 0). The flags say Z = 0, so it jumped to loop[/i]. After [color=#e5c07b][code]Run[/code][/color] stops, it says how many instructions ran and why Run stopped (the end of the program, a breakpoint, a key to type, or Pause).

[color=#61afef][b]What happens next[/b][/color]
The instruction ▶ points at, and what it [i]will[/i] do with the values the registers hold now. picosim finds this out exactly, by running that instruction on a copy of the machine and throwing the copy away, so your program is not touched. Two lines follow:
[ul]​[b]Then[/b] — where the program goes after it: the next line, back up to the top of a loop, into a function, or back to the code that called the function.
​[b]Why[/b] — what the instruction is for: saving registers at the start of a function, setting the flags for the branch on the next line, deciding whether to go round a loop again… When the line has a comment in your file, the comment is quoted too, so good comments make better explanations.[/ul]

[color=#61afef][b]More detail[/b][/color]
Tick [b]More detail[/b] in the panel's corner for the full picture. It is remembered.

[table=2][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Detail[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]What it says[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]How this instruction works[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]One or two sentences about the instruction itself: what [code]movs[/code] does, what the S means, when a [code]bne[/code] jumps.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]What changed[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Every register and flag that changed, old → new, with what each flag means, and anything printed.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]PC[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Where the PC moved: on by 2 (or 4) to the next instruction, or a jump.[/cell][/table]

[table=1][cell bg=#2a2a2a border=#61afef padding=14,9,14,9 expand=1][color=#61afef][b]Try this[/b][/color]   Before you press Step, read [b]What happens next[/b] and work out the new values yourself. Then step and check them against [b]What just happened[/b] and the yellow registers.[/cell][/table]

[color=#61afef][b]While Run is on[/b][/color]
Explanations pause: the panel says the program is running and is not updated, so Run is not slowed down. When Run stops, the panel explains where and why, and what comes next.
1.name: Explain this step
1.sum:
[b]Explain this step[/b] (top right) describes every step as you take it. [b]What just happened[/b] says in plain words what the instruction did, with the real values. [b]What happens next[/b] says what the next instruction will do, where the program goes after it ([b]Then[/b]) and what that is for ([b]Why[/b], often using the comment on that line of the program). It is exact: picosim really runs the next instruction on a copy of the machine to find out.

Tick [b]More detail[/b] for exactly what changed (registers, flags), how the instruction works. While [color=#e5c07b][code]Run[/code][/color] is on, the panel waits, then explains where Run stopped. Click its title to fold it away.

1.full:
[font_size=26][b]Registers panel[/b][/font_size]

Top left. The processor's 16 registers, each holding one 32-bit number. Values changed by the last step are [color=#f2cc60]yellow[/color].

[table=2][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Register[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Its job[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]R0–R7[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Your values. Almost every instruction can use these, so use them first. R0 also carries the character for [code]putchar[/code] and [code]getchar[/code].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]R8–R12[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]More storage, but most Cortex-M0+ instructions cannot use them (see [url=instructions][color=#61afef][u]Instructions[/u][/color][/url]).[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]SP[/b] (R13)[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Stack pointer: where the stack is. [code]push[/code] moves it down and [code]pop[/code] moves it back up.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]LR[/b] (R14)[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Link register: where to come back to. [code]bl[/code] puts the return address here before it jumps.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]PC[/b] (R15)[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Program counter: the address of the next instruction. It goes up by 2 (or 4) after each instruction, and jumps on a branch.[/cell][/table]

When a program is loaded, the built-in OS has already called your main, so PC is [code]0x00003000[/code] (main), LR is [code]0x00000007[/code] (where main returns to, in the OS), R0 is [code]0x00003001[/code] (left over from the OS) and SP is [code]0x00010000[/code] (the top of RAM). The others start at 0.

[color=#61afef][b]Hex, decimal or signed[/b][/color]
The menu at the panel's top right shows every register as [color=#e5c07b][code]Hex[/code][/color] ([code]0x0000002A[/code]), [color=#e5c07b][code]Decimal[/code][/color] ([code]42[/code]) or [color=#e5c07b][code]Signed[/code][/color] (decimal, where values from [code]0x80000000[/code] up are negative, so [code]0xFFFFFFFF[/code] is −1). Hover a register to see all of these at once, plus its 32 bits in binary. See [url=numbers][color=#61afef][u]Hex, binary and ASCII[/u][/color][/url].

[color=#61afef][b]Flags[/b][/color]
The four check boxes N, Z, C and V are the flags: a tick means 1. They change only after an instruction that sets them, such as [code]cmp[/code], [code]adds[/code] or [code]movs[/code]. Hover one for what it means, or read [url=branches][color=#61afef][u]Flags and branches[/u][/color][/url].

[color=#61afef][b]What changed[/b][/color]
Under the flags, a yellow line names each register the last step changed, its new value as a number (and as a character when it is one), and the line of your file that changed it, for example [code]R0 = 72 = 0x48 = 'H'   ← movs r0, #'H'   (line 22)[/code]. Hovering a yellow register says the same. The PC is left out, because every step changes it. After [color=#e5c07b][code]Run[/code][/color], [color=#e5c07b][code]◀ Step back[/code][/color] or a value you typed, the line says so instead of naming one instruction.

[color=#61afef][b]Editing[/b][/color]
Click a register, type a new value — hex like [code]0x1F[/code] or decimal like [code]31[/code] — and press [color=#e5c07b][code]Enter[/code][/color]. Click a flag to toggle it. This is a quick way to try "what if R1 were 9?" without editing the file; [color=#e5c07b][code]Reload[/code][/color] puts everything back.

[color=#61afef][b]Status line[/b][/color]
The bottom line counts the instructions run since the program was loaded. [color=#e5c07b][code]Reload[/code][/color] sets it back to 0.

[color=#61afef][b]Bigger text[/b][/color]
Drag the bars below and beside the panel to make it larger — the text and fields scale up to fill the space.
1.name: Registers
1.sum:
The Registers panel (top left) shows the CPU's 16 registers: R0–R12 hold your values, [b]SP[/b] points at the stack, [b]LR[/b] holds a function's return address and [b]PC[/b] is the address of the next instruction. Whatever the last step changed turns [color=#f2cc60]yellow[/color], and the line under the flags says which line of your file changed it.

The four check boxes are the flags N Z C V. The menu at the top right shows the values in [color=#e5c07b][code]Hex[/code][/color], [color=#e5c07b][code]Decimal[/code][/color] or [color=#e5c07b][code]Signed[/code][/color]; hover a register to see every form at once, or click one, type a new value and press [color=#e5c07b][code]Enter[/code][/color] ([color=#e5c07b][code]Reload[/code][/color] puts everything back).

1.full:
[font_size=26][b]Disassembly[/b][/font_size]

Below the Registers. Your program as the CPU sees it, one instruction per row. The row with ▶ is the instruction that runs next. With [color=#e5c07b][code]Follow PC[/code][/color] ticked the list scrolls to it automatically.

[table=3][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Column[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Example[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Meaning[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]●[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Breakpoint column: click it to set or clear a breakpoint (below).[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Address[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]▶3002[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Where in memory the instruction is, in hex. Each instruction is 2 bytes, so addresses go up by 2. [code]bl[/code] is 4 bytes.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Raw[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]2048[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The instruction as the CPU stores it: 16 bits in hex ([code]bl[/code] has two groups). The assembler made this from your line.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Label[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]main[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The label at this address, if there is one.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Instruction[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]movs r0, #0x48[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The instruction turned back into assembly from the raw bits, the way the CPU sees it.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Source[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]22  movs r0, #'H'  @ R0 = …[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The line of your file it came from: its line number, your code and your comment. Hover it to see the whole line.[/cell][/table]

Compare the [b]Instruction[/b] and [b]Source[/b] columns to see what the assembler did with your line:
[ul]Constants are shown in hex: [code]movs r0, #'H'[/code] becomes [code]movs r0, #0x48[/code], and [code]#10[/code] becomes [code]#0xa[/code].
Some lines are stored in a shorter form: [code]adds r4, r4, #1[/code] becomes [code]adds r4, #1[/code], which does the same thing. A few instructions have a second name: [code]bcs[/code] shows as [code]bhs[/code].
Branches and calls show the label they go to ([code]bl putchar[/code], [code]bne loop[/code]), and the Label column shows where that label is.
The first rows, from [code]0000[/code] to [code]0016[/code], are the built-in OS ([code]_start[/code], [code]putchar[/code], [code]getchar[/code]); their Source is the OS's file, [code]os.s[/code]. Your program starts at [code]3000[/code], the [code]main[/code] row. At Level 1 ▶ never stops in them.[/ul]

[color=#61afef][b]Breakpoints[/b][/color]
Click the narrow first column of a row to put a red ● there; click again to remove it. [color=#e5c07b][code]Run[/code][/color] stops when it reaches a breakpoint, [i]before[/i] running that instruction. Use one to run straight to the part you want to study, then step from there.
1.name: Disassembly
1.sum: The Disassembly lists your program one instruction per row: its address, its bits ([b]Raw[/b]), its label, the instruction as the CPU sees it and the line of your file it came from ([b]Source[/b]). The row with ▶ runs next. Click a row's first column to put a [b]breakpoint[/b] (a red ●) there: [color=#e5c07b][code]Run[/code][/color] stops just before that instruction.

1.full:
[font_size=26][b]USB Serial console[/b][/font_size]

Bottom right. Shows what your program prints with [code]putchar[/code].

[color=#61afef][b]Typing input[/b][/color]
[ul]Click in the output area and type: each key is sent immediately (what [code]getchar[/code] expects).
Or type a whole line in the box below and press [color=#e5c07b][code]Enter[/code][/color] — it is sent followed by a carriage return.[/ul]
When the program is waiting in [code]getchar[/code], the console header says so. [color=#e5c07b][code]Clear[/code][/color] empties the output.
1.name: Serial console
1.sum: The serial console (bottom right) shows what your program prints with [code]putchar[/code]. When the program calls [code]getchar[/code] it waits for a key: click in the console and type (each key is sent at once), or type a line in the box underneath and press [color=#e5c07b][code]Enter[/code][/color]. [color=#e5c07b][code]Clear[/code][/color] empties it.

1.full:
[font_size=26][b]Layout and zoom[/b][/font_size]

[ul]​[b]Resize panels[/b] by dragging the bars between them. The registers panel's text grows with it.
​[b]Zoom[/b] the whole window with [color=#e5c07b][code]−[/code][/color] / [color=#e5c07b][code]+[/code][/color] in the toolbar, [color=#e5c07b][code]Ctrl/Cmd +[/code][/color] / [color=#e5c07b][code]Ctrl/Cmd −[/code][/color], or [color=#e5c07b][code]Ctrl/Cmd[/code][/color] + mouse wheel. Click the percentage (or [color=#e5c07b][code]Ctrl/Cmd 0[/code][/color]) to reset. The zoom is remembered.
​[b]Colours:[/b] [color=#e5c07b][code]View[/code][/color] in the toolbar picks System, Blue, Dark or Light. It is remembered too.
Zoom stops at the largest size where the whole toolbar still fits, so no button is ever cut off.[/ul]

Where each panel is, and what every toolbar button does, is in [url=tour][color=#61afef][u]The screen at a glance[/u][/color][/url]. Which panels and buttons you see depends on the [color=#e5c07b][code]Level[/code][/color] menu.
1.name: Layout and zoom
1.sum: Drag the bars between the panels to resize them; a panel you make bigger also gets bigger text. Zoom the whole window with [color=#e5c07b][code]−[/code][/color] / [color=#e5c07b][code]+[/code][/color] in the toolbar, [color=#e5c07b][code]Ctrl/Cmd +[/code][/color] / [color=#e5c07b][code]Ctrl/Cmd −[/code][/color] or [color=#e5c07b][code]Ctrl/Cmd[/code][/color] + mouse wheel, and click the percentage to fit the window again. [color=#e5c07b][code]View[/code][/color] picks the colours (System, Blue, Dark or Light). picosim remembers all of these.

1.full:
[font_size=26][b]Keyboard shortcuts[/b][/font_size]

[table=2][cell][color=#e5c07b][code]S  or  F10[/code][/color]    [/cell][cell]Step instruction: run one instruction (hold to repeat)[/cell][cell][color=#e5c07b][code]B[/code][/color]    [/cell][cell]Step back: undo the last step (hold to repeat)[/cell][cell][color=#e5c07b][code]Space  or  F5[/code][/color]    [/cell][cell]Run / Pause[/cell][cell][color=#e5c07b][code]F1[/code][/color]    [/cell][cell]open this guide[/cell][cell][color=#e5c07b][code]?[/code][/color]    [/cell][cell]open Ask picosim, the help chat[/cell][cell][color=#e5c07b][code]Ctrl/Cmd+O[/code][/color]    [/cell][cell]open a .s file[/cell][cell][color=#e5c07b][code]Ctrl/Cmd+R[/code][/color]    [/cell][cell]reload (start the program over)[/cell][cell][color=#e5c07b][code]Ctrl/Cmd + / −[/code][/color]    [/cell][cell]zoom in / out[/cell][cell][color=#e5c07b][code]Ctrl/Cmd 0[/code][/color]    [/cell][cell]reset zoom[/cell][cell][color=#e5c07b][code]Esc[/code][/color]    [/cell][cell]close this guide[/cell][/table]

The letter keys work on every keyboard: on a Mac, F11 shows the desktop and the F keys need Fn, so use S, B, C and Space there. They only work in Simulator mode, and not while you are typing in a box or in the serial console (those keys go to your program).
1.name: Keyboard shortcuts
1.sum: [color=#e5c07b][code]S[/code][/color] steps one instruction, [color=#e5c07b][code]B[/code][/color] steps back, [color=#e5c07b][code]Space[/code][/color] runs or pauses, [color=#e5c07b][code]F1[/code][/color] opens this guide, [color=#e5c07b][code]Ctrl/Cmd+O[/code][/color] opens a file and [color=#e5c07b][code]Ctrl/Cmd+R[/code][/color] reloads it. Holding a step key repeats it. The keys work only in Simulator mode, and not while you are typing in a box or in the serial console.

1.full:
[font_size=26][b]Troubleshooting[/b][/font_size]

[font_size=21][b]While it runs[/b][/font_size]

[color=#61afef][b]Nothing happens when I press Step or Run[/b][/color]
The program has halted (the status text says [i]halted[/i]) — press [color=#e5c07b][code]Reload[/code][/color]. Or no program is loaded.

[color=#61afef][b]R0 already holds 0x00003001 and LR 0x00000007 before I press anything[/b][/color]
picosim's built-in OS has already run its start-up and called your [code]main[/code]: R0 is left over from that, and LR is where main returns to. Your program does not need them. See [url=running][color=#61afef][u]How a program runs[/u][/color][/url].

[color=#61afef][b]Run is very slow[/b][/color]
Move the [color=#e5c07b][code]Speed[/code][/color] slider to the right. At the starting speed (8 cyc/s) Run does about one instruction a second, so you can watch it. [b]Max[/b] finishes almost at once.

[color=#61afef][b]The program stops and waits[/b][/color]
It is in [code]getchar[/code], waiting for a key (the status text says [i]waiting for input[/i]). Click the serial console and type a key.

[color=#61afef][b]It prints a strange character instead of my number[/b][/color]
[code]putchar[/code] prints the character whose [i]code[/i] is in R0. Add [code]'0'[/code] to a number from 0 to 9 first; numbers of 10 or more need one digit at a time. See [url=numbers][color=#61afef][u]Hex, binary and ASCII[/u][/color][/url].

[color=#61afef][b]A value I saved in R0–R3 changed after bl putchar[/b][/color]
Functions are allowed to change R0–R3 (and LR). Keep values you need in R4–R7, and add those registers to [code]main[/code]'s [code]push[/code] and [code]pop[/code].

[color=#61afef][b]I can't find a button or panel from the guide[/b][/color]
Some appear only at higher levels. Raise the [color=#e5c07b][code]Level[/code][/color] menu in the toolbar; see [url=start][color=#61afef][u]Start here[/u][/color][/url].

[font_size=21][b]When it will not load[/b][/font_size]
The [b]Could not load program[/b] box shows the assembler's message. The number after the file name is the line, for example [code]add.s:12: Error: …[/code] is line 12. Fix the file, save it and press [color=#e5c07b][code]Reload[/code][/color].

[table=2][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]The message says[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]What is usually wrong[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]cannot honor width suffix[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]A missing S ([code]add[/code] instead of [code]adds[/code], [code]mov r0, #1[/code] instead of [code]movs[/code]), or a register from R8 to R12. Use R0–R7. See [url=instructions][color=#61afef][u]Instructions[/u][/color][/url].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]invalid immediate: 300 is out of range[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The constant is too big (or negative). [code]movs[/code], [code]cmp[/code] and two-register [code]adds[/code] / [code]subs[/code] take 0 to 255.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]immediate value out of range[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Three-register [code]adds r0, r1, #9[/code] takes only 0 to 7. Use [code]adds r0, #9[/code] on the same register, or put the constant in a register first.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]bad arguments to instruction[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]A missing comma or # (write [code]movs r0, #1[/code]), or a misspelt register.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]undefined reference to …[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]A branch or [code]bl[/code] to a label that does not exist. Check the spelling, and that the label line ends in a colon.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]The program has no main: label[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Put [code]main:[/code] on the line before your first instruction.[/cell][/table]

[color=#61afef][b]"Simulator backend disconnected"[/b][/color]
The Python backend stopped. Close picosim and start it again with [code]picosim --gui[/code].

[font_size=21][b]"CPU fault: …" in the console[/b][/font_size]
Your program did something that would crash a real Pico, and the message says what and where. The most common ones:
[ul]​[b]Undefined instruction[/b] — not a Cortex-M0+ instruction (for example code written for a Cortex-M4), or the program ran into data.
​[b]Bus fault[/b] — the address is not RAM (0x0000–0xFFFF). The two most common causes at first: [code]main[/code] has no [code]pop {…, pc}[/code] at the end, so the CPU runs on through empty memory until it reaches [code]0x00010000[/code]; or [code]main[/code] pops without a matching [code]push {…, lr}[/code] at the start, so the pop reads past the top of RAM. Later on, a pointer that went wrong or a stack that grew too far (too many PUSHes without POPs) do the same.[/ul]
Press [color=#e5c07b][code]Reload[/code][/color] to start again.
1.name: Troubleshooting
1.sum:
Most problems have a quick fix. If Step does nothing, the program has finished: press [color=#e5c07b][code]Reload[/code][/color]. If it is waiting, type a key in the serial console. If Run is slow, move the [color=#e5c07b][code]Speed[/code][/color] slider to the right. If the program will not load, the [b]Could not load program[/b] box gives the line number and what is wrong: fix that line and save.

A [b]CPU fault[/b] message in the console means the program did something that would crash a real Pico. The most common cause is a [code]main[/code] without [code]pop {…, pc}[/code] at its end. The details list every message you may see, with what to do.

1.full:
[font_size=26][b]Ask picosim[/b][/font_size]

Click [color=#e5c07b][code]Ask[/code][/color] in the toolbar, or press [color=#e5c07b][code]?[/code][/color], and type a question in your own words. Typos are fine. Some good ones:

[table=2][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Ask about[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]For example[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Your program right now[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1][i]Why did it stop?[/i] · [i]What just happened?[/i] · [i]What happens next?[/i] · [i]Why is R0 72?[/i] · [i]Why is it waiting?[/i][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Errors and crashes[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1][i]What does this error mean?[/i] (or paste the error) · [i]Why did it crash?[/i][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]The buttons and panels[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1][i]What does Step over do?[/i] · [i]How do I set a breakpoint?[/i] · [i]How do I see decimal?[/i][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Assembly[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1][i]What does LDR do?[/i] · [i]movs vs mov?[/i] · [i]What is the Z flag?[/i] · [i]What is 0x2A in decimal?[/i][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Challenges[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1][i]What is the challenge?[/i] · [i]Did I pass?[/i] · [i]Give me a hint[/i][/cell][/table]

Follow-ups work too: [i]why?[/i], [i]tell me more[/i], [i]what about R1?[/i]. Chips under the conversation suggest questions that fit what is on screen, such as [i]Why did it crash?[/i] after a fault.

[color=#61afef][b]Hints, not answers[/b][/color]
It never writes your code or a challenge's solution, and nothing you type changes that. Ask for the answer and you get the next small hint: first the idea and the guide page, then where to look, then what kind of change to make. After three hints it stops: ask your teacher, or look the topic up online. Load errors and CPU faults are different: it tells you exactly what the assembler or the CPU complained about, because fixing those is not the exercise.

[color=#61afef][b]Where answers come from[/b][/color]
Each answer has a small tag. [b]built-in answer[/b] and [b]from the guide[/b] come from picosim itself: this guide and your program as it runs, so they match what you see. Above your Level it gives a short answer and says which Level covers it. 👍 and 👎 tell your teacher what helps; [b]Report[/b] saves the question and answer (without personal details) for them.
Please don't type personal details (phone numbers, addresses, passwords): the chat leaves them out. If something is really wrong, beyond picosim, talk to a teacher or another adult you trust.

[color=#61afef][b]For teachers: AI help[/b][/color]
By default everything works offline. A teacher can let questions the built-in answers cannot handle go to Claude, an AI made by Anthropic: run [code]picosim --chat-setup[/code] to see (and create) the config file, set [code]"ai": "on"[/code] there, install the extra with [code]pip install -e .[lb]ai][/code] (it needs Python 3.10 or newer) and set an Anthropic API key in [code]ANTHROPIC_API_KEY[/code]. The question, a summary of the machine and the student's program (personal data removed) are then sent to Anthropic, so check your school's rules first; the window shows a notice while AI is on. AI answers are tagged [b]AI answer[/b], follow the same hints-only rule, and are withdrawn if they show too much code. The config also sets the model, [code]max_ai_per_hour[/code] (20), a [code]helpline[/code] for the wellbeing reply and [code]log_unanswered[/code]. There is no setting for full answers.
Reports go to [code]chat_reports.jsonl[/code] and 👍 / 👎 counts to [code]chat_feedback.json[/code], next to the config. Write your own hints for a challenge with [code]@ Hint:[/code] lines (see [url=challenges][color=#61afef][u]Challenges[/u][/color][/url]).
1.name: Ask picosim
1.sum:
[color=#e5c07b][code]Ask[/code][/color] (top right, or the [color=#e5c07b][code]?[/code][/color] key) opens a chat where you can ask questions in your own words: [i]Why did my program stop?[/i], [i]Why is R0 72?[/i], [i]What does LDR do?[/i], [i]How do I set a breakpoint?[/i] It looks at your program as it runs and answers from this guide, with a link to the page and often a [b]Show me[/b] button that points at the control.

It gives [b]hints, never finished answers[/b]: ask it for the solution to a challenge and it gives the next small hint instead, up to three. If you need more help than that, ask your teacher, or look the topic up online. It only knows about picosim, ARM assembly and the Pico.

1.full:
[font_size=26][b]Glossary[/b][/font_size]

[table=2][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Word[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Meaning[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Address[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]A number that says where in memory something is, like a house number. Shown in hex, such as [code]3000[/code].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]ASCII[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The code that gives each character a number: 'A' is [code]0x41[/code]. See [url=numbers][color=#61afef][u]Hex, binary and ASCII[/u][/color][/url].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Assembler[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The program that turns your [code].s[/code] file into the bits the CPU runs. picosim runs it when you Open or Reload.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Assembly language[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Writing a program as the processor's own instructions, one per line, with names instead of bits.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Bit[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]One binary digit, 0 or 1. A register has 32.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Branch[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]An instruction that jumps to another place in the program, always ([code]b[/code]) or only if a condition holds ([code]bne[/code], …).[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Breakpoint[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]A red ● on a Disassembly row: Run stops just before that instruction.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Built-in OS[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]picosim's tiny operating system at addresses [code]0000[/code]–[code]2FFF[/code]. It starts your [code]main[/code] and provides [code]putchar[/code] and [code]getchar[/code].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Byte[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]8 bits: two hex digits, 0 to 255.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Clock cycle[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]One tick of the CPU's clock. An instruction takes several. You will see them at Level 3.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Comment[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Text after [code]@[/code] that the assembler ignores; it is for people.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Cortex-M0+[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The processor inside the Pico's RP2040 chip. picosim runs only its instructions.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]CPU fault[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]A mistake that would crash a real Pico, such as running something that is not an instruction. picosim stops and explains it in the console.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Directive[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]A line starting with a dot, such as [code].thumb[/code]: an instruction to the assembler, not to the CPU.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Disassembly[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Your program shown back from the bits in memory: see [url=memory][color=#61afef][u]Disassembly[/u][/color][/url].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Flags[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]N, Z, C and V: four bits describing the last result, used by conditional branches. See [url=branches][color=#61afef][u]Flags and branches[/u][/color][/url].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Function[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]A piece of code you call with [code]bl[/code] that returns with [code]bx lr[/code] or [code]pop {…, pc}[/code]. [code]putchar[/code] is one.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Halted[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The program has finished (or faulted) and the CPU has stopped. Press Reload to start again.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Hex[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Base 16, written with [code]0x[/code] in front: [code]0x2A[/code] = 42.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Immediate[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]A constant written inside the instruction after a [code]#[/code], as in [code]movs r0, #5[/code].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Instruction[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]One step for the CPU, such as [code]adds r2, r0, r1[/code].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Label[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]A name followed by a colon, such as [code]loop:[/code]; it stands for the address of the next line.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]LR[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Link register (R14): holds the address a function returns to.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Mnemonic[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The name of an instruction: [code]movs[/code], [code]adds[/code], [code]bne[/code].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Operand[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]What an instruction works on: the registers and constants after the mnemonic.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]PC[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Program counter (R15): the address of the next instruction.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Register[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]One of 16 storage boxes inside the CPU, each holding a 32-bit number.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Serial console[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The text panel on the right: what your program prints, and where you type to it.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]SP and the stack[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The stack is memory used to save registers ([code]push[/code] / [code]pop[/code]); SP (R13) points to its top.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Thumb[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The 16-bit instruction set the Cortex-M0+ runs (a few instructions, like [code]bl[/code], are 32 bits).[/cell][/table]
1.name: Glossary
1.sum: Short meanings of the words used in picosim and in this guide, in alphabetical order. More words appear as you raise the Level.

2.full:
[font_size=26][b]Start here[/b][/font_size]

picosim runs programs written in [b]assembly language[/b] — the instructions the Raspberry Pi Pico's processor understands — and lets you watch them run one step at a time. Try anything: nothing can break, and [color=#e5c07b][code]Reload[/code][/color] always starts your program over.

[color=#61afef][b]Your first five minutes[/b][/color]
[ol type=1]Click [color=#e5c07b][code]Examples[/code][/color] in the toolbar and pick [b]Say hello[/b]. Your program appears in the Disassembly list on the left; the row marked ▶ is the instruction that runs next. The [b]Source[/b] column shows the line of your file that each row came from.
Press [color=#e5c07b][code]Step instruction[/code][/color] ([color=#e5c07b][code]S[/code][/color]) three times. These first three instructions belong to picosim's small [b]built-in OS[/b], which starts your program: R0 briefly holds [code]0x00002FFC[/code] and then [code]0x00003001[/code]. Now ▶ is on [code]main[/code], the first line of [i]your[/i] program.
Step twice more and look at the [url=registers][color=#61afef][u]Registers[/u][/color][/url]: the one that just changed turns [color=#f2cc60]yellow[/color]. After [code]movs r0, #'H'[/code], R0 holds [code]0x00000048[/code], the [url=numbers][color=#61afef][u]ASCII code[/u][/color][/url] for the letter H.
Step three more times. [code]bl putchar[/code] jumps into the OS's [code]putchar[/code] (address [code]0010[/code]), [code]svc #2[/code] prints the [b]H[/b] in the [url=serial][color=#61afef][u]serial console[/u][/color][/url] on the right, and [code]bx lr[/code] comes back to the next line of your program. ([color=#e5c07b][code]Step over[/code][/color] does all three at once.)
Press [color=#e5c07b][code]Run[/code][/color] ([color=#e5c07b][code]Space[/code][/color]) to let the rest go by itself. When the status text at the top says [b]halted[/b], the program has finished; press [color=#e5c07b][code]Reload[/code][/color] to watch it again.[/ol]
Each time you step, the [url=explain][color=#61afef][u]Explain this step[/u][/color][/url] panel at the top right says what that instruction did and what the next one will do, so you can follow along without guessing.

[table=1][cell bg=#2a2a2a border=#61afef padding=14,9,14,9 expand=1][color=#61afef][b]Stuck?[/b][/color]   Nothing you do here can break anything, and [color=#e5c07b][code]Reload[/code][/color] always starts the program over. [url=running][color=#61afef][u]How a program runs[/u][/color][/url] explains each of the steps above.[/cell][/table]

[color=#61afef][b]Words you will meet[/b][/color]
[ul]​[b]Register[/b] — a small storage box inside the processor that holds one number. R0–R12 are for your values; SP, LR and PC have special jobs.
​[b]PC[/b] (program counter) — the address of the next instruction. Watch it move as you step.
​[b]Hex[/b] — numbers written in base 16 with a [code]0x[/code] in front: [code]0x2A[/code] = 42. Hover a register to see it in decimal, or switch the Registers panel's [color=#e5c07b][code]Hex[/code][/color] menu to [color=#e5c07b][code]Decimal[/code][/color].
​[b]Flags[/b] N Z C V — four yes/no facts about the last result (negative? zero? …) that branches like [code]BNE[/code] use to decide where to go.[/ul]
More words are in the [url=glossary][color=#61afef][u]Glossary[/u][/color][/url].

[color=#61afef][b]What to read next[/b][/color]
If you missed the first class, read these in order. Each takes a few minutes:
[ol type=1]​[url=tour][color=#61afef][u]The screen at a glance[/u][/color][/url] — every button and panel you can see.
​[url=running][color=#61afef][u]How a program runs[/u][/color][/url] — what happens when you press Step and Run.
​[url=numbers][color=#61afef][u]Hex, binary and ASCII[/u][/color][/url] — how to read the numbers on screen.
​[url=instructions][color=#61afef][u]Instructions[/u][/color][/url] and [url=branches][color=#61afef][u]Flags and branches[/u][/color][/url] — what each line of a program does.
​[url=examples][color=#61afef][u]Level 1 examples[/u][/color][/url] — step through them with a guide beside you.
​[url=programs][color=#61afef][u]Writing programs[/u][/color][/url] — write, save and run your own.[/ol]

[color=#61afef][b]New at Level 2[/b][/color]
[ol type=1]​[url=memmap][color=#61afef][u]Memory and addresses[/u][/color][/url] — bytes, words and where things are.
​[url=loadstore][color=#61afef][u]Loads and stores[/u][/color][/url] — moving numbers between memory and registers.
​[url=stack][color=#61afef][u]The stack and functions[/u][/color][/url] — calling your own functions safely.
​[url=gpio][color=#61afef][u]GPIO: controlling pins[/u][/color][/url] — lighting LEDs and reading buttons.
​[url=examples2][color=#61afef][u]Level 2 examples[/u][/color][/url] — step through them with a guide beside you.
​[url=memory][color=#61afef][u]Disassembly & memory[/u][/color][/url] — the Memory tab and the stack view.
​[url=pico][color=#61afef][u]Raspberry Pi Pico board[/u][/color][/url] — reading and clicking the pins.
​[url=hardware][color=#61afef][u]Running on a real Pico[/u][/color][/url] — Flash your program to a board.[/ol]

[color=#61afef][b]Levels: see more when you are ready[/b][/color]
The [color=#e5c07b][code]Level[/code][/color] menu (top right) decides how much of picosim is shown. Each level adds to the one before:
[ul]​[b]1 · Basics[/b] — Run programs one instruction at a time and watch the registers and the serial console
​[b]2 · Memory & I/O[/b] — Adds the Memory tab, the stack and the Raspberry Pi Pico board with its pins   [color=#f2cc60]← you are here[/color]
​[b]3 · Inside the CPU[/b] — Adds the CPU diagram: step through every clock cycle on the datapath
​[b]4 · Pipeline & performance[/b] — Adds the Pico's 2-stage pipeline and the Performance window[/ul]
Your teacher will tell you when to change level. Changing it never changes your program. When you raise it, picosim switches on what is new (the Memory tab, the CPU diagram, the pipeline), says what appeared in a strip under the toolbar, and outlines each new button and panel with a [color=#f2cc60][b]NEW[/b][/color] tag for a few seconds.

[table=1][cell bg=#2a2a2a border=#61afef padding=14,9,14,9 expand=1][color=#61afef][b]Tip[/b][/color]   The list on the left gets longer at each level. Click a section's heading (such as [b]▾ GETTING STARTED[/b]) to fold its topics away, and click it again to bring them back. picosim remembers which sections you folded.[/cell][/table]
2.name: Start here
2.sum:
picosim runs programs written in [b]assembly language[/b], the instructions the Raspberry Pi Pico's processor understands, and lets you watch them one step at a time. To begin, click [color=#e5c07b][code]Examples[/code][/color] and pick [b]Say hello[/b]. Press [color=#e5c07b][code]Step instruction[/code][/color] ([color=#e5c07b][code]S[/code][/color]) to run one instruction: whatever changed turns [color=#f2cc60]yellow[/color] in the Registers, the [url=explain][color=#61afef][u]Explain this step[/u][/color][/url] panel says what happened and what comes next, and anything printed appears in the serial console. [color=#e5c07b][code]Run[/code][/color] ([color=#e5c07b][code]Space[/code][/color]) lets the program go by itself, [color=#e5c07b][code]◀ Step back[/code][/color] ([color=#e5c07b][code]B[/code][/color]) undoes a step and [color=#e5c07b][code]Reload[/code][/color] starts over. Nothing you do can break anything.

The [color=#e5c07b][code]Level[/code][/color] menu (top right) decides how much of picosim you see: start at Level 1 and move up when your class does. Then read [url=tour][color=#61afef][u]The screen at a glance[/u][/color][/url] and [url=running][color=#61afef][u]How a program runs[/u][/color][/url]; the [url=glossary][color=#61afef][u]Glossary[/u][/color][/url] explains any word you do not know.

2.full:
[font_size=26][b]The screen at a glance[/b][/font_size]

Before a program is loaded, picosim shows a welcome page with the examples; click one to open it. After that the window has a toolbar across the top and these panels:

[table=2][cell bg=#2a2a2a border=#474747 padding=16,12,16,12 expand=1][b]Registers[/b]
[color=#8c8c8c]the CPU's 16 registers and flags[/color]

[b]Disassembly[/b]
[color=#8c8c8c]your program, one instruction per row[/color]

[b]Raspberry Pi Pico board[/b]
[color=#8c8c8c]the chip's pins[/color][/cell][cell bg=#2a2a2a border=#474747 padding=16,12,16,12 expand=1][b]Explain this step[/b]
[color=#8c8c8c]what the last step did, and what happens next[/color]

[b]Serial console[/b]
[color=#8c8c8c]what your program prints, and the keys you type[/color][/cell][/table]

Click a panel's name to read about it: [url=registers][color=#61afef][u]Registers[/u][/color][/url], [url=memory][color=#61afef][u]Disassembly[/u][/color][/url], [url=explain][color=#61afef][u]Explain this step[/u][/color][/url], [url=serial][color=#61afef][u]Serial console[/u][/color][/url]. Drag the bars between panels to resize them.

[color=#61afef][b]The toolbar, left to right[/b][/color]
[table=2][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Control[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]What it does[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#e5c07b][code]Open…[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Open a [code].s[/code] file of your own ([color=#e5c07b][code]Ctrl/Cmd+O[/code][/color]).[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#e5c07b][code]Examples[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Open one of the example programs. One marked [i](Level 2)[/i] or higher is meant for later, but opens all the same.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#e5c07b][code]Reload[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Read the file again and start the program from the beginning ([color=#e5c07b][code]Ctrl/Cmd+R[/code][/color]). Use it after you save a change, or to watch again.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#e5c07b][code]⚙ Settings[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Only for programs that have settings, such as which pin an LED is on. See [url=programs][color=#61afef][u]Writing programs[/u][/color][/url].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#e5c07b][code]◀ Step back[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Undo the last step ([color=#e5c07b][code]B[/code][/color]; hold it to keep going back). Registers, flags, memory, pins and the console go back to what they were.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#e5c07b][code]Step instruction[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Run exactly one instruction, then stop ([color=#e5c07b][code]S[/code][/color] or [color=#e5c07b][code]F10[/code][/color]; hold it to keep stepping).[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#e5c07b][code]Step over[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]On a [code]bl[/code] line, run the whole function call and stop on the line after it ([color=#e5c07b][code]O[/code][/color]). On any other line it is the same as Step instruction.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#e5c07b][code]Run[/code][/color] / [color=#e5c07b][code]Pause[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Let the program run by itself; press again to pause ([color=#e5c07b][code]Space[/code][/color] or [color=#e5c07b][code]F5[/code][/color]). It stops at the end, at a breakpoint, or on a CPU fault.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#e5c07b][code]Speed[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]How fast Run goes, in clock cycles per second ([code]cyc/s[/code]). An instruction takes several clock cycles (about 6 or 7 on average in the Level 1 examples), so the starting speed of 8 cyc/s runs about one instruction a second. [b]Max[/b] runs as fast as possible.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#e5c07b][code]Simulator[/code][/color] menu[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Switch to [b]Pico (USB serial)[/b] to run on a real board: see [url=hardware][color=#61afef][u]Running on a real Pico[/u][/color][/url].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Status text[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]How many instructions have run, and why the program stopped: [b]halted[/b] (finished), [b]waiting for input[/b] (type a key in the console) or [b]stopped by a CPU fault[/b] (read the console).[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#e5c07b][code]−[/code][/color] [color=#e5c07b][code]100%[/code][/color] [color=#e5c07b][code]+[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Zoom the whole window. Click the percentage to fit it to the window again.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#e5c07b][code]View[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The colour scheme: [b]System[/b] (follows your computer's light or dark setting), [b]Blue[/b], [b]Dark[/b] or [b]Light[/b]; and [b]Show the tour again[/b].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#e5c07b][code]Level[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]How much of picosim to show (you are on 2 · Memory & I/O). See [url=start][color=#61afef][u]Start here[/u][/color][/url].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#e5c07b][code]Guide[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]This guide ([color=#e5c07b][code]F1[/code][/color]). [color=#e5c07b][code]Esc[/code][/color] closes it.[/cell][/table]

Buttons that cannot be used right now are greyed out: for example Step and Run after the program has halted, until you press [color=#e5c07b][code]Reload[/code][/color].

[color=#61afef][b]The tour[/b][/color]
The first time you load a program, a short tour points out Step, Explain this step, the Registers, the Disassembly, the console and this guide, one at a time. [color=#e5c07b][code]Next ▶[/code][/color] moves on and [color=#e5c07b][code]Skip tour[/code][/color] (or [color=#e5c07b][code]Esc[/code][/color]) ends it. To see it again, choose [color=#e5c07b][code]View[/code][/color] ▸ [b]Show the tour again[/b].
2.name: The screen at a glance
2.sum:
Across the top is the toolbar: [color=#e5c07b][code]Open…[/code][/color] and [color=#e5c07b][code]Examples[/code][/color] load a program, [color=#e5c07b][code]Reload[/code][/color] starts it over, [color=#e5c07b][code]◀ Step back[/code][/color], [color=#e5c07b][code]Step instruction[/code][/color] and [color=#e5c07b][code]Run[/code][/color] move through it, and [color=#e5c07b][code]Speed[/code][/color] sets how fast Run goes. Below it, the [b]Registers[/b] (top left) show the numbers the CPU is working on, the [b]Disassembly[/b] under them lists your program with ▶ on the next instruction, [b]Explain this step[/b] (top right) describes each step, and the [b]serial console[/b] (bottom right) shows what the program prints; the [b]Pico board[/b] (bottom left) shows the chip's pins and the [b]Memory[/b] tab shows the bytes in memory.

Hover any button for a reminder of what it does. A greyed-out button cannot be used right now: for example Step after the program has finished, until you press [color=#e5c07b][code]Reload[/code][/color]. [color=#e5c07b][code]View[/code][/color] ▸ [b]Show the tour again[/b] replays the short first-run tour.

2.full:
[font_size=26][b]How a program runs[/b][/font_size]

Every program runs the same way: a small [b]built-in OS[/b] starts it, it runs one instruction at a time, it calls the OS to print, and it ends by returning to the OS. Here is the [b]Say hello[/b] example with every instruction the CPU runs, the OS's included, exactly as [color=#e5c07b][code]Step instruction[/code][/color] shows it from Level 2. Open it from [color=#e5c07b][code]Examples[/code][/color] and step along.

[table=4][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Step[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Address[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Instruction[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]What happens[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]1[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0000[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]ldr r0, [lb]pc, #8][/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]OS: R0 = [code]0x00002FFC[/code], the address where picosim stored the address of your [code]main[/code].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]2[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0002[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]ldr r0, [lb]r0][/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]OS: R0 = [code]0x00003001[/code], the address of [code]main[/code] ([code]3000[/code]). The extra 1 means "Thumb code"; every Pico code address has it.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]3[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0004[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]blx r0[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]OS: calls [code]main[/code]. LR = [code]0x00000007[/code] (where to come back to), PC = [code]0x00003000[/code].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]4[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]3000[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]push {r7, lr}[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Your program starts. Saves R7 and LR on the stack, so SP goes down by 8 to [code]0x0000FFF8[/code].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]5[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]3002[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]movs r0, #'H'[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]R0 = [code]0x00000048[/code], the character H. The Z flag is cleared.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]6[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]3004[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]bl putchar[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Calls the OS's putchar: LR = [code]0x00003009[/code] (the next line, plus 1), PC = [code]0x00000010[/code].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]7[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0010[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]svc #2[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]OS: a [i]supervisor call[/i] asks picosim to print the character in R0. [b]H[/b] appears in the console.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]8[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0012[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]bx lr[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]OS: returns to the address in LR, the line after the [code]bl[/code] ([code]3008[/code]).[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]9–20[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The same three steps print [code]i[/code], [code]![/code] and a new line.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]21[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]301A[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]movs r0, #0[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]R0 = 0, which means "finished without errors". The result is zero, so the Z flag turns on.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]22[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]301C[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]pop {r7, pc}[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Takes R7 and the saved LR back off the stack, putting the LR value into PC: this returns to the OS. SP is back to [code]0x00010000[/code].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]23[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0006[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]bkpt #0[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]OS: [i]breakpoint[/i] instruction. The simulator stops and the status text says [color=#f2cc60][b]halted[/b][/color].[/cell][/table]

[table=1][cell bg=#2a2a2a border=#61afef padding=14,9,14,9 expand=1][color=#61afef][b]Step over[/b][/color]   Steps 1–3 and the [code]svc[/code] / [code]bx lr[/code] after every [code]bl putchar[/code] are the OS, not your file. On a [code]bl[/code] line, [color=#e5c07b][code]Step over[/code][/color] ([color=#e5c07b][code]O[/code][/color]) runs the whole call and stops on the line after it, so you can skip what you do not want to watch.[/cell][/table]

[color=#61afef][b]Step, Run and breakpoints[/b][/color]
[ul]​[color=#e5c07b][code]Step instruction[/code][/color] ([color=#e5c07b][code]S[/code][/color]) runs exactly one instruction, the OS's too; [color=#e5c07b][code]Step over[/code][/color] ([color=#e5c07b][code]O[/code][/color]) runs a whole [code]bl[/code] call.
​[color=#e5c07b][code]Run[/code][/color] ([color=#e5c07b][code]Space[/code][/color]) keeps going at the [url=tour][color=#61afef][u]Speed[/u][/color][/url] you chose, until the program halts, reaches a breakpoint, or you press [color=#e5c07b][code]Pause[/code][/color]. If the program is waiting for a key ([code]getchar[/code]), Run waits too and carries on once you type one in the console.
A [b]breakpoint[/b] (click the first column of a Disassembly row) makes Run stop just before that instruction. Then you can Step from there.
​[color=#e5c07b][code]◀ Step back[/code][/color] ([color=#e5c07b][code]B[/code][/color]) undoes the last step, so you can go back and watch a line again. Everything goes back with it, the console's text too. A key you typed for [code]getchar[/code] is handed to the program again when it gets there.
You can mix them: Run to a breakpoint, Step a few lines, Run again.[/ul]

[color=#61afef][b]Starting again[/b][/color]
When the program has halted, Step and Run are greyed out. [color=#e5c07b][code]Reload[/code][/color] reads the file again and starts it from the beginning, with every register and flag reset. When you save your file, picosim reloads it by itself. The console keeps what was printed before, under a grey [code][lb]loaded …][/code] line that marks the new start; [color=#e5c07b][code]Clear[/code][/color] empties it.

[color=#61afef][b]Where the numbers come from[/b][/color]
The addresses are always the same: the OS is at [code]0000[/code]–[code]2FFF[/code] and your program starts at [code]3000[/code]. The stack is at the top of memory, just below [code]0x00010000[/code]. See [url=programs][color=#61afef][u]Memory map[/u][/color][/url].
2.name: How a program runs
2.sum:
Every program runs the same way: picosim's small [b]built-in OS[/b] calls your [code]main[/code], the CPU runs one instruction at a time from top to bottom (unless a branch jumps somewhere else), the program calls functions such as [code]putchar[/code] to print, and [code]main[/code] ends with [code]pop {…, pc}[/code], which returns to the OS. The OS then stops the processor and the status text says [b]halted[/b]. From Level 2 you also step through the OS's instructions: three at the start and two inside each putchar; [color=#e5c07b][code]Step over[/code][/color] ([color=#e5c07b][code]O[/code][/color]) runs a whole call in one step.

[color=#e5c07b][code]Step instruction[/code][/color] runs one instruction. [color=#e5c07b][code]Run[/code][/color] keeps going until the program ends, reaches a [b]breakpoint[/b] (click a row's first column in the Disassembly) or you press [color=#e5c07b][code]Pause[/code][/color]. [color=#e5c07b][code]◀ Step back[/code][/color] undoes a step, and [color=#e5c07b][code]Reload[/code][/color] starts again. The full details walk through Say hello line by line, with the real values.

2.full:
[font_size=26][b]Writing programs[/b][/font_size]

A program is a plain text file whose name ends in [code].s[/code], written in ARM [b]Thumb[/b] assembly language for the GNU assembler. Here is a complete one:

[table=1][cell bg=#0e0e0e border=#474747 padding=14,10,14,10 expand=1][code]        .syntax unified
        .cpu cortex-m0plus
        .thumb

main:
        push    {r7, lr}        @ save the return address
        movs    r0, #'H'        @ R0 = the letter H
        bl      putchar         @ print the letter in R0
        movs    r0, #0
        pop     {r7, pc}        @ return: the program halts[/code][/cell][/table]

[color=#61afef][b]The parts of a program[/b][/color]
[table=3][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Part[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Example[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]What it is[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Directive[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code].thumb[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]An order to the assembler, not an instruction for the CPU. Start every program with the same three lines shown above: they choose the Pico's instruction set.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Label[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]main:[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]A name for the address of the next instruction, written at the start of a line and ending in a colon. Branches and calls jump to labels.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Instruction[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]movs r0, #'H'[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]One step for the CPU: the [b]mnemonic[/b] ([code]movs[/code]) says what to do, the [b]operands[/b] ([code]r0[/code], [code]#'H'[/code]) say what to do it to. One per line.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Immediate[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]#72[/code][/color]  [color=#56b6c2][code]#0x48[/code][/color]  [color=#56b6c2][code]#'H'[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]A constant written into the instruction, after a #. Decimal, hex and a character in quotes all mean the same number here.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Comment[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]@ print it[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Everything after @ is ignored by the assembler. Use comments to explain your code.[/cell][/table]

Indentation and capital letters do not matter ([code]MOVS R0, #5[/code] is fine), but commas between operands do. [url=instructions][color=#61afef][u]Instructions[/u][/color][/url] lists what each instruction does.

[color=#61afef][b]Edit and save[/b][/color]
picosim runs your file but does not edit it. Use any plain-text code editor (VS Code, for example).
[ol type=1]Start from an example: open it from the [code]examples[/code] folder in your editor and use [i]Save As[/i] to save a copy in your own folder, with a name ending in [code].s[/code].
In picosim, click [color=#e5c07b][code]Open…[/code][/color] ([color=#e5c07b][code]Ctrl/Cmd+O[/code][/color]) and pick your file.
Change the file in your editor and save it. picosim notices and loads it again by itself, from the beginning (the console says [code][lb]… changed on disk: reloading][/code]). [color=#e5c07b][code]Reload[/code][/color] ([color=#e5c07b][code]Ctrl/Cmd+R[/code][/color]) does the same by hand.[/ol]
If the assembler finds a mistake, a [b]Could not load program[/b] box lists each one: the line number, that line of your file, what is wrong and what usually causes it. Fix the line and save; picosim tries again as soon as you save. [url=trouble][color=#61afef][u]Troubleshooting[/u][/color][/url] explains the common messages.

[color=#61afef][b]Entry point and ending[/b][/color]
Execution starts at [code]main:[/code] (the label [code]asm_main:[/code] also works, and is what the Pico build uses). The built-in OS calls [code]main[/code] like a function, so it should begin with [code]push {…, lr}[/code] and end with [code]pop {…, pc}[/code]. When it returns, the OS runs [code]BKPT[/code] and the simulator halts. Press [color=#e5c07b][code]Reload[/code][/color] to run it again. See [url=running][color=#61afef][u]How a program runs[/u][/color][/url].

[color=#61afef][b]Input and output[/b][/color]
[ul]​[code]bl putchar[/code] — prints the character in [code]r0[/code] to the [url=serial][color=#61afef][u]serial console[/u][/color][/url].
​[code]bl getchar[/code] — waits for one key typed in the console and returns it in [code]r0[/code].[/ul]
They behave the same on a real Pico, so the same file runs on both. Both may change R0–R3, so keep values you need afterwards in R4–R7 (and add those registers to [code]push[/code] and [code]pop[/code], as the [url=examples][color=#61afef][u]Count with a loop[/u][/color][/url] example does).

[color=#61afef][b]Settings[/b][/color]
Some programs have settings, such as which pin an LED is on. When a program has them, [color=#e5c07b][code]⚙ Settings[/code][/color] appears next to [color=#e5c07b][code]Reload[/code][/color]: pick your values and click [color=#e5c07b][code]Apply and reload[/code][/color]. picosim remembers them for you and uses them when it runs or flashes the program; the file itself is not changed (a • on the button means you changed something). Not sure what your circuit uses? Open the [b]Buttons and LEDs[/b] example and set its FIND_PINS setting to [i]find my pins[/i].
To give your own program settings, end an [code].equ[/code] line with a comment that starts with [code]<-[/code], for example [code].equ LED_PIN, 15  @ <- the GPIO number of your LED[/code]. A comment like [code]@ <- 1: wired to GND; 0: wired to 3V3[/code] becomes a menu.

[color=#61afef][b]Memory map[/b][/color]
[ul]​[code]0x0000–0x2FFF[/code] — the built-in OS
​[code]0x3000–0xFFFF[/code] — your code and data; the stack starts at the top of RAM ([code]SP = 0x00010000[/code]) and grows down
​[code]0x10000[/code] and up — memory-mapped I/O. The GPIO registers of the RP2040 are here: SIO at [code]0xD0000000[/code], IO_BANK0 at [code]0x40014000[/code], PADS_BANK0 at [code]0x4001C000[/code] (and RESETS at [code]0x4000C000[/code]). Writing them changes the [url=pico][color=#61afef][u]Pico board[/u][/color][/url]'s pins. A pin follows the SIO registers only after its IO_BANK0 CTRL register is set to function 5 (SIO), as on the real chip. Any other address stops the program with a bus fault.[/ul]

[color=#61afef][b]Like the real chip[/b][/color]
picosim runs only Cortex-M0+ (ARMv6-M) instructions and stops with an explanation wherever the Pico would crash (a HardFault): a word or halfword access to an address that is not a multiple of its size, a jump through a register to an address with bit 0 clear (mark such labels with [code].thumb_func[/code]), or an instruction the M0+ does not have. See [url=trouble][color=#61afef][u]Troubleshooting[/u][/color][/url].
2.name: Writing programs
2.sum:
A program is a plain text file whose name ends in [code].s[/code]. It starts with three lines ([code].syntax unified[/code], [code].cpu cortex-m0plus[/code], [code].thumb[/code]), then the label [code]main:[/code] and one instruction per line; anything after [code]@[/code] is a comment. [code]main[/code] begins with [code]push {r7, lr}[/code] and ends with [code]pop {r7, pc}[/code], and [code]bl putchar[/code] prints the character in R0.

Write and save the file in any text editor (VS Code, for example); picosim reloads it by itself when you save. [color=#e5c07b][code]Open…[/code][/color] ([color=#e5c07b][code]Ctrl/Cmd+O[/code][/color]) loads a file. If the assembler finds a mistake, a box lists each wrong line and what usually fixes it. The easiest start is a copy of an example.

2.full:
[font_size=26][b]Challenges[/b][/font_size]

Some examples end their opening comment with a [b]challenge[/b]: a small change to make, which picosim checks for you. The task is shown in a strip under the toolbar. When the program finishes, the strip turns [color=#98c379]green[/color] if you did it. If not, it lists each check: what was wanted and what your program did instead. Change your file, save it (picosim reloads it) and run it again. A stock example fails its own challenge, because you have not changed it yet.
Not every example has one: the LED and button programs never finish, so there is nothing to check at the end. [color=#e5c07b][code]About challenges[/code][/color] opens this page and [color=#e5c07b][code]✕[/code][/color] hides the strip until you load another program.

[color=#61afef][b]Writing your own (for teachers)[/b][/color]
Put the lines in the comment at the top of the file, before the first instruction:
[code]@ Challenge: Change the two numbers so it prints 9, and R3 is still 1.
@ Expect: output "9\n"
@ Expect: R3 = 1[/code]
[table=2][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Line[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]What it checks[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]@ Challenge: …[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The task the strip shows. Optional; without it, the strip lists the checks.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]@ Expect: output "…"[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Everything the program printed, from start to finish, must be exactly this text. Write it in quotes; [code]\n[/code] is a new line (what [code]movs r0, #10[/code] + [code]bl putchar[/code] prints).[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]@ Expect: R2 = 7[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The register's value when the program finishes. R0–R12, SP and LR; the value may be decimal, hex ([code]0x64[/code]), negative ([code]-1[/code]) or a character ([code]'H'[/code]).[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]@ Hint: …[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Your own hint for [url=ask][color=#61afef][u]Ask picosim[/u][/color][/url]. When a student asks for help with the challenge, it gives these first, one per request, in order, before its own hints. Optional.[/cell][/table]

Use as many Expect lines as you like; all must pass. Checks run only in the simulator, and not when the program stops with a CPU fault. A line picosim cannot read is reported in the console when the file loads, and the rest of the program still runs.
2.name: Challenges
2.sum: Some examples set a [b]challenge[/b]: a small change for you to make, shown in a strip under the toolbar. Change the file, save it and run the program to the end: the strip turns [color=#98c379]green[/color] if your program did it, or lists what is still wrong. Teachers can add their own with [code]@ Challenge:[/code] and [code]@ Expect:[/code] comment lines (see the details).

2.full:
[font_size=26][b]Hex, binary and ASCII[/b][/font_size]

Inside the computer every value is a pattern of bits (0s and 1s). A register holds 32 of them. picosim shows them in [b]hexadecimal[/b] (hex), base 16, because each hex digit stands for exactly 4 bits, so 32 bits are always 8 hex digits.

[color=#61afef][b]The 16 hex digits[/b][/color]
[table=6][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Hex[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Decimal[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Binary[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Hex[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Decimal[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Binary[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]0[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]0[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0000[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]8[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]8[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]1000[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]1[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]1[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0001[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]9[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]9[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]1001[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]2[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]2[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0010[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]A[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]10[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]1010[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]3[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]3[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0011[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]B[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]11[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]1011[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]5[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]5[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0101[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]D[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]13[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]1101[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]E[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]14[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]1110[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a
