With [b]Follow loads and stores[/b] ticked, the view moves to them by itself.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]The stack[/b] (right)[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Each word from SP up to the top of RAM as a box, the newest at the bottom with the [b]◀ SP[/b] tag. Each box says what put it there, such as [i]LR saved by push {r7, lr} (line 20)[/i], or that it looks like a return address, and boxes are grouped by the function that pushed them. A word the last step popped is shown faded just below SP, with the register it went into.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]Inspector[/b] (bottom)[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Hover a byte to see everything about it: its address and label, what kind of byte it is, its value in hex, decimal and as a character, the word it belongs to (put together lowest byte first), and which registers point to it.[/cell][/table]

[ul]​[b]Show[/b] — [color=#e5c07b][code]Bytes[/code][/color] (every byte in hex), [color=#e5c07b][code]Words[/code][/color] (4 bytes put together into one number, so [code]64 00 00 00[/code] shows as [code]00000064[/code]) or [color=#e5c07b][code]Characters[/code][/color] (each byte as the character it codes, [code]\0[/code] for the 0 that ends a string).
​[b]Go to[/b] — type an address ([code]0x3000[/code]) or any label of your program, data labels included ([code]numbers[/code]), and press [color=#e5c07b][code]Enter[/code][/color]. [color=#e5c07b][code]PC[/code][/color], [color=#e5c07b][code]SP[/code][/color] and [color=#e5c07b][code]main[/code][/color] jump straight there. The mouse wheel scrolls the bytes.
​[b]Changing memory[/b] — click a byte to select it (an orange outline), type new bytes in hex on the right ([code]2a 00 00 00[/code]) and press [color=#e5c07b][code]Enter[/code][/color]: a quick way to try your program on different data without editing the file. [color=#e5c07b][code]◀ Step back[/code][/color] and [color=#e5c07b][code]Reload[/code][/color] undo it.[/ul]
[table=1][cell bg=#2a2a2a border=#61afef padding=14,9,14,9 expand=1][color=#61afef][b]Try this[/b][/color]   Open [b]Add up a list in memory[/b], tick Follow loads and stores and step through the loop. Each [code]ldr r0, [lb]r1][/code] outlines the next number, and the [b]R1 ↓[/b] tag moves 4 bytes along each pass: R1 is a pointer walking through the list.[/cell][/table]
2.name: Disassembly & memory
2.sum:
The Disassembly lists your program one instruction per row: its address, its bits ([b]Raw[/b]), its label, the instruction as the CPU sees it and the line of your file it came from ([b]Source[/b]). The row with ▶ runs next. Click a row's first column to put a [b]breakpoint[/b] (a red ●) there: [color=#e5c07b][code]Run[/code][/color] stops just before that instruction.

The [b]Memory[/b] tab shows memory as a place: a map of where everything lives, the bytes coloured by what they are (with labels and pointer tags on them), the stack as boxes that say what put each word there, and, after each step, which bytes it read or wrote. Hover a byte to have it explained; click one to change it.

2.full:
[font_size=26][b]Raspberry Pi Pico board[/b][/font_size]

Bottom left, under Disassembly. A to-scale drawing of the Raspberry Pi Pico, lying on its side with the USB connector on the left, showing what your program does to the chip's GPIO pins. [url=gpio][color=#61afef][u]GPIO: controlling pins[/u][/color][/url] explains how a program controls them.

[color=#61afef][b]Reading the pins[/b][/color]
The 40 gold pads are the header pins, numbered 1–20 along the bottom edge and 21–40 along the top. Each GPIO pad is labelled with its GP number; a small [b]out[/b] or [color=#61afef]in[/color] under the label says which way it is set (a floating input shows neither). Power pins (GND, 3V3, VSYS, VBUS, …) are labelled in grey and red. On the pad itself:

[table=2][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]On the pad[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Means[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#98c379][b]1[/b][/color] on green[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]An output your program drives high.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]0[/b] on dark grey[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Low: an output driven low, or an input held low (by a click or a pull-down).[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#61afef][b]1[/b][/color] on blue[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]An input reading high (clicked high, or held by a pull-up).[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]nothing[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Floating: nothing drives the pin and it has no pull resistor. Your program reads it as 0.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#f2cc60]yellow ring[/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Changed by the last step.[/cell][/table]

The same key is drawn above the board. Hover any pin for its header number, GP number, direction, level and pull (for example [i]Pin 20: GP15 — output, high (1)[/i]).

[color=#61afef][b]Under the board[/b][/color]
[ul]​[b]Last I/O write[/b] — the last I/O register the current instruction wrote, decoded: [code]SIO GPIO_OUT_XOR ← 0x00008000[/code] or [code]IO_BANK0 GPIO15_CTRL ← 0x00000005[/code].
​[b]Changed by the last step[/b] — which pins changed, for example [code]GP15 → 1[/code].[/ul]

[color=#61afef][b]The on-board LED[/b][/color]
The drawing's LED lights when GP25 is high, as on a Raspberry Pi Pico. Real boards differ (on a Pico W that LED is wired to the Wi-Fi chip, not to GP25), so for programs that should work on any board, wire your own LED to a GPIO pin: see the [b]Blink an LED[/b] example.

[color=#61afef][b]Driving inputs[/b][/color]
Click an [i]input[/i] pin to drive it like a switch: floating (Z) → 1 → 0 → floating. Your program sees it when it reads [code]GPIO_IN[/code]. A pin with a pull-up already reads 1, so for a button to GND click it [i]twice[/i] (1, then 0) to "press" it. Output pins cannot be clicked: your program controls them.

[color=#61afef][b]Live from your board[/b][/color]
In [color=#e5c07b][code]Pico (USB serial)[/code][/color] mode, while a board you flashed from picosim is connected, the drawing shows your [i]real[/i] board's pins instead: the subtitle turns green and says LIVE. The pins update as your program runs (about 50 times a second), and pins that just changed get a yellow ring. You cannot click pins in this mode; use your real buttons. An input with nothing connected reads 0.

[color=#61afef][b]Full window[/b][/color]
Click [color=#e5c07b][code]⛶ Enlarge[/code][/color] in the board's corner to fill the window with it; [color=#e5c07b][code]✕ Close[/code][/color] or [color=#e5c07b][code]Esc[/code][/color] returns.
2.name: Raspberry Pi Pico board
2.sum:
The drawing of the Raspberry Pi Pico (bottom left) shows what your program does to the chip's pins. A pin your program drives high shows a green [b]1[/b], one driven low a dark [b]0[/b], and an input reading high a blue [b]1[/b]; a [color=#f2cc60]yellow[/color] ring marks a pin the last step changed. Hover a pin for its numbers and state.

Click an [i]input[/i] pin to drive it like a switch: floating → 1 → 0 → floating. In [b]Pico (USB serial)[/b] mode, with a board you flashed connected, the drawing shows your real board's pins instead.

2.full:
[font_size=26][b]USB Serial console[/b][/font_size]

Bottom right. Shows what your program prints with [code]putchar[/code].

[color=#61afef][b]Typing input[/b][/color]
[ul]Click in the output area and type: each key is sent immediately (what [code]getchar[/code] expects).
Or type a whole line in the box below and press [color=#e5c07b][code]Enter[/code][/color] — it is sent followed by a carriage return.[/ul]
When the program is waiting in [code]getchar[/code], the console header says so. [color=#e5c07b][code]Clear[/code][/color] empties the output.
2.name: Serial console
2.sum: The serial console (bottom right) shows what your program prints with [code]putchar[/code]. When the program calls [code]getchar[/code] it waits for a key: click in the console and type (each key is sent at once), or type a line in the box underneath and press [color=#e5c07b][code]Enter[/code][/color]. [color=#e5c07b][code]Clear[/code][/color] empties it.

2.full:
[font_size=26][b]Layout and zoom[/b][/font_size]

[ul]​[b]Resize panels[/b] by dragging the bars between them. The registers panel's text grows with it.
​[b]Zoom[/b] the whole window with [color=#e5c07b][code]−[/code][/color] / [color=#e5c07b][code]+[/code][/color] in the toolbar, [color=#e5c07b][code]Ctrl/Cmd +[/code][/color] / [color=#e5c07b][code]Ctrl/Cmd −[/code][/color], or [color=#e5c07b][code]Ctrl/Cmd[/code][/color] + mouse wheel. Click the percentage (or [color=#e5c07b][code]Ctrl/Cmd 0[/code][/color]) to reset. The zoom is remembered.
​[b]Colours:[/b] [color=#e5c07b][code]View[/code][/color] in the toolbar picks System, Blue, Dark or Light. It is remembered too.
Zoom stops at the largest size where the whole toolbar still fits, so no button is ever cut off.
The Pico board can fill the window — see [url=pico][color=#61afef][u]Raspberry Pi Pico board[/u][/color][/url].[/ul]

Where each panel is, and what every toolbar button does, is in [url=tour][color=#61afef][u]The screen at a glance[/u][/color][/url]. Which panels and buttons you see depends on the [color=#e5c07b][code]Level[/code][/color] menu.
2.name: Layout and zoom
2.sum: Drag the bars between the panels to resize them; a panel you make bigger also gets bigger text. Zoom the whole window with [color=#e5c07b][code]−[/code][/color] / [color=#e5c07b][code]+[/code][/color] in the toolbar, [color=#e5c07b][code]Ctrl/Cmd +[/code][/color] / [color=#e5c07b][code]Ctrl/Cmd −[/code][/color] or [color=#e5c07b][code]Ctrl/Cmd[/code][/color] + mouse wheel, and click the percentage to fit the window again. [color=#e5c07b][code]View[/code][/color] picks the colours (System, Blue, Dark or Light). picosim remembers all of these.

2.full:
[font_size=26][b]Running on a real Pico[/b][/font_size]

The same [code].s[/code] file that runs in the simulator can run on a real Raspberry Pi Pico (or any RP2040 board) plugged into your computer by USB. picosim turns it into a [code].uf2[/code] file, the format the Pico loads programs from, and copies it to the board. This is called [b]flashing[/b], because the program is stored in the board's flash memory and stays there after you unplug it.

[color=#61afef][b]What you need[/b][/color]
[ul]The board and a USB cable that carries data (some cables only charge).
The tools from [code]installation.md[/code]: the ARM compiler, git and, ideally, [code]picotool[/code]. Your teacher has probably installed them already.[/ul]

[color=#61afef][b]Steps[/b][/color]
[ol type=1]Load your program in picosim and check it in the Simulator first.
Choose [b]Pico (USB serial)[/b] in the toolbar's mode menu (it says [b]Simulator[/b] until you change it). The port menu, [color=#e5c07b][code]⟳[/code][/color], [color=#e5c07b][code]Connect[/code][/color] and [color=#e5c07b][code]Flash[/code][/color] appear.
Click [color=#e5c07b][code]Flash[/code][/color]. picosim builds the program with the Pico SDK and uploads it; the console shows each step. The very first build downloads the SDK and takes a few minutes; later ones take seconds. It uploads with [code]picotool[/code] if that is installed; otherwise it copies the file to the board's [code]RPI-RP2[/code] drive, which appears when you [b]hold the BOOTSEL button while plugging the board in[/b].
When the upload finishes, picosim connects to the board by itself and the console talks to it: what the board prints appears in green, and keys you type go to the board. The board waits up to 5 seconds for this connection before your program starts, so nothing it prints is lost. If it does not connect, pick the port marked [i](Pico)[/i] ([color=#e5c07b][code]⟳[/code][/color] refreshes the list) and click [color=#e5c07b][code]Connect[/code][/color].
The [url=pico][color=#61afef][u]Pico board[/u][/color][/url] drawing turns LIVE and shows your real board's pins.[/ol]

[color=#61afef][b]What is different on the board[/b][/color]
[ul]The build defines [code]PICOSIM_HARDWARE[/code], so a program can use bigger delays on the board ([code].ifdef PICOSIM_HARDWARE[/code], as the LED examples do): the real chip runs millions of instructions a second.
Your [color=#e5c07b][code]⚙ Settings[/code][/color] values (pins and wiring) are built in.
Your [code]main:[/code] is renamed [code]asm_main[/code] and called by the Pico SDK after it has started USB. When [code]main[/code] returns, the board does not halt: it waits, with USB still running, so its last output stays in the console and the next Flash works.
Stepping, the registers, the Memory tab and the CPU diagram work only in [b]Simulator[/b] mode. Switch back to it to debug.[/ul]

[color=#61afef][b]If Flash fails[/b][/color]
The status text says [i]Flash failed — see console[/i]; the console shows why:

[table=2][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]The console says[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]What to do[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]picotool could not find or access the Pico[/code] or [code]Put the Pico in BOOTSEL mode[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Unplug the board, hold BOOTSEL, plug it back in, let go, and click Flash again.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]'picotool' was not found and no RPI-RP2 volume is mounted[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]No picotool: put the board in BOOTSEL mode as above, so its drive appears.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]git is not on PATH[/code], [code]ARM GNU C/C++ compiler was not found[/code] or [code]has no C library (newlib)[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]A tool is missing: see [code]installation.md[/code] or ask your teacher.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]an assembler error[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Your program does not assemble: fix it in the Simulator first.[/cell][/table]
2.name: Running on a real Pico
2.sum:
The same [code].s[/code] file can run on a real Raspberry Pi Pico plugged in by USB. Choose [b]Pico (USB serial)[/b] in the mode menu and click [color=#e5c07b][code]Flash[/code][/color]: picosim builds your program, copies it to the board and connects the console, so you see what the board prints. If picotool is not installed, hold the board's [b]BOOTSEL[/b] button while you plug it in, so it appears as a drive.

The first build takes a few minutes because it downloads the Pico SDK; later ones take seconds. If Flash fails the console says why, and the details list what to do. Stepping, the registers and the CPU diagram work only in Simulator mode.

2.full:
[font_size=26][b]Keyboard shortcuts[/b][/font_size]

[table=2][cell][color=#e5c07b][code]S  or  F10[/code][/color]    [/cell][cell]Step instruction: run one instruction (hold to repeat)[/cell][cell][color=#e5c07b][code]B[/code][/color]    [/cell][cell]Step back: undo the last step (hold to repeat)[/cell][cell][color=#e5c07b][code]O[/code][/color]    [/cell][cell]Step over: run a whole bl call, stop on the line after it[/cell][cell][color=#e5c07b][code]Space  or  F5[/code][/color]    [/cell][cell]Run / Pause[/cell][cell][color=#e5c07b][code]F1[/code][/color]    [/cell][cell]open this guide[/cell][cell][color=#e5c07b][code]?[/code][/color]    [/cell][cell]open Ask picosim, the help chat[/cell][cell][color=#e5c07b][code]Ctrl/Cmd+O[/code][/color]    [/cell][cell]open a .s file[/cell][cell][color=#e5c07b][code]Ctrl/Cmd+R[/code][/color]    [/cell][cell]reload (start the program over)[/cell][cell][color=#e5c07b][code]Ctrl/Cmd + / −[/code][/color]    [/cell][cell]zoom in / out[/cell][cell][color=#e5c07b][code]Ctrl/Cmd 0[/code][/color]    [/cell][cell]reset zoom[/cell][cell][color=#e5c07b][code]Esc[/code][/color]    [/cell][cell]close this guide, the enlarged Pico board or a component card[/cell][/table]

The letter keys work on every keyboard: on a Mac, F11 shows the desktop and the F keys need Fn, so use S, B, C and Space there. They only work in Simulator mode, and not while you are typing in a box or in the serial console (those keys go to your program).
2.name: Keyboard shortcuts
2.sum: [color=#e5c07b][code]S[/code][/color] steps one instruction, [color=#e5c07b][code]B[/code][/color] steps back, [color=#e5c07b][code]Space[/code][/color] runs or pauses, [color=#e5c07b][code]O[/code][/color] steps over a call, [color=#e5c07b][code]F1[/code][/color] opens this guide, [color=#e5c07b][code]Ctrl/Cmd+O[/code][/color] opens a file and [color=#e5c07b][code]Ctrl/Cmd+R[/code][/color] reloads it. Holding a step key repeats it. The keys work only in Simulator mode, and not while you are typing in a box or in the serial console.

2.full:
[font_size=26][b]Troubleshooting[/b][/font_size]

[font_size=21][b]While it runs[/b][/font_size]

[color=#61afef][b]Nothing happens when I press Step or Run[/b][/color]
The program has halted (the status text says [i]halted[/i]) — press [color=#e5c07b][code]Reload[/code][/color]. Or no program is loaded, or you are in Pico mode — switch to Simulator.

[color=#61afef][b]I pressed Step and ended up in code I did not write[/b][/color]
That is the built-in OS, at addresses below [code]3000[/code]. The first three instructions of every run are the OS starting your [code]main[/code], and each [code]bl putchar[/code] goes into the OS for two instructions ([code]svc #2[/code], [code]bx lr[/code]) before coming back. Keep stepping, or use [color=#e5c07b][code]Step over[/code][/color] on the [code]bl[/code] line. See [url=running][color=#61afef][u]How a program runs[/u][/color][/url].

[color=#61afef][b]R0 suddenly holds 0x00002FFC or 0x00003001[/b][/color]
Those are from the OS's first two instructions, before your program starts. Your own code starts at [code]main[/code].

[color=#61afef][b]Run is very slow[/b][/color]
Move the [color=#e5c07b][code]Speed[/code][/color] slider to the right. At the starting speed (8 cyc/s) Run does about one instruction a second, so you can watch it. [b]Max[/b] finishes almost at once.

[color=#61afef][b]The program stops and waits[/b][/color]
It is in [code]getchar[/code], waiting for a key (the status text says [i]waiting for input[/i]). Click the serial console and type a key.

[color=#61afef][b]It prints a strange character instead of my number[/b][/color]
[code]putchar[/code] prints the character whose [i]code[/i] is in R0. Add [code]'0'[/code] to a number from 0 to 9 first; numbers of 10 or more need one digit at a time. See [url=numbers][color=#61afef][u]Hex, binary and ASCII[/u][/color][/url].

[color=#61afef][b]A value I saved in R0–R3 changed after bl putchar[/b][/color]
Functions are allowed to change R0–R3 (and LR). Keep values you need in R4–R7, and add those registers to [code]main[/code]'s [code]push[/code] and [code]pop[/code].

[color=#61afef][b]The program never halts, and ▶ is stuck on a bx lr[/b][/color]
A function called another function (even putchar) without saving LR first, so its [code]bx lr[/code] jumps back to itself forever. Add [code]push {lr}[/code] at its start and end it with [code]pop {pc}[/code]. See [url=stack][color=#61afef][u]The stack and functions[/u][/color][/url].

[color=#61afef][b]Go to in the Memory tab does nothing[/b][/color]
Type the label exactly as it is in your file (capital letters matter), or an address starting with [code]0x[/code], then press [color=#e5c07b][code]Enter[/code][/color]. Reload first if you have just added the label.

[color=#61afef][b]My data is not in the Disassembly[/b][/color]
Data after [code].data[/code] is not listed there: look at it in the Memory tab (Go to its label).

[color=#61afef][b]I can't find a button or panel from the guide[/b][/color]
Some appear only at higher levels. Raise the [color=#e5c07b][code]Level[/code][/color] menu in the toolbar; see [url=start][color=#61afef][u]Start here[/u][/color][/url].

[font_size=21][b]When it will not load[/b][/font_size]
The [b]Could not load program[/b] box shows the assembler's message. The number after the file name is the line, for example [code]add.s:12: Error: …[/code] is line 12. Fix the file, save it and press [color=#e5c07b][code]Reload[/code][/color].

[table=2][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]The message says[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]What is usually wrong[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]cannot honor width suffix[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]A missing S ([code]add[/code] instead of [code]adds[/code], [code]mov r0, #1[/code] instead of [code]movs[/code]), or a register from R8 to R12. Use R0–R7. See [url=instructions][color=#61afef][u]Instructions[/u][/color][/url].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]invalid immediate: 300 is out of range[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The constant is too big (or negative). [code]movs[/code], [code]cmp[/code] and two-register [code]adds[/code] / [code]subs[/code] take 0 to 255.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]immediate value out of range[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Three-register [code]adds r0, r1, #9[/code] takes only 0 to 7. Use [code]adds r0, #9[/code] on the same register, or put the constant in a register first.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]bad arguments to instruction[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]A missing comma or # (write [code]movs r0, #1[/code]), or a misspelt register.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]undefined reference to …[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]A branch or [code]bl[/code] to a label that does not exist. Check the spelling, and that the label line ends in a colon.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]The program has no main: label[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Put [code]main:[/code] on the line before your first instruction.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]invalid offset, value too big[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]A load or store offset that is too big, negative or not a multiple of the size; or, on an [code]ldr rX, =…[/code] line, a literal pool too far away (put [code].ltorg[/code] after a [code]b[/code] or [code]pop[/code]). See [url=loadstore][color=#61afef][u]Loads and stores[/u][/color][/url].[/cell][/table]

[color=#61afef][b]"Simulator backend disconnected"[/b][/color]
The Python backend stopped. Close picosim and start it again with [code]picosim --gui[/code].

[font_size=21][b]Pins[/b][/font_size]

[color=#61afef][b]A pin will not respond to clicks[/b][/color]
Only input pins can be driven. If your program configured the pin as an output (via [code]GPIO_OE[/code]), it controls the pin.

[color=#61afef][b]My program sets GPIO_OE and GPIO_OUT but the pin stays blank[/b][/color]
The pin is not connected to the SIO yet: write 5 (function SIO) to its IO_BANK0 CTRL register at [code]0x40014004 + 8 × pin[/code] first. The real RP2040 needs this too. Hover the pin for a reminder. See [url=gpio][color=#61afef][u]GPIO: controlling pins[/u][/color][/url].

[font_size=21][b]On a real Pico[/b][/font_size]

[color=#61afef][b]There is no Flash button[/b][/color]
Choose [b]Pico (USB serial)[/b] in the mode menu (it says [b]Simulator[/b]). Flash needs a loaded [code].s[/code] file.

[color=#61afef][b]Flash failed[/b][/color]
The console shows the reason; the table in [url=hardware][color=#61afef][u]Running on a real Pico[/u][/color][/url] says what to do. Most often the board is not in BOOTSEL mode: unplug it, hold BOOTSEL, plug it in, let go, and Flash again.

[color=#61afef][b]Nothing appears in the console after Flash[/b][/color]
Check that a port marked [i](Pico)[/i] is chosen and that the button says [b]Disconnect[/b] (it is connected); if not, press [color=#e5c07b][code]⟳[/code][/color] and [color=#e5c07b][code]Connect[/code][/color]. A board waits only 5 seconds for the console before it starts, so a short program may have finished before you connected: Flash again.

[font_size=21][b]"CPU fault: …" in the console[/b][/font_size]
Your program did something that would crash a real Pico, and the message says what and where. The most common ones:
[ul]​[b]Undefined instruction[/b] — not a Cortex-M0+ instruction (for example code written for a Cortex-M4), or the program ran into data.
​[b]Bus fault[/b] — the address is not RAM (0x0000–0xFFFF) or a simulated I/O register. The two most common causes at first: [code]main[/code] has no [code]pop {…, pc}[/code] at the end, so the CPU runs on through empty memory until it reaches [code]0x00010000[/code]; or [code]main[/code] pops without a matching [code]push {…, lr}[/code] at the start, so the pop reads past the top of RAM. Later on, a pointer that went wrong or a stack that grew too far (too many PUSHes without POPs) do the same.
​[b]… with bit 0 clear[/b] — BX, BLX or POP {PC} jumped to an even address. Put [code].thumb_func[/code] on the line before a label whose address you load with [code]ldr r0, =label[/code].
​[b]Unaligned access[/b] — LDR/STR need an address that is a multiple of 4, LDRH/STRH a multiple of 2. Use LDRB/STRB for single bytes, and put [code].align 2[/code] before word data.[/ul]
Press [color=#e5c07b][code]Reload[/code][/color] to start again.
2.name: Troubleshooting
2.sum:
Most problems have a quick fix. If Step does nothing, the program has finished: press [color=#e5c07b][code]Reload[/code][/color]. If it is waiting, type a key in the serial console. If Run is slow, move the [color=#e5c07b][code]Speed[/code][/color] slider to the right. If the program will not load, the [b]Could not load program[/b] box gives the line number and what is wrong: fix that line and save.

A [b]CPU fault[/b] message in the console means the program did something that would crash a real Pico. The most common cause is a [code]main[/code] without [code]pop {…, pc}[/code] at its end. The details list every message you may see, with what to do.

2.full:
[font_size=26][b]Ask picosim[/b][/font_size]

Click [color=#e5c07b][code]Ask[/code][/color] in the toolbar, or press [color=#e5c07b][code]?[/code][/color], and type a question in your own words. Typos are fine. Some good ones:

[table=2][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Ask about[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]For example[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Your program right now[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1][i]Why did it stop?[/i] · [i]What just happened?[/i] · [i]What happens next?[/i] · [i]Why is R0 72?[/i] · [i]Why is it waiting?[/i][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Errors and crashes[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1][i]What does this error mean?[/i] (or paste the error) · [i]Why did it crash?[/i][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]The buttons and panels[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1][i]What does Step over do?[/i] · [i]How do I set a breakpoint?[/i] · [i]How do I see decimal?[/i][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Assembly[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1][i]What does LDR do?[/i] · [i]movs vs mov?[/i] · [i]What is the Z flag?[/i] · [i]What is 0x2A in decimal?[/i][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Challenges[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1][i]What is the challenge?[/i] · [i]Did I pass?[/i] · [i]Give me a hint[/i][/cell][/table]

Follow-ups work too: [i]why?[/i], [i]tell me more[/i], [i]what about R1?[/i]. Chips under the conversation suggest questions that fit what is on screen, such as [i]Why did it crash?[/i] after a fault.

[color=#61afef][b]Hints, not answers[/b][/color]
It never writes your code or a challenge's solution, and nothing you type changes that. Ask for the answer and you get the next small hint: first the idea and the guide page, then where to look, then what kind of change to make. After three hints it stops: ask your teacher, or look the topic up online. Load errors and CPU faults are different: it tells you exactly what the assembler or the CPU complained about, because fixing those is not the exercise.

[color=#61afef][b]Where answers come from[/b][/color]
Each answer has a small tag. [b]built-in answer[/b] and [b]from the guide[/b] come from picosim itself: this guide and your program as it runs, so they match what you see. Above your Level it gives a short answer and says which Level covers it. 👍 and 👎 tell your teacher what helps; [b]Report[/b] saves the question and answer (without personal details) for them.
Please don't type personal details (phone numbers, addresses, passwords): the chat leaves them out. If something is really wrong, beyond picosim, talk to a teacher or another adult you trust.

[color=#61afef][b]For teachers: AI help[/b][/color]
By default everything works offline. A teacher can let questions the built-in answers cannot handle go to Claude, an AI made by Anthropic: run [code]picosim --chat-setup[/code] to see (and create) the config file, set [code]"ai": "on"[/code] there, install the extra with [code]pip install -e .[lb]ai][/code] (it needs Python 3.10 or newer) and set an Anthropic API key in [code]ANTHROPIC_API_KEY[/code]. The question, a summary of the machine and the student's program (personal data removed) are then sent to Anthropic, so check your school's rules first; the window shows a notice while AI is on. AI answers are tagged [b]AI answer[/b], follow the same hints-only rule, and are withdrawn if they show too much code. The config also sets the model, [code]max_ai_per_hour[/code] (20), a [code]helpline[/code] for the wellbeing reply and [code]log_unanswered[/code]. There is no setting for full answers.
Reports go to [code]chat_reports.jsonl[/code] and 👍 / 👎 counts to [code]chat_feedback.json[/code], next to the config. Write your own hints for a challenge with [code]@ Hint:[/code] lines (see [url=challenges][color=#61afef][u]Challenges[/u][/color][/url]).
2.name: Ask picosim
2.sum:
[color=#e5c07b][code]Ask[/code][/color] (top right, or the [color=#e5c07b][code]?[/code][/color] key) opens a chat where you can ask questions in your own words: [i]Why did my program stop?[/i], [i]Why is R0 72?[/i], [i]What does LDR do?[/i], [i]How do I set a breakpoint?[/i] It looks at your program as it runs and answers from this guide, with a link to the page and often a [b]Show me[/b] button that points at the control.

It gives [b]hints, never finished answers[/b]: ask it for the solution to a challenge and it gives the next small hint instead, up to three. If you need more help than that, ask your teacher, or look the topic up online. It only knows about picosim, ARM assembly and the Pico.

2.full:
[font_size=26][b]Glossary[/b][/font_size]

[table=2][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Word[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Meaning[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Address[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]A number that says where in memory something is, like a house number. Shown in hex, such as [code]3000[/code].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Alignment[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]A word must be at an address that is a multiple of 4, a halfword at a multiple of 2. See [url=memmap][color=#61afef][u]Memory and addresses[/u][/color][/url].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]ASCII[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The code that gives each character a number: 'A' is [code]0x41[/code]. See [url=numbers][color=#61afef][u]Hex, binary and ASCII[/u][/color][/url].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Assembler[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The program that turns your [code].s[/code] file into the bits the CPU runs. picosim runs it when you Open or Reload.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Assembly language[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Writing a program as the processor's own instructions, one per line, with names instead of bits.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Bit[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]One binary digit, 0 or 1. A register has 32.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]BOOTSEL[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The button on the Pico. Hold it while plugging the board in and it appears as a drive (RPI-RP2) you can copy a program to.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Branch[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]An instruction that jumps to another place in the program, always ([code]b[/code]) or only if a condition holds ([code]bne[/code], …).[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Breakpoint[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]A red ● on a Disassembly row: Run stops just before that instruction.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Built-in OS[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]picosim's tiny operating system at addresses [code]0000[/code]–[code]2FFF[/code]. It starts your [code]main[/code] and provides [code]putchar[/code] and [code]getchar[/code].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Byte[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]8 bits: two hex digits, 0 to 255.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Calling convention[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The rules functions follow: arguments and result in R0–R3, R4–R7 kept, LR saved. See [url=stack][color=#61afef][u]The stack and functions[/u][/color][/url].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Clock cycle[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]One tick of the CPU's clock. An instruction takes several. You will see them at Level 3.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Comment[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Text after [code]@[/code] that the assembler ignores; it is for people.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Cortex-M0+[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The processor inside the Pico's RP2040 chip. picosim runs only its instructions.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]CPU fault[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]A mistake that would crash a real Pico, such as running something that is not an instruction. picosim stops and explains it in the console.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Directive[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]A line starting with a dot, such as [code].thumb[/code]: an instruction to the assembler, not to the CPU.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Disassembly[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Your program shown back from the bits in memory: see [url=memory][color=#61afef][u]Disassembly[/u][/color][/url].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Flags[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]N, Z, C and V: four bits describing the last result, used by conditional branches. See [url=branches][color=#61afef][u]Flags and branches[/u][/color][/url].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Flash[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]To copy a program into the Pico's flash memory, where it stays when the power is off. Also the name of that memory.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Floating[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]An input pin that nothing drives: it could read 0 or 1. A pull resistor prevents it.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Function[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]A piece of code you call with [code]bl[/code] that returns with [code]bx lr[/code] or [code]pop {…, pc}[/code]. [code]putchar[/code] is one.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]GPIO[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]General-purpose input/output: a pin your program can drive high or low, or read. See [url=gpio][color=#61afef][u]GPIO: controlling pins[/u][/color][/url].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Halfword[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]2 bytes, 16 bits. Most Thumb instructions are one halfword.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Halted[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The program has finished (or faulted) and the CPU has stopped. Press Reload to start again.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Hex[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Base 16, written with [code]0x[/code] in front: [code]0x2A[/code] = 42.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Immediate[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]A constant written inside the instruction after a [code]#[/code], as in [code]movs r0, #5[/code].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Instruction[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]One step for the CPU, such as [code]adds r2, r0, r1[/code].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Label[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]A name followed by a colon, such as [code]loop:[/code]; it stands for the address of the next line.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Leaf function[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]A function that calls no other function, so it need not save LR.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Literal pool[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Numbers the assembler stores after your code for [code]ldr rX, =value[/code]; listed as [code].word[/code] rows.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Little-endian[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Storing a word's lowest byte at the lowest address: [code]0x0000300D[/code] is stored as [code]0D 30 00 00[/code].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Load / store[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Copy a value from memory into a register ([code]ldr[/code]) or from a register into memory ([code]str[/code]).[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]LR[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Link register (R14): holds the address a function returns to.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Mask[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]A number with a 1 in the bits you care about, such as [code]1 << 15[/code] for GP15.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Memory-mapped I/O[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Controlling hardware by reading and writing special addresses with ordinary loads and stores.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Mnemonic[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The name of an instruction: [code]movs[/code], [code]adds[/code], [code]bne[/code].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Operand[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]What an instruction works on: the registers and constants after the mnemonic.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]PC[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Program counter (R15): the address of the next instruction.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Pointer[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]A register (or word) holding an address: [code][lb]r1][/code] means the memory R1 points at.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Polling[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Reading an input over and over in a loop to see when it changes.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Pull-up / pull-down[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]A weak resistor inside the chip that holds an input at 1 (up) or 0 (down) while nothing else drives it.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Register[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]One of 16 storage boxes inside the CPU, each holding a 32-bit number.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Serial console[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The text panel on the right: what your program prints, and where you type to it.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]SIO[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Single-cycle I/O: the block at 0xD0000000 whose registers set, clear and read the GPIO pins in one clock cycle.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]SP and the stack[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The stack is memory used to save registers ([code]push[/code] / [code]pop[/code]); SP (R13) points to its top. See [url=memory][color=#61afef][u]the Memory tab[/u][/color][/url].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Thumb[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The 16-bit instruction set the Cortex-M0+ runs (a few instructions, like [code]bl[/code], are 32 bits).[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Thumb bit[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Bit 0 of an address you jump to with BX, BLX or POP {PC}. It must be 1, meaning "Thumb code"; the instruction itself is fetched from the even address.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]UF2[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The file format the Pico loads programs from. Flash makes one from your [code].s[/code] file.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Word[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]4 bytes, 32 bits: what one register holds.[/cell][/table]
2.name: Glossary
2.sum: Short meanings of the words used in picosim and in this guide, in alphabetical order. More words appear as you raise the Level.

3.full:
[font_size=26][b]Start here[/b][/font_size]

picosim runs programs written in [b]assembly language[/b] — the instructions the Raspberry Pi Pico's processor understands — and lets you watch them run one step at a time. Try anything: nothing can break, and [color=#e5c07b][code]Reload[/code][/color] always starts your program over.

[color=#61afef][b]Your first five minutes[/b][/color]
[ol type=1]Click [color=#e5c07b][code]Examples[/code][/color] in the toolbar and pick [b]Say hello[/b]. Your program appears in the Disassembly list on the left; the row marked ▶ is the instruction that runs next. The [b]Source[/b] column shows the line of your file that each row came from.
Press [color=#e5c07b][code]Step instruction[/code][/color] ([color=#e5c07b][code]S[/code][/color]) three times. These first three instructions belong to picosim's small [b]built-in OS[/b], which starts your program: R0 briefly holds [code]0x00002FFC[/code] and then [code]0x00003001[/code]. Now ▶ is on [code]main[/code], the first line of [i]your[/i] program.
Step twice more and look at the [url=registers][color=#61afef][u]Registers[/u][/color][/url]: the one that just changed turns [color=#f2cc60]yellow[/color]. After [code]movs r0, #'H'[/code], R0 holds [code]0x00000048[/code], the [url=numbers][color=#61afef][u]ASCII code[/u][/color][/url] for the letter H.
Step three more times. [code]bl putchar[/code] jumps into the OS's [code]putchar[/code] (address [code]0010[/code]), [code]svc #2[/code] prints the [b]H[/b] in the [url=serial][color=#61afef][u]serial console[/u][/color][/url] on the right, and [code]bx lr[/code] comes back to the next line of your program. ([color=#e5c07b][code]Step over[/code][/color] does all three at once.)
Press [color=#e5c07b][code]Run[/code][/color] ([color=#e5c07b][code]Space[/code][/color]) to let the rest go by itself. When the status text at the top says [b]halted[/b], the program has finished; press [color=#e5c07b][code]Reload[/code][/color] to watch it again.[/ol]
Each time you step, the [url=explain][color=#61afef][u]Explain this step[/u][/color][/url] panel at the top right says what that instruction did and what the next one will do, so you can follow along without guessing.

[table=1][cell bg=#2a2a2a border=#61afef padding=14,9,14,9 expand=1][color=#61afef][b]Stuck?[/b][/color]   Nothing you do here can break anything, and [color=#e5c07b][code]Reload[/code][/color] always starts the program over. [url=running][color=#61afef][u]How a program runs[/u][/color][/url] explains each of the steps above.[/cell][/table]

[color=#61afef][b]Words you will meet[/b][/color]
[ul]​[b]Register[/b] — a small storage box inside the processor that holds one number. R0–R12 are for your values; SP, LR and PC have special jobs.
​[b]PC[/b] (program counter) — the address of the next instruction. Watch it move as you step.
​[b]Hex[/b] — numbers written in base 16 with a [code]0x[/code] in front: [code]0x2A[/code] = 42. Hover a register to see it in decimal, or switch the Registers panel's [color=#e5c07b][code]Hex[/code][/color] menu to [color=#e5c07b][code]Decimal[/code][/color].
​[b]Flags[/b] N Z C V — four yes/no facts about the last result (negative? zero? …) that branches like [code]BNE[/code] use to decide where to go.[/ul]
More words are in the [url=glossary][color=#61afef][u]Glossary[/u][/color][/url].

[color=#61afef][b]What to read next[/b][/color]
If you missed the first class, read these in order. Each takes a few minutes:
[ol type=1]​[url=tour][color=#61afef][u]The screen at a glance[/u][/color][/url] — every button and panel you can see.
​[url=running][color=#61afef][u]How a program runs[/u][/color][/url] — what happens when you press Step and Run.
​[url=numbers][color=#61afef][u]Hex, binary and ASCII[/u][/color][/url] — how to read the numbers on screen.
​[url=instructions][color=#61afef][u]Instructions[/u][/color][/url] and [url=branches][color=#61afef][u]Flags and branches[/u][/color][/url] — what each line of a program does.
​[url=examples][color=#61afef][u]Level 1 examples[/u][/color][/url] — step through them with a guide beside you.
​[url=programs][color=#61afef][u]Writing programs[/u][/color][/url] — write, save and run your own.[/ol]

[color=#61afef][b]New at Level 2[/b][/color]
[ol type=1]​[url=memmap][color=#61afef][u]Memory and addresses[/u][/color][/url] — bytes, words and where things are.
​[url=loadstore][color=#61afef][u]Loads and stores[/u][/color][/url] — moving numbers between memory and registers.
​[url=stack][color=#61afef][u]The stack and functions[/u][/color][/url] — calling your own functions safely.
​[url=gpio][color=#61afef][u]GPIO: controlling pins[/u][/color][/url] — lighting LEDs and reading buttons.
​[url=examples2][color=#61afef][u]Level 2 examples[/u][/color][/url] — step through them with a guide beside you.
​[url=memory][color=#61afef][u]Disassembly & memory[/u][/color][/url] — the Memory tab and the stack view.
​[url=pico][color=#61afef][u]Raspberry Pi Pico board[/u][/color][/url] — reading and clicking the pins.
​[url=hardware][color=#61afef][u]Running on a real Pico[/u][/color][/url] — Flash your program to a board.[/ol]

[color=#61afef][b]New at Level 3[/b][/color]
[ol type=1]​[url=cpuintro][color=#61afef][u]The big picture[/u][/color][/url] — clock cycles, the datapath and the control unit.
​[url=blocks][color=#61afef][u]Building blocks[/u][/color][/url] — registers, the bus, muxes and the ALU.
​[url=diagram][color=#61afef][u]Datapath diagram[/u][/color][/url] — how to read the CPU diagram.
​[url=cycles][color=#61afef][u]Cycle by cycle[/u][/color][/url] — the panel under the diagram.
​[url=tutorial][color=#61afef][u]Tutorial: one ADDS[/u][/color][/url] — an ADDS, all six cycles, with real values.
​[url=kinds][color=#61afef][u]Other instructions[/u][/color][/url] — the other kinds of instruction.
​[url=signals][color=#61afef][u]Control signals[/u][/color][/url] — what every signal name means.[/ol]

[color=#61afef][b]Levels: see more when you are ready[/b][/color]
The [color=#e5c07b][code]Level[/code][/color] menu (top right) decides how much of picosim is shown. Each level adds to the one before:
[ul]​[b]1 · Basics[/b] — Run programs one instruction at a time and watch the registers and the serial console
​[b]2 · Memory & I/O[/b] — Adds the Memory tab, the stack and the Raspberry Pi Pico board with its pins
​[b]3 · Inside the CPU[/b] — Adds the CPU diagram: step through every clock cycle on the datapath   [color=#f2cc60]← you are here[/color]
​[b]4 · Pipeline & performance[/b] — Adds the Pico's 2-stage pipeline and the Performance window[/ul]
Your teacher will tell you when to change level. Changing it never changes your program. When you raise it, picosim switches on what is new (the Memory tab, the CPU diagram, the pipeline), says what appeared in a strip under the toolbar, and outlines each new button and panel with a [color=#f2cc60][b]NEW[/b][/color] tag for a few seconds.

[table=1][cell bg=#2a2a2a border=#61afef padding=14,9,14,9 expand=1][color=#61afef][b]Tip[/b][/color]   The list on the left gets longer at each level. Click a section's heading (such as [b]▾ GETTING STARTED[/b]) to fold its topics away, and click it again to bring them back. picosim remembers which sections you folded.[/cell][/table]
3.name: Start here
3.sum:
picosim runs programs written in [b]assembly language[/b], the instructions the Raspberry Pi Pico's processor understands, and lets you watch them one step at a time. To begin, click [color=#e5c07b][code]Examples[/code][/color] and pick [b]Say hello[/b]. Press [color=#e5c07b][code]Step instruction[/code][/color] ([color=#e5c07b][code]S[/code][/color]) to run one instruction: whatever changed turns [color=#f2cc60]yellow[/color] in the Registers, the [url=explain][color=#61afef][u]Explain this step[/u][/color][/url] panel says what happened and what comes next, and anything printed appears in the serial console. [color=#e5c07b][code]Run[/code][/color] ([color=#e5c07b][code]Space[/code][/color]) lets the program go by itself, [color=#e5c07b][code]◀ Step back[/code][/color] ([color=#e5c07b][code]B[/code][/color]) undoes a step and [color=#e5c07b][code]Reload[/code][/color] starts over. Nothing you do can break anything.

The [color=#e5c07b][code]Level[/code][/color] menu (top right) decides how much of picosim you see: start at Level 1 and move up when your class does. Then read [url=tour][color=#61afef][u]The screen at a glance[/u][/color][/url] and [url=running][color=#61afef][u]How a program runs[/u][/color][/url]; the [url=glossary][color=#61afef][u]Glossary[/u][/color][/url] explains any word you do not know.

3.full:
[font_size=26][b]The screen at a glance[/b][/font_size]

Before a program is loaded, picosim shows a welcome page with the examples; click one to open it. After that the window has a toolbar across the top and these panels:

[table=2][cell bg=#2a2a2a border=#474747 padding=16,12,16,12 expand=1][b]Registers[/b]
[color=#8c8c8c]the CPU's 16 registers and flags[/color]

[b]Disassembly[/b]
[color=#8c8c8c]your program, one instruction per row[/color]

[b]Raspberry Pi Pico board[/b]
[color=#8c8c8c]the chip's pins[/color][/cell][cell bg=#2a2a2a border=#474747 padding=16,12,16,12 expand=1][b]Explain this step[/b]
[color=#8c8c8c]what the last step did, and what happens next[/color]

[b]CPU diagram[/b] (when shown)
[color=#8c8c8c]the datapath, cycle by cycle[/color]

[b]Serial console[/b]
[color=#8c8c8c]what your program prints, and the keys you type[/color][/cell][/table]

Click a panel's name to read about it: [url=registers][color=#61afef][u]Registers[/u][/color][/url], [url=memory][color=#61afef][u]Disassembly[/u][/color][/url], [url=explain][color=#61afef][u]Explain this step[/u][/color][/url], [url=serial][color=#61afef][u]Serial console[/u][/color][/url]. Drag the bars between panels to resize them.

[color=#61afef][b]The toolbar, left to right[/b][/color]
[table=2][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Control[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]What it does[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#e5c07b][code]Open…[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Open a [code].s[/code] file of your own ([color=#e5c07b][code]Ctrl/Cmd+O[/code][/color]).[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#e5c07b][code]Examples[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Open one of the example programs. One marked [i](Level 2)[/i] or higher is meant for later, but opens all the same.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#e5c07b][code]Reload[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Read the file again and start the program from the beginning ([color=#e5c07b][code]Ctrl/Cmd+R[/code][/color]). Use it after you save a change, or to watch again.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#e5c07b][code]⚙ Settings[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Only for programs that have settings, such as which pin an LED is on. See [url=programs][color=#61afef][u]Writing programs[/u][/color][/url].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#e5c07b][code]◀ Step back[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Undo the last step ([color=#e5c07b][code]B[/code][/color]; hold it to keep going back). Registers, flags, memory, pins and the console go back to what they were. Partway through an instruction it goes back one clock cycle.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#e5c07b][code]Step instruction[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Run exactly one instruction, then stop ([color=#e5c07b][code]S[/code][/color] or [color=#e5c07b][code]F10[/code][/color]; hold it to keep stepping).[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#e5c07b][code]Step over[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]On a [code]bl[/code] line, run the whole function call and stop on the line after it ([color=#e5c07b][code]O[/code][/color]). On any other line it is the same as Step instruction.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#e5c07b][code]Step cycle[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Run one clock cycle of the CPU ([color=#e5c07b][code]C[/code][/color] or [color=#e5c07b][code]F11[/code][/color]). See [url=cycles][color=#61afef][u]Cycle by cycle[/u][/color][/url].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#e5c07b][code]Run[/code][/color] / [color=#e5c07b][code]Pause[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Let the program run by itself; press again to pause ([color=#e5c07b][code]Space[/code][/color] or [color=#e5c07b][code]F5[/code][/color]). It stops at the end, at a breakpoint, or on a CPU fault.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#e5c07b][code]Speed[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]How fast Run goes, in clock cycles per second ([code]cyc/s[/code]). An instruction takes several clock cycles (about 6 or 7 on average in the Level 1 examples), so the starting speed of 8 cyc/s runs about one instruction a second. [b]Max[/b] runs as fast as possible.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#e5c07b][code]Simulator[/code][/color] menu[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Switch to [b]Pico (USB serial)[/b] to run on a real board: see [url=hardware][color=#61afef][u]Running on a real Pico[/u][/color][/url].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Status text[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]How many instructions have run and clock cycles, and why the program stopped: [b]halted[/b] (finished), [b]waiting for input[/b] (type a key in the console) or [b]stopped by a CPU fault[/b] (read the console).[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#e5c07b][code]−[/code][/color] [color=#e5c07b][code]100%[/code][/color] [color=#e5c07b][code]+[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Zoom the whole window. Click the percentage to fit it to the window again.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#e5c07b][code]Show CPU Diagram[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Show the CPU diagram on the right. See [url=diagram][color=#61afef][u]Datapath diagram[/u][/color][/url].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#e5c07b][code]View[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The colour scheme: [b]System[/b] (follows your computer's light or dark setting), [b]Blue[/b], [b]Dark[/b] or [b]Light[/b]; and [b]Show the tour again[/b].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#e5c07b][code]Level[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]How much of picosim to show (you are on 3 · Inside the CPU). See [url=start][color=#61afef][u]Start here[/u][/color][/url].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#e5c07b][code]Guide[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]This guide ([color=#e5c07b][code]F1[/code][/color]). [color=#e5c07b][code]Esc[/code][/color] closes it.[/cell][/table]

Buttons that cannot be used right now are greyed out: for example Step and Run after the program has halted, until you press [color=#e5c07b][code]Reload[/code][/color].

[color=#61afef][b]The tour[/b][/color]
The first time you load a program, a short tour points out Step, Explain this step, the Registers, the Disassembly, the console and this guide, one at a time. [color=#e5c07b][code]Next ▶[/code][/color] moves on and [color=#e5c07b][code]Skip tour[/code][/color] (or [color=#e5c07b][code]Esc[/code][/color]) ends it. To see it again, choose [color=#e5c07b][code]View[/code][/color] ▸ [b]Show the tour again[/b].
3.name: The screen at a glance
3.sum:
Across the top is the toolbar: [color=#e5c07b][code]Open…[/code][/color] and [color=#e5c07b][code]Examples[/code][/color] load a program, [color=#e5c07b][code]Reload[/code][/color] starts it over, [color=#e5c07b][code]◀ Step back[/code][/color], [color=#e5c07b][code]Step instruction[/code][/color] and [color=#e5c07b][code]Run[/code][/color] move through it, and [color=#e5c07b][code]Speed[/code][/color] sets how fast Run goes. Below it, the [b]Registers[/b] (top left) show the numbers the CPU is working on, the [b]Disassembly[/b] under them lists your program with ▶ on the next instruction, [b]Explain this step[/b] (top right) describes each step, and the [b]serial console[/b] (bottom right) shows what the program prints; the [b]Pico board[/b] (bottom left) shows the chip's pins and the [b]Memory[/b] tab shows the bytes in memory; [color=#e5c07b][code]Show CPU Diagram[/code][/color] adds a drawing of the processor's insides.

Hover any button for a reminder of what it does. A greyed-out button cannot be used right now: for example Step after the program has finished, until you press [color=#e5c07b][code]Reload[/code][/color]. [color=#e5c07b][code]View[/code][/color] ▸ [b]Show the tour again[/b] replays the short first-run tour.

3.full:
[font_size=26][b]How a program runs[/b][/font_size]

Every program runs the same way: a small [b]built-in OS[/b] starts it, it runs one instruction at a time, it calls the OS to print, and it ends by returning to the OS. Here is the [b]Say hello[/b] example with every instruction the CPU runs, the OS's included, exactly as [color=#e5c07b][code]Step instruction[/code][/color] shows it from Level 2. Open it from [color=#e5c07b][code]Examples[/code][/color] and step along.

[table=4][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Step[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Address[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Instruction[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]What happens[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]1[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0000[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]ldr r0, [lb]pc, #8][/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]OS: R0 = [code]0x00002FFC[/code], the address where picosim stored the address of your [code]main[/code].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]2[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0002[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]ldr r0, [lb]r0][/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]OS: R0 = [code]0x00003001[/code], the address of [code]main[/code] ([code]3000[/code]). The extra 1 means "Thumb code"; every Pico code address has it.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]3[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0004[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]blx r0[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]OS: calls [code]main[/code]. LR = [code]0x00000007[/code] (where to come back to), PC = [code]0x00003000[/code].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]4[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]3000[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]push {r7, lr}[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Your program starts. Saves R7 and LR on the stack, so SP goes down by 8 to [code]0x0000FFF8[/code].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]5[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]3002[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]movs r0, #'H'[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]R0 = [code]0x00000048[/code], the character H. The Z flag is cleared.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]6[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]3004[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]bl putchar[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Calls the OS's putchar: LR = [code]0x00003009[/code] (the next line, plus 1), PC = [code]0x00000010[/code].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]7[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0010[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]svc #2[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]OS: a [i]supervisor call[/i] asks picosim to print the character in R0. [b]H[/b] appears in the console.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]8[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0012[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]bx lr[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]OS: returns to the address in LR, the line after the [code]bl[/code] ([code]3008[/code]).[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]9–20[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The same three steps print [code]i[/code], [code]![/code] and a new line.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]21[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]301A[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]movs r0, #0[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]R0 = 0, which means "finished without errors". The result is zero, so the Z flag turns on.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]22[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]301C[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]pop {r7, pc}[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Takes R7 and the saved LR back off the stack, putting the LR value into PC: this returns to the OS. SP is back to [code]0x00010000[/code].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]23[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0006[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]bkpt #0[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]OS: [i]breakpoint[/i] instruction. The simulator stops and the status text says [color=#f2cc60][b]halted[/b][/color].[/cell][/table]

[table=1][cell bg=#2a2a2a border=#61afef padding=14,9,14,9 expand=1][color=#61afef][b]Step over[/b][/color]   Steps 1–3 and the [code]svc[/code] / [code]bx lr[/code] after every [code]bl putchar[/code] are the OS, not your file. On a [code]bl[/code] line, [color=#e5c07b][code]Step over[/code][/color] ([color=#e5c07b][code]O[/code][/color]) runs the whole call and stops on the line after it, so you can skip what you do not want to watch.[/cell][/table]

[color=#61afef][b]Step, Run and breakpoints[/b][/color]
[ul]​[color=#e5c07b][code]Step instruction[/code][/color] ([color=#e5c07b][code]S[/code][/color]) runs exactly one instruction, the OS's too; [color=#e5c07b][code]Step over[/code][/color] ([color=#e5c07b][code]O[/code][/color]) runs a whole [code]bl[/code] call.
​[color=#e5c07b][code]Run[/code][/color] ([color=#e5c07b][code]Space[/code][/color]) keeps going at the [url=tour][color=#61afef][u]Speed[/u][/color][/url] you chose, until the program halts, reaches a breakpoint, or you press [color=#e5c07b][code]Pause[/code][/color]. If the program is waiting for a key ([code]getchar[/code]), Run waits too and carries on once you type one in the console.
A [b]breakpoint[/b] (click the first column of a Disassembly row) makes Run stop just before that instruction. Then you can Step from there.
​[color=#e5c07b][code]◀ Step back[/code][/color] ([color=#e5c07b][code]B[/code][/color]) undoes the last step, so you can go back and watch a line again. Everything goes back with it, the console's text too. A key you typed for [code]getchar[/code] is handed to the program again when it gets there.
You can mix them: Run to a breakpoint, Step a few lines, Run again.[/ul]

[color=#61afef][b]Starting again[/b][/color]
When the program has halted, Step and Run are greyed out. [color=#e5c07b][code]Reload[/code][/color] reads the file again and starts it from the beginning, with every register and flag reset. When you save your file, picosim reloads it by itself. The console keeps what was printed before, under a grey [code][lb]loaded …][/code] line that marks the new start; [color=#e5c07b][code]Clear[/code][/color] empties it.

[color=#61afef][b]Where the numbers come from[/b][/color]
The addresses are always the same: the OS is at [code]0000[/code]–[code]2FFF[/code] and your program starts at [code]3000[/code]. The stack is at the top of memory, just below [code]0x00010000[/code]. See [url=programs][color=#61afef][u]Memory map[/u][/color][/url].
3.name: How a program runs
3.sum:
Every program runs the same way: picosim's small [b]built-in OS[/b] calls your [code]main[/code], the CPU runs one instruction at a time from top to bottom (unless a branch jumps somewhere else), the program calls functions such as [code]putchar[/code] to print, and [code]main[/code] ends with [code]pop {…, pc}[/code], which returns to the OS. The OS then stops the processor and the status text says [b]halted[/b]. From Level 2 you also step through the OS's instructions: three at the start and two inside each putchar; [color=#e5c07b][code]Step over[/code][/color] ([color=#e5c07b][code]O[/code][/color]) runs a whole call in one step.

[color=#e5c07b][code]Step instruction[/code][/color] runs one instruction. [color=#e5c07b][code]Run[/code][/color] keeps going until the program ends, reaches a [b]breakpoint[/b] (click a row's first column in the Disassembly) or you press [color=#e5c07b][code]Pause[/code][/color]. [color=#e5c07b][code]◀ Step back[/code][/color] undoes a step, and [color=#e5c07b][code]Reload[/code][/color] starts again. The full details walk through Say hello line by line, with the real values.

3.full:
[font_size=26][b]Writing programs[/b][/font_size]

A program is a plain text file whose name ends in [code].s[/code], written in ARM [b]Thumb[/b] assembly language for the GNU assembler. Here is a complete one:

[table=1][cell bg=#0e0e0e border=#474747 padding=14,10,14,10 expand=1][code]        .syntax unified
        .cpu cortex-m0plus
        .thumb

main:
        push    {r7, lr}        @ save the return address
        movs    r0, #'H'        @ R0 = the letter H
        bl      putchar         @ print the letter in R0
        movs    r0, #0
        pop     {r7, pc}        @ return: the program halts[/code][/cell][/table]

[color=#61afef][b]The parts of a program[/b][/color]
[table=3][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Part[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Example[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]What it is[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Directive[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code].thumb[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]An order to the assembler, not an instruction for the CPU. Start every program with the same three lines shown above: they choose the Pico's instruction set.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Label[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]main:[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]A name for the address of the next instruction, written at the start of a line and ending in a colon. Branches and calls jump to labels.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Instruction[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]movs r0, #'H'[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]One step for the CPU: the [b]mnemonic[/b] ([code]movs[/code]) says what to do, the [b]operands[/b] ([code]r0[/code], [code]#'H'[/code]) say what to do it to. One per line.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Immediate[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]#72[/code][/color]  [color=#56b6c2][code]#0x48[/code][/color]  [color=#56b6c2][code]#'H'[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]A constant written into the instruction, after a #. Decimal, hex and a character in quotes all mean the same number here.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Comment[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]@ print it[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Everything after @ is ignored by the assembler. Use comments to explain your code.[/cell][/table]

Indentation and capital letters do not matter ([code]MOVS R0, #5[/code] is fine), but commas between operands do. [url=instructions][color=#61afef][u]Instructions[/u][/color][/url] lists what each instruction does.

[color=#61afef][b]Edit and save[/b][/color]
picosim runs your file but does not edit it. Use any plain-text code editor (VS Code, for example).
[ol type=1]Start from an example: open it from the [code]examples[/code] folder in your editor and use [i]Save As[/i] to save a copy in your own folder, with a name ending in [code].s[/code].
In picosim, click [color=#e5c07b][code]Open…[/code][/color] ([color=#e5c07b][code]Ctrl/Cmd+O[/code][/color]) and pick your file.
Change the file in your editor and save it. picosim notices and loads it again by itself, from the beginning (the console says [code][lb]… changed on disk: reloading][/code]). [color=#e5c07b][code]Reload[/code][/color] ([color=#e5c07b][code]Ctrl/Cmd+R[/code][/color]) does the same by hand.[/ol]
If the assembler finds a mistake, a [b]Could not load program[/b] box lists each one: the line number, that line of your file, what is wrong and what usually causes it. Fix the line and save; picosim tries again as soon as you save. [url=trouble][color=#61afef][u]Troubleshooting[/u][/color][/url] explains the common messages.

[color=#61afef][b]Entry point and ending[/b][/color]
Execution starts at [code]main:[/code] (the label [code]asm_main:[/code] also works, and is what the Pico build uses). The built-in OS calls [code]main[/code] like a function, so it should begin with [code]push {…, lr}[/code] and end with [code]pop {…, pc}[/code]. When it returns, the OS runs [code]BKPT[/code] and the simulator halts. Press [color=#e5c07b][code]Reload[/code][/color] to run it again. See [url=running][color=#61afef][u]How a program runs[/u][/color][/url].

[color=#61afef][b]Input and output[/b][/color]
[ul]​[code]bl putchar[/code] — prints the character in [code]r0[/code] to the [url=serial][color=#61afef][u]serial console[/u][/color][/url].
​[code]bl getchar[/code] — waits for one key typed in the console and returns it in [code]r0[/code].[/ul]
They behave the same on a real Pico, so the same file runs on both. Both may change R0–R3, so keep values you need afterwards in R4–R7 (and add those registers to [code]push[/code] and [code]pop[/code], as the [url=examples][color=#61afef][u]Count with a loop[/u][/color][/url] example does).

[color=#61afef][b]Settings[/b][/color]
Some programs have settings, such as which pin an LED is on. When a program has them, [color=#e5c07b][code]⚙ Settings[/code][/color] appears next to [color=#e5c07b][code]Reload[/code][/color]: pick your values and click [color=#e5c07b][code]Apply and reload[/code][/color]. picosim remembers them for you and uses them when it runs or flashes the program; the file itself is not changed (a • on the button means you changed something). Not sure what your circuit uses? Open the [b]Buttons and LEDs[/b] example and set its FIND_PINS setting to [i]find my pins[/i].
To give your own program settings, end an [code].equ[/code] line with a comment that starts with [code]<-[/code], for example [code].equ LED_PIN, 15  @ <- the GPIO number of your LED[/code]. A comment like [code]@ <- 1: wired to GND; 0: wired to 3V3[/code] becomes a menu.

[color=#61afef][b]Memory map[/b][/color]
[ul]​[code]0x0000–0x2FFF[/code] — the built-in OS
​[code]0x3000–0xFFFF[/code] — your code and data; the stack starts at the top of RAM ([code]SP = 0x00010000[/code]) and grows down
​[code]0x10000[/code] and up — memory-mapped I/O. The GPIO registers of the RP2040 are here: SIO at [code]0xD0000000[/code], IO_BANK0 at [code]0x40014000[/code], PADS_BANK0 at [code]0x4001C000[/code] (and RESETS at [code]0x4000C000[/code]). Writing them changes the [url=pico][color=#61afef][u]Pico board[/u][/color][/url]'s pins. A pin follows the SIO registers only after its IO_BANK0 CTRL register is set to function 5 (SIO), as on the real chip. Any other address stops the program with a bus fault.[/ul]

[color=#61afef][b]Like the real chip[/b][/color]
picosim runs only Cortex-M0+ (ARMv6-M) instructions and stops with an explanation wherever the Pico would crash (a HardFault): a word or halfword access to an address that is not a multiple of its size, a jump through a register to an address with bit 0 clear (mark such labels with [code].thumb_func[/code]), or an instruction the M0+ does not have. See [url=trouble][color=#61afef][u]Troubleshooting[/u][/color][/url].
3.name: Writing programs
3.sum:
A program is a plain text file whose name ends in [code].s[/code]. It starts with three lines ([code].syntax unified[/code], [code].cpu cortex-m0plus[/code], [code].thumb[/code]), then the label [code]main:[/code] and one instruction per line; anything after [code]@[/code] is a comment. [code]main[/code] begins with [code]push {r7, lr}[/code] and ends with [code]pop {r7, pc}[/code], and [code]bl putchar[/code] prints the character in R0.

Write and save the file in any text editor (VS Code, for example); picosim reloads it by itself when you save. [color=#e5c07b][code]Open…[/code][/color] ([color=#e5c07b][code]Ctrl/Cmd+O[/code][/color]) loads a file. If the assembler finds a mistake, a box lists each wrong line and what usually fixes it. The easiest start is a copy of an example.

3.full:
[font_size=26][b]Challenges[/b][/font_size]

Some examples end their opening comment with a [b]challenge[/b]: a small change to make, which picosim checks for you. The task is shown in a strip under the toolbar. When the program finishes, the strip turns [color=#98c379]green[/color] if you did it. If not, it lists each check: what was wanted and what your program did instead. Change your file, save it (picosim reloads it) and run it again. A stock example fails its own challenge, because you have not changed it yet.
Not every example has one: the LED and button programs never finish, so there is nothing to check at the end. [color=#e5c07b][code]About challenges[/code][/color] opens this page and [color=#e5c07b][code]✕[/code][/color] hides the strip until you load another program.

[color=#61afef][b]Writing your own (for teachers)[/b][/color]
Put the lines in the comment at the top of the file, before the first instruction:
[code]@ Challenge: Change the two numbers so it prints 9, and R3 is still 1.
@ Expect: output "9\n"
@ Expect: R3 = 1[/code]
[table=2][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Line[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]What it checks[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]@ Challenge: …[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The task the strip shows. Optional; without it, the strip lists the checks.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]@ Expect: output "…"[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Everything the program printed, from start to finish, must be exactly this text. Write it in quotes; [code]\n[/code] is a new line (what [code]movs r0, #10[/code] + [code]bl putchar[/code] prints).[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]@ Expect: R2 = 7[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The register's value when the program finishes. R0–R12, SP and LR; the value may be decimal, hex ([code]0x64[/code]), negative ([code]-1[/code]) or a character ([code]'H'[/code]).[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]@ Hint: …[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Your own hint for [url=ask][color=#61afef][u]Ask picosim[/u][/color][/url]. When a student asks for help with the challenge, it gives these first, one per request, in order, before its own hints. Optional.[/cell][/table]

Use as many Expect lines as you like; all must pass. Checks run only in the simulator, and not when the program stops with a CPU fault. A line picosim cannot read is reported in the console when the file loads, and the rest of the program still runs.
3.name: Challenges
3.sum: Some examples set a [b]challenge[/b]: a small change for you to make, shown in a strip under the toolbar. Change the file, save it and run the program to the end: the strip turns [color=#98c379]green[/color] if your program did it, or lists what is still wrong. Teachers can add their own with [code]@ Challenge:[/code] and [code]@ Expect:[/code] comment lines (see the details).

3.full:
[font_size=26][b]Hex, binary and ASCII[/b][/font_size]

Inside the computer every value is a pattern of bits (0s and 1s). A register holds 32 of them. picosim shows them in [b]hexadecimal[/b] (hex), base 16, because each hex digit stands for exactly 4 bits, so 32 bits are always 8 hex digits.
