[color=#61afef][b]The 16 hex digits[/b][/color]

padding=10,5,16,5][b]F[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]15[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]1111[/code][/cell][/table]

[color=#61afef][b]Reading a hex number[/b][/color]
Hex numbers start with [code]0x[/code] so you can tell them apart from decimal. Each place is worth 16 times the one to its right (1, 16, 256, 4096, …):
[ul]​[code]0x48[/code] = 4 × 16 + 8 = [b]72[/b]
​[code]0x2A[/code] = 2 × 16 + 10 = [b]42[/b]
​[code]0x3000[/code] = 3 × 4096 = [b]12288[/b][/ul]
Leading zeros change nothing: the Registers panel's [code]0x00000048[/code] is just [code]0x48[/code]. And to turn hex into binary, write each digit as its 4 bits: [code]0x48[/code] = [code]0100 1000[/code].

[table=1][cell bg=#2a2a2a border=#61afef padding=14,9,14,9 expand=1][color=#61afef][b]Shortcut[/b][/color]   Hover any register to see its value in hex, decimal, signed decimal and binary at once, or switch the Registers panel's menu from [color=#e5c07b][code]Hex[/code][/color] to [color=#e5c07b][code]Decimal[/code][/color].[/cell][/table]

[color=#61afef][b]Negative numbers[/b][/color]
The same 32 bits can be read two ways. As [b]unsigned[/b], [code]0xFFFFFFFF[/code] is 4 294 967 295. As [b]signed[/b] (two's complement), every value from [code]0x80000000[/code] up is negative, and [code]0xFFFFFFFF[/code] is −1, [code]0xFFFFFFFE[/code] is −2, and so on. The top bit (bit 31) is 1 for a negative number; that is what the N flag reports. Choose [color=#e5c07b][code]Signed[/code][/color] in the Registers panel's menu to see registers this way.

[color=#61afef][b]Characters are numbers too (ASCII)[/b][/color]
A character is stored as its [b]ASCII code[/b]. [code]putchar[/code] prints the character whose code is in R0. The ones you will use most:

[table=3][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Characters[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Hex[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Decimal[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0[/code] [code]1[/code] … [code]9[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0x30[/code] – [code]0x39[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]48 – 57[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]A[/code] [code]B[/code] … [code]Z[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0x41[/code] – [code]0x5A[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]65 – 90[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]a[/code] [code]b[/code] … [code]z[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0x61[/code] – [code]0x7A[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]97 – 122[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]space[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0x20[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]32[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]![/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0x21[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]33[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]new line[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0x0A[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]10[/cell][/table]

In your program you can write the character in quotes and let the assembler look up its code: [code]movs r0, #'H'[/code] is the same as [code]movs r0, #0x48[/code] and [code]movs r0, #72[/code]. (The Disassembly always shows the hex.)

[color=#61afef][b]Printing a number[/b][/color]
To print the [i]number[/i] 7 you must print the [i]character[/i] '7', whose code is 7 + [code]0x30[/code] = [code]0x37[/code]. So add [code]'0'[/code] (that is, [code]0x30[/code]) before calling putchar:

[table=1][cell bg=#0e0e0e border=#474747 padding=14,10,14,10 expand=1][code]        movs    r0, #7
        adds    r0, #'0'        @ R0 = 0x37, the character '7'
        bl      putchar[/code][/cell][/table]

This works only for 0–9. For 10 it gives [code]0x3A[/code], which is the character [b]:[/b] — to print bigger numbers you must print one digit at a time.
3.name: Hex, binary and ASCII
3.sum:
The CPU stores everything as bits (0s and 1s), and picosim shows them in [b]hexadecimal[/b]: base 16, with the digits 0–9 and A–F and [code]0x[/code] in front. One hex digit is exactly 4 bits, so a 32-bit register is 8 hex digits. For example [code]0x2A[/code] = 2 × 16 + 10 = 42. Hover a register to see its value in decimal and binary too.

Characters are numbers as well ([b]ASCII[/b]): 'H' is 72 ([code]0x48[/code]) and the digits '0' to '9' are 48 to 57. That is why printing the number 7 needs the character '7': add [code]'0'[/code] (48) before calling putchar.

3.full:
[font_size=26][b]Instructions[/b][/font_size]

Every instruction in the Level 1 examples. In the forms, [b]Rd[/b] is the register that gets the result, [b]Rn[/b] and [b]Rm[/b] are registers it reads, and [b]#imm[/b] is a constant.

Write [code]movs[/code], [code]adds[/code] and [code]subs[/code] with the [b]S[/b] on the end (it means "set the flags").   2. Use registers [b]R0 to R7[/b]. Break either rule and the assembler says [i]cannot honor width suffix[/i].[/cell][/table]

The [b]Flags[/b] column lists the flags each instruction sets; the others keep their old values. [url=branches][color=#61afef][u]Flags and branches[/u][/color][/url] explains them.

[color=#61afef][b]Jumping[/b][/color]
[table=3][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Form[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Example[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]What it does[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]b label[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]b done[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Always jump to the label.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]b<cond> label[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]bne loop[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Jump only if a condition on the flags is true, otherwise go on to the next line. See [url=branches][color=#61afef][u]Flags and branches[/u][/color][/url].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]bl label[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]bl putchar[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Call a function: put the address of the next line in LR, then jump.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]bx lr[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]bx lr[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Jump to the address in LR: how a function returns.[/cell][/table]

[color=#61afef][b]Saving registers: push and pop[/b][/color]
[table=3][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Form[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Example[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]What it does[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]push {list}[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]push {r4, lr}[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Save the listed registers on the stack (SP goes down 4 bytes per register).[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]pop {list}[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]pop {r4, pc}[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Load them back (SP goes up again). Popping into PC jumps to the saved address.[/cell][/table]

Every example's [code]main[/code] begins with [code]push {r7, lr}[/code] (or [code]{r4, lr}[/code]) and ends with [code]pop {r7, pc}[/code]. The reason: [code]bl putchar[/code] overwrites LR, so the address [code]main[/code] must return to is saved first and popped straight into PC at the end.
Registers are pushed in pairs because the ARM rules for calling functions keep the stack in steps of 8 bytes; R7 is there just to make the pair. If you use R4–R7, put them in the list too, so your program leaves them as it found them.

[color=#61afef][b]Other instructions you may meet[/b][/color]
[table=2][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Form[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]What it does[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]ands Rd, Rm[/code][/color]  [color=#56b6c2][code]orrs Rd, Rm[/code][/color]  [color=#56b6c2][code]eors Rd, Rm[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Bitwise AND, OR and exclusive OR: Rd = Rd op Rm, bit by bit.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]lsls Rd, Rm, #n[/code][/color]  [color=#56b6c2][code]lsrs Rd, Rm, #n[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Shift Rm's bits left or right by n places into Rd (left by 1 doubles, right by 1 halves an unsigned number).[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]muls Rd, Rm, Rd[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Rd = Rm × Rd. The register that gets the result must also be the last one.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]mov Rd, Rm[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Copy without setting flags; this one also works with R8–R12.[/cell][/table]

Loads and stores ([code]ldr[/code], [code]str[/code]) are in the [b]Add up a list in memory[/b] example.
Mnemonics can be written in capitals or not. picosim runs only the instructions the Pico's Cortex-M0+ processor has; the ARMv6-M Architecture Reference Manual lists them all.
3.name: Instructions
3.sum:
Each line of a program is one [b]instruction[/b]: its name (the mnemonic, such as [code]movs[/code] or [code]adds[/code]) and what it works on (registers such as [code]r0[/code] and constants such as [code]#5[/code]). The Level 1 examples use [code]movs[/code] (put a value in a register), [code]adds[/code] and [code]subs[/code] (add and subtract), [code]cmp[/code] (compare), [code]b[/code] and the conditional branches (jump), [code]bl[/code] (call a function) and [code]push[/code] / [code]pop[/code] (save and restore registers).

Two rules avoid most mistakes: write [code]movs[/code], [code]adds[/code] and [code]subs[/code] with the [b]S[/b] on the end, and use registers [b]R0 to R7[/b]. A constant in [code]movs[/code], [code]cmp[/code] or two-register [code]adds[/code] / [code]subs[/code] must be 0 to 255; the three-register form ([code]adds r0, r1, #3[/code]) takes only 0 to 7.

3.full:
[font_size=26][b]Flags and branches[/b][/font_size]

A program decides what to do next in two steps: an instruction such as [code]cmp[/code] sets the [b]flags[/b], and then a conditional [b]branch[/b] reads them and either jumps or carries on.

[color=#61afef][b]The four flags[/b][/color]
[table=3][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Flag[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Name[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]It is 1 when the result…[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]N[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Negative[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]is negative: bit 31 of the result is 1.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]Z[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Zero[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]is zero. After [code]cmp a, b[/code] this means a = b.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]C[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Carry[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]carried out of bit 31 (adding), or did [i]not[/i] need to borrow (subtracting or [code]cmp[/code]). After [code]cmp a, b[/code], C = 1 means a ≥ b as unsigned numbers.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]V[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Overflow[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]was too big or too small to fit as a signed number, such as 0x7FFFFFFF + 1.[/cell][/table]

Instructions that end in [b]S[/b] ([code]movs[/code], [code]adds[/code], [code]subs[/code], …) and [code]cmp[/code] set the flags. Branches, [code]bl[/code], [code]push[/code] and [code]pop[/code] never change them, so a flag keeps its value until the next flag-setting instruction. The flags are the N Z C V boxes in the [url=registers][color=#61afef][u]Registers panel[/u][/color][/url].

[color=#61afef][b]What cmp does[/b][/color]
[code]cmp r4, #6[/code] works out R4 − 6, sets the flags from the answer, and throws the answer away. From the [b]Count with a loop[/b] example:

[table=6][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]R4[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]R4 − 6[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]N[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Z[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]C[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]bne loop[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]2[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]−4[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]1[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]0[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]0[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]jumps back (not equal)[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]5[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]−1[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]1[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]0[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]0[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]jumps back (not equal)[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]6[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]0[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]0[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#f2cc60][b]1[/b][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]1[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]goes on to the next line[/cell][/table]

[color=#61afef][b]Conditional branches[/b][/color]
Write the condition after [code]b[/code]. Each one reads like a question about the [code]cmp[/code] before it, [code]cmp a, b[/code]:

[table=4][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Branch[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Jumps if[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Use for[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Flags tested[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]beq[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]a = b[/cell][cell padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]bne[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]a ≠ b[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]any numbers[/cell][cell instruction[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]N = 1[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]bpl[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]result positive or zero[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]after any S instruction[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]N = 0[/cell][/table]

[b]Signed or unsigned?[/b] If your values can be negative, use the signed branches. For character codes, addresses and counts that never go below 0, either kind works while the numbers are small; the unsigned ones are the safe choice.

[color=#61afef][b]Pattern: a loop[/b][/color]
[table=1][cell bg=#0e0e0e border=#474747 padding=14,10,14,10 expand=1][code]        movs    r4, #0          @ i = 0
loop:
        @ ... the loop body: what to repeat ...
        adds    r4, #1          @ i = i + 1
        cmp     r4, #10
        blt     loop            @ i < 10? go round again[/code][/cell][/table]

The body runs 10 times, with R4 = 0, 1, … 9. Keep the counter in R4–R7: [code]putchar[/code] may change R0–R3.

[color=#61afef][b]Pattern: if / else[/b][/color]
[table=1][cell bg=#0e0e0e border=#474747 padding=14,10,14,10 expand=1][code]        cmp     r0, r1
        bgt     bigger          @ R0 > R1?
        movs    r2, r1          @ no:  R2 = R1
        b       done
bigger:
        movs    r2, r0          @ yes: R2 = R0
done:                           @ R2 = the larger of R0 and R1[/code][/cell][/table]

The [code]b done[/code] matters: without it the "no" path would run on into the "yes" path.

[table=1][cell bg=#2a2a2a border=#61afef padding=14,9,14,9 expand=1][color=#61afef][b]Watch it happen[/b][/color]   Set a breakpoint on a branch, press Run, and look at the flags each time it stops. Then press Step instruction once to see whether it jumped.[/cell][/table]
3.name: Flags and branches
3.sum:
A program makes decisions in two steps. First an instruction such as [code]cmp r4, #6[/code] compares two numbers and sets the four [b]flags[/b]: N (negative), Z (zero), C (carry) and V (overflow). Then a conditional branch such as [code]bne loop[/code] reads the flags and either jumps to the label or carries on with the next line.

[code]beq[/code] jumps if the numbers were equal and [code]bne[/code] if they were not; [code]blt[/code], [code]bgt[/code], [code]ble[/code] and [code]bge[/code] compare signed numbers, and [code]blo[/code], [code]bhi[/code], [code]bls[/code] and [code]bhs[/code] unsigned ones. A loop works this way: change a counter, compare it, and branch back while the loop is not finished.

3.full:
[font_size=26][b]Level 1 examples[/b][/font_size]

Open each one from [color=#e5c07b][code]Examples[/code][/color] and keep this page beside it. Every example file also starts with a short [i]What to watch[/i] comment. Remember that the first three steps, and the two steps after each [code]bl putchar[/code], are the [url=running][color=#61afef][u]built-in OS[/u][/color][/url] ([color=#e5c07b][code]Step over[/code][/color] skips them).

[font_size=21][b]1 · Say hello[/b][/font_size]   [color=#8c8c8c]01_hello.s · 23 instructions[/color]
Prints [code]Hi![/code] one letter at a time. Shows how [code]movs[/code] puts a character's code in R0 and how [code]bl putchar[/code] prints it.
[ul]Before each [code]bl putchar[/code], R0 holds the code: [code]0x48[/code] H, [code]0x69[/code] i, [code]0x21[/code] !, [code]0x0A[/code] new line.
Watch LR change on every [code]bl[/code] ([code]0x00003009[/code], [code]0x0000300F[/code], …): it is always the address of the next line, plus 1.
​[url=running][color=#61afef][u]How a program runs[/u][/color][/url] goes through this example line by line.[/ul]
[b]Try it:[/b] make it print your initials. Copy a [code]movs[/code] / [code]bl putchar[/code] pair for each letter, and use [code]#' '[/code] for a space.

[font_size=21][b]2 · Add two numbers[/b][/font_size]   [color=#8c8c8c]02_add.s · 20 instructions[/color]
Puts 3 and 4 in registers, adds and subtracts them, and prints the sum.
[ul]R0 = 3, R1 = 4, then [code]adds r2, r0, r1[/code] makes R2 = 7 and [code]subs r3, r1, r0[/code] makes R3 = 1.
The [code]subs[/code] turns the C flag on: 4 − 3 did not need to borrow.
​[code]adds r0, #'0'[/code] turns 7 into [code]0x37[/code], the character '7', which is printed. See [url=numbers][color=#61afef][u]Printing a number[/u][/color][/url].[/ul]
[b]Try it:[/b] change 3 and 4 in the file (keep the sum under 10), save and press [color=#e5c07b][code]Reload[/code][/color]. Or, without editing: when ▶ reaches [code]movs r0, r2[/code], click R2 in the Registers panel, type 5, press Enter, then Run. It prints 5.

[font_size=21][b]3 · Count with a loop[/b][/font_size]   [color=#8c8c8c]03_count_loop.s · 52 instructions[/color]
Prints [b]12345[/b] with a loop: the same five lines run once for each digit.
[ul]R4 is the counter. It is kept in R4, not R0–R3, because putchar may change those; that is why [code]main[/code] pushes R4.
In the Disassembly, the row labelled [code]loop[/code] is where [code]bne loop[/code] jumps back to; it shows as [code]bne #0x3004[/code].
After [code]cmp r4, #6[/code]: while R4 is less than 6, N = 1 and Z = 0, so [code]bne[/code] jumps back. When R4 reaches 6, Z = 1 and the loop ends. The table in [url=branches][color=#61afef][u]Flags and branches[/u][/color][/url] shows the values.[/ul]
[b]Try it:[/b] put a breakpoint on the [code]bne[/code] row and press Run several times to see the flags on each pass. Then make it count to 9 (change [code]#6[/code] to [code]#10[/code]).

[url=examples2][color=#61afef][u]Level 2 examples[/u][/color][/url] covers the rest: memory ([code]ldr[/code] / [code]str[/code]), an LED, typing, functions and buttons.
3.name: Level 1 examples
3.sum:
Three examples for Level 1, opened from [color=#e5c07b][code]Examples[/code][/color]: [b]Say hello[/b] prints [code]Hi![/code] one letter at a time ([code]movs[/code] and [code]bl putchar[/code]), [b]Add two numbers[/b] adds 3 and 4 and prints 7, and [b]Count with a loop[/b] prints [code]12345[/code] with a loop ([code]cmp[/code] and [code]bne[/code]). Each file starts with a comment that says what to watch.

Step through each one with [url=explain][color=#61afef][u]Explain this step[/u][/color][/url] open, then try the change suggested in its [b]Try it[/b] line or its challenge.

3.full:
[font_size=26][b]Memory and addresses[/b][/font_size]

The CPU has only 16 registers. Everything else — your program's instructions, its data, the stack — lives in [b]memory[/b]. Memory is one long row of bytes, and each byte has a number, its [b]address[/b], like a house number on a very long street.

[color=#61afef][b]Bytes, halfwords and words[/b][/color]
[table=5][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Size[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Bytes[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Bits[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Holds (unsigned)[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Load / store with[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]byte[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]1[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]8[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]0 to 255[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]ldrb[/code][/color] [color=#56b6c2][code]strb[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]halfword[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]2[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]16[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]0 to 65 535[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]ldrh[/code][/color] [color=#56b6c2][code]strh[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]word[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]4[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]32[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]0 to 4 294 967 295[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]ldr[/code][/color] [color=#56b6c2][code]str[/code][/color][/cell][/table]

A register holds exactly one word. Most Thumb instructions are one halfword (2 bytes) long, which is why the PC usually moves on by 2.

[color=#61afef][b]Little-endian: the low byte comes first[/b][/color]
A word takes 4 bytes in a row. The RP2040 stores the [i]lowest[/i] byte at the [i]lowest[/i] address; this is called [b]little-endian[/b]. In the [b]Call a function[/b] example, the word [code]0x0000300D[/code] pushed onto the stack at [code]0xFFF4[/code] sits in memory like this:

[table=5][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Address[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]FFF4[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]FFF5[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]FFF6[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]FFF7[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Byte[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0D[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]30[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]00[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]00[/code][/cell][/table]

So in the Memory tab's hex dump you read a word's bytes [i]backwards[/i]: [code]0D 30 00 00[/code] is the word [code]0x0000300D[/code]. The Stack view under the dump puts the bytes back together for you.

[color=#61afef][b]Alignment[/b][/color]
A word must start at an address that is a multiple of 4 (in hex, ending in 0, 4, 8 or C), and a halfword at a multiple of 2. The Cortex-M0+ cannot load a word from [code]0x3002[/code]: picosim stops with an [b]Unaligned access[/b] CPU fault there, as a real Pico would. Bytes can be anywhere. Put [code].align 2[/code] before [code].word[/code] data that comes after bytes or strings.

[color=#61afef][b]picosim's memory map[/b][/color]
[table=2][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Addresses[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]What is there[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0x0000[/code] – [code]0x2FFF[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The built-in OS: [code]_start[/code], [code]putchar[/code], [code]getchar[/code].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0x3000[/code] upward[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Your program: first its instructions (and their literal pools), then its [code].data[/code], in the order they are in your file.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]… up to [code]0xFFFF[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Free RAM. The stack starts at the top and grows [i]down[/i] towards your program.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0x00010000[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]SP's starting value: just past the end of RAM. The first [code]push[/code] stores below it.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0x4000C000[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]RESETS (see [url=gpio][color=#61afef][u]GPIO[/u][/color][/url]).[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0x40014000[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]IO_BANK0: which part of the chip controls each pin.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0x4001C000[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]PADS_BANK0: each pin's pull-up and pull-down resistors.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0xD0000000[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]SIO: set, clear and read the pins.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]anything else[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Nothing: reading or writing it stops the program with a [b]bus fault[/b].[/cell][/table]

[table=1][cell bg=#2a2a2a border=#61afef padding=14,9,14,9 expand=1][color=#61afef][b]Real chip[/b][/color]   RAM here is 64 KB ([code]0x10000[/code] bytes) and starts at 0. The real RP2040 has 264 KB of RAM at [code]0x20000000[/code] and runs your program from flash at [code]0x10000000[/code]. So never type a fixed RAM address into a program: use labels, and the same file works in both places. The I/O addresses are the real chip's.[/cell][/table]

[color=#61afef][b]Seeing it[/b][/color]
Open the [url=memory][color=#61afef][u]Memory tab[/u][/color][/url] next to Disassembly, type a label such as [code]numbers[/code] (or an address such as [code]0x3000[/code]) in [b]Go to[/b] and press [color=#e5c07b][code]Enter[/code][/color]. Its map shows the table above as a picture, with PC and SP marked; bytes the last step read are outlined in [color=#61afef]blue[/color] and bytes it wrote in [color=#f2cc60]yellow[/color].
3.name: Memory and addresses
3.sum:
Memory is one long row of bytes, and each byte has a number called its [b]address[/b]. A [b]word[/b] is 4 bytes (what one register holds) and a halfword 2. picosim keeps its built-in OS at [code]0x0000[/code]–[code]0x2FFF[/code], your program from [code]0x3000[/code] upward and the stack at the top, just below [code]0x10000[/code]; the Pico's hardware (its pins) is at high addresses such as [code]0xD0000000[/code].

A word is stored lowest byte first ([b]little-endian[/b]), so [code]0x0000300D[/code] appears in memory as [code]0D 30 00 00[/code]. A word must start at an address that is a multiple of 4, and a halfword at a multiple of 2; otherwise the program stops with a fault, as on a real Pico.

3.full:
[font_size=26][b]Loads and stores[/b][/font_size]

The ALU only works on registers. To use a number that is in memory, the program must [b]load[/b] it into a register, work on it there, and [b]store[/b] the result back. ARM processors are built this way, which is why they are called [i]load/store[/i] machines.

[color=#61afef][b]The forms[/b][/color]
[table=3][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Form[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Example[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]What it does[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]ldr Rd, [lb]Rn][/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]ldr r0, [lb]r1][/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]R0 = the word in memory at the address in R1.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]ldr Rd, [lb]Rn, #imm][/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]ldr r0, [lb]r1, #4][/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]R0 = the word at R1 + 4. imm is 0 to 124, a multiple of 4.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]ldr Rd, [lb]Rn, Rm][/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]ldr r0, [lb]r1, r2][/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]R0 = the word at R1 + R2.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]str Rd, [lb]Rn, #imm][/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]str r2, [lb]r1][/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The word at R1 (+ imm) = R2. The same three forms as ldr.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]ldrb[/code][/color] / [color=#56b6c2][code]strb[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]ldrb r0, [lb]r4][/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]One byte. ldrb fills the other 24 bits of the register with 0. imm is 0 to 31.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]ldrh[/code][/color] / [color=#56b6c2][code]strh[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]ldrh r0, [lb]r1, #2][/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]One halfword. imm is 0 to 62, even.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]ldr Rd, [lb]sp, #imm][/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]ldr r0, [lb]sp, #4][/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]A word on the stack. imm is 0 to 1020, a multiple of 4.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]ldr Rd, =value[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]ldr r1, =numbers[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]R1 = any 32-bit number, or the address of a label (below).[/cell][/table]

[table=1][cell bg=#2a2a2a border=#61afef padding=14,9,14,9 expand=1][color=#61afef][b]Brackets[/b][/color]   Square brackets mean [i]the memory at this address[/i]. [code]r1[/code] is the number in R1; [code][lb]r1][/code] is whatever is stored at the address R1 holds. The register in brackets is a [b]pointer[/b]: it points at the data.[/cell][/table]

As with arithmetic, use R0–R7: [code]ldr r8, [lb]r1][/code] gives [i]cannot honor width suffix[/i]. An offset that is too big, not a multiple of the size, or negative gives [i]invalid offset, value too big[/i].

[color=#61afef][b]Getting an address: ldr Rd, =label[/b][/color]
[code]movs[/code] can only make 0 to 255, but addresses such as [code]0x3024[/code] and I/O addresses such as [code]0xD0000024[/code] are much bigger. [code]ldr r1, =numbers[/code] asks the assembler to store the number in memory just after your code, in a [b]literal pool[/b], and to load it from there:
[ul]In the Disassembly it shows as [code]ldr r1, [lb]pc, #0x18][/code]: "the word 0x18 bytes on from here".
After your last instruction you will see rows such as [code].word 0x00003024[/code]. Those are the pool: data, not instructions. The CPU never runs them, because the program's last instruction (a [code]pop[/code] or [code]b[/code]) jumps away first.[/ul]
A pool must be within about 1 KB [i]after[/i] the ldr that uses it. In a long program the assembler says [i]invalid offset, value too big[/i] on the ldr line; put [code].ltorg[/code] on a line the CPU never reaches (just after a [code]b[/code] or [code]pop {…, pc}[/code]) and the assembler places a pool there.

[color=#61afef][b]Putting data in your program[/b][/color]
[table=3][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Directive[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Example[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]What it makes[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code].data[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code].data[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Everything after it is data, placed after your code. These lines are not listed in the Disassembly: look at them in the Memory tab.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code].word[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]numbers: .word 10, 20, 30, 40[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Words (4 bytes each). The label is the address of the first one.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code].hword[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code].hword 500[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Halfwords (2 bytes).[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code].byte[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code].byte 1, 2, 3[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Single bytes.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code].asciz[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]msg: .asciz "Hi\n"[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The string's characters, then a 0 byte that marks its end.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code].ascii[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code].ascii "Hi"[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The characters only, with no 0 at the end.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code].align 2[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code].align 2[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Skip ahead to the next multiple of 4, so a .word after bytes or strings is aligned.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code].equ[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code].equ COUNT, 4[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]A name for a number. It takes no memory: the assembler swaps the name for the number everywhere.[/cell][/table]

Data you put after your code [i]without[/i] [code].data[/code] (as the Buttons and LEDs example does with its messages) is listed in the Disassembly as [code].word[/code] and [code].ascii[/code] rows.

[color=#61afef][b]Example: adding up a list[/b][/color]
From the [b]Add up a list in memory[/b] example:

[table=1][cell bg=#0e0e0e border=#474747 padding=14,10,14,10 expand=1][code]        ldr     r1, =numbers    @ R1 = the address of the first number
        movs    r2, #0          @ R2 = running total
        movs    r3, #4          @ R3 = how many numbers are left
loop:
        ldr     r0, [lb]r1]        @ R0 = the number at address R1
        adds    r2, r2, r0      @ add it to the total
        adds    r1, #4          @ the next word is 4 bytes further on
        subs    r3, #1          @ one fewer left (sets Z when it reaches 0)
        bne     loop

        ldr     r1, =total      @ R1 = the address of "total"
        str     r2, [lb]r1]        @ store the total in memory[/code][/cell][/table]

What each pass loads and adds up:

[table=5][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Pass[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]R1 (pointer)[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]R0 = [lb]r1][/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]R2 (total)[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]R3 (left)[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]1[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0x3024[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]10 ([code]0x0A[/code])[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]10 ([code]0x0A[/code])[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]3[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]2[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0x3028[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]20 ([code]0x14[/code])[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]30 ([code]0x1E[/code])[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]2[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]3[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0x302C[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]30 ([code]0x1E[/code])[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]60 ([code]0x3C[/code])[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]1[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]4[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0x3030[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]40 ([code]0x28[/code])[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]100 ([code]0x64[/code])[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]0, so Z = 1 and the loop ends[/cell][/table]

R1 is shown at the moment of the load; [code]adds r1, #4[/code] then moves it on by one word. Finally [code]ldr r1, =total[/code] makes R1 = [code]0x3034[/code] and [code]str r2, [lb]r1][/code] writes the bytes [code]64 00 00 00[/code] there.

[color=#61afef][b]Arrays: element number n[/b][/color]
Element [i]n[/i] of a word array (counting from 0) is at [i]start + 4 × n[/i]. Multiplying by 4 is a shift left by 2:

[table=1][cell bg=#0e0e0e border=#474747 padding=14,10,14,10 expand=1][code]        ldr     r1, =numbers    @ R1 = the address of element 0
        movs    r3, #2          @ n = 2
        lsls    r2, r3, #2      @ R2 = n × 4 = 8
        ldr     r0, [lb]r1, r2]    @ R0 = element 2 = 30[/code][/cell][/table]

For a byte array the step is 1, so no shift is needed: [code]ldrb r0, [lb]r1, r3][/code].

[color=#61afef][b]Strings[/b][/color]
A string is a row of character bytes that ends with a 0 byte ([code].asciz[/code] adds it). To print one, load each byte with [code]ldrb[/code] until you reach the 0:

[table=1][cell bg=#0e0e0e border=#474747 padding=14,10,14,10 expand=1][code]print:                          @ prints the string whose address is in R0
        push    {r4, lr}
        movs    r4, r0          @ R4 = the address of the next character
1:      ldrb    r0, [lb]r4]        @ R0 = that character
        cmp     r0, #0
        beq     2f              @ the 0 byte: the end of the string
        bl      putchar
        adds    r4, #1          @ the next character is 1 byte on
        b       1b
2:      pop     {r4, pc}[/code][/cell][/table]

[code]1:[/code] and [code]2:[/code] are [b]local labels[/b]: [code]1b[/code] means "the nearest 1: [b]b[/b]ack" and [code]2f[/code] "the nearest 2: [b]f[/b]orward", so you can reuse the same numbers in every function. Call it with [code]ldr r0, =msg[/code] and [code]bl print[/code].
3.name: Loads and stores
3.sum:
The ALU works only on registers, so a value in memory must be [b]loaded[/b] into a register ([code]ldr[/code]), worked on, and [b]stored[/b] back ([code]str[/code]). The address goes in square brackets: [code]ldr r0, [lb]r1][/code] means "R0 = the word at the address in R1". [code]ldrb[/code] / [code]strb[/code] move one byte and [code]ldrh[/code] / [code]strh[/code] a halfword.

To put an address, or any number bigger than 255, into a register, write [code]ldr r1, =label[/code]: the assembler stores the number just after your code and loads it from there. Data such as [code]numbers: .word 10, 20[/code] goes after a [code].data[/code] line.

3.full:
[font_size=26][b]The stack and functions[/b][/font_size]

A [b]function[/b] is a piece of code you can call from anywhere and that comes back when it is done. [code]bl name[/code] calls it: it puts the return address (the line after the [code]bl[/code], plus 1) in [b]LR[/b] and jumps. The function ends with [code]bx lr[/code], which jumps back to the address in LR.

[color=#61afef][b]The problem: there is only one LR[/b][/color]
If a function calls another function — even [code]putchar[/code] — that second [code]bl[/code] overwrites LR, and the first function no longer knows where to return. So a function that calls anything must save LR first, and the place to save it is the [b]stack[/b].

[table=1][cell bg=#2a2a2a border=#f2cc60 padding=14,9,14,9 expand=1][color=#f2cc60][b]If you forget[/b][/color]   A function that calls putchar and then ends with [code]bx lr[/code] without saving LR jumps back into itself, to its own [code]bx lr[/code], forever. The program never halts. In picosim you see ▶ stuck on that one row while Run keeps going.[/cell][/table]

[color=#61afef][b]The stack[/b][/color]
The stack is the top part of RAM, used like a pile of plates: the last thing put on is the first taken off. [b]SP[/b] (the stack pointer) holds the address of the item on top. The stack grows [i]down[/i]: SP starts at [code]0x00010000[/code], just past the end of RAM.
[ul]​[code]push {r4, lr}[/code] moves SP down by 4 bytes per register (8 here), then stores the registers there, the lowest-numbered register at the lowest address.
​[code]pop {r4, pc}[/code] loads them back in the same order and moves SP up again. Popping into PC is a jump: it returns, using the LR value that was pushed.[/ul]

[color=#61afef][b]Watch it: the Call a function example[/b][/color]
These are the real values from stepping [b]Call a function[/b] with [color=#e5c07b][code]Step instruction[/code][/color] (the step numbers count from the first OS instruction):

[table=5][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Step[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Instruction[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]SP after[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]LR after[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]What happens[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]4[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]push {r7, lr}[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0xFFF8[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0x00000007[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1][code]main[/code] saves R7 and its own return address (into the OS).[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]6[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]bl twice[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0xFFF8[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0x00003009[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Call: LR = the address of the next line ([code]3008[/code]) + 1.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]8[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]bx lr[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0xFFF8[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0x00003009[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1][code]twice[/code] returns. It calls nothing, so it never touched the stack.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]9[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]bl print_digit[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0xFFF8[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0x0000300D[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Call the second function.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]10[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]push {lr}[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0xFFF4[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0x0000300D[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1][code]print_digit[/code] saves its return address, because it is about to call putchar.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]12[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]bl putchar[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0xFFF4[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0x0000302D[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]LR is overwritten, but the saved copy is safe on the stack.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]15[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]pop {pc}[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0xFFF8[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0x0000302D[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]PC = the saved [code]0x300D[/code] with bit 0 cleared, [code]0x300C[/code]: back in main.[/cell][/table]

The stack at step 12 (Memory tab → Stack, or Go to [color=#e5c07b][code]SP[/code][/color]):

[table=3][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Address[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Holds[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Put there by[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0xFFF4[/code]  ← SP[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0x0000300D[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]print_digit: its return address (into main)[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0xFFF8[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0x00000000[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]main: R7[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0xFFFC[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0x00000007[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]main: its return address (into the OS)[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0x10000[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]the end of RAM: where SP started[/cell][/table]

[color=#61afef][b]The rules every function follows[/b][/color]
So that functions written by different people work together, ARM sets rules for the registers (the [b]calling convention[/b]). Simplified:

[table=2][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Registers[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Rule[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]R0–R3[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Arguments go in here, the first in R0. The result comes back in R0. A function may change all four, so do not expect them to survive a [code]bl[/code].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]R4–R7[/b] (and R8–R11)[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]A function that uses them must leave them as it found them: push them at the start, pop them at the end.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]LR[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Changed by every [code]bl[/code]. Push it if your function calls another function.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]SP[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Must be back where it started when the function returns: every push needs a matching pop.[/cell][/table]

putchar and getchar follow these rules, which is why the examples keep their counters in R4. The rules also ask that the stack moves in steps of 8 bytes whenever a library function such as putchar is called on the real Pico; that is why [code]main[/code] pushes a [i]pair[/i] of registers. A small function of your own (like print_digit) can push just [code]{lr}[/code].

[color=#61afef][b]A template[/b][/color]
[table=1][cell bg=#0e0e0e border=#474747 padding=14,10,14,10 expand=1][code]my_function:                    @ takes a number in R0, returns one in R0
        push    {r4, lr}        @ save R4 (we use it) and the return address
        @ ... the work: R4 is ours to use here ...
        pop     {r4, pc}        @ put R4 back and return[/code][/cell][/table]

A function that calls nothing and uses only R0–R3 (a [b]leaf[/b] function, like [code]twice[/code]) needs no push at all: it ends with [code]bx lr[/code].

[color=#61afef][b]Common mistakes[/b][/color]
[ul]​[b]Forgetting push {lr}[/b] in a function that calls another: it loops forever on its own [code]bx lr[/code].
​[b]Push and pop that do not match[/b]: the wrong value lands in PC. A [code]pop {r7, pc}[/code] with no push before it reads past the top of RAM and stops with a bus fault.
​[b]Pushing inside a loop[/b] without popping: SP keeps going down until the stack runs over your data and code.[/ul]
3.name: The stack and functions
3.sum:
A [b]function[/b] is code you call with [code]bl name[/code] and that comes back with [code]bx lr[/code]: [code]bl[/code] puts the return address in LR before it jumps. A function that calls another function must save LR first, because the second [code]bl[/code] overwrites it. It saves it on the stack with [code]push {…, lr}[/code] and returns with [code]pop {…, pc}[/code].

The [b]stack[/b] is memory at the top of RAM. SP points at its top, and it grows down: each push moves SP down 4 bytes per register. The rules: arguments and results go in R0–R3, a function may change R0–R3, and it must put R4–R7 back as it found them.

3.full:
[font_size=26][b]GPIO: controlling pins[/b][/font_size]

The RP2040 has 30 [b]GPIO[/b] pins (general-purpose input/output), GP0 to GP29. Your program can use each one as:
[ul]an [b]output[/b]: the program makes it [b]high[/b] (3.3 V, a 1) or [b]low[/b] (0 V, a 0) — enough to light an LED through a resistor;
an [b]input[/b]: the program reads whether something outside, such as a button, holds it high or low.[/ul]

[color=#61afef][b]Memory-mapped I/O[/b][/color]
There are no special instructions for pins. The chip's control registers sit at memory addresses, and you use them with ordinary [code]str[/code] and [code]ldr[/code]. [code]str r4, [lb]r5][/code] with R5 = [code]0xD000001C[/code] does not change memory at all: it flips a pin. This is called [b]memory-mapped I/O[/b].

[color=#61afef][b]One bit per pin[/b][/color]
Each of these registers has one bit for each pin: bit [i]n[/i] is GP[i]n[/i]. A number with just that one bit set is the pin's [b]mask[/b], [code]1 << n[/code] (1 shifted left n places):

[table=3][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Pin[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Mask (hex)[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Mask (binary, low 16 bits)[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]GP0[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0x00000001[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0000 0000 0000 0001[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]GP2[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0x00000004[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0000 0000 0000 0100[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]GP15[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0x00008000[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]1000 0000 0000 0000[/code][/cell][/table]

In a program write [code]ldr r4, =1 << 15[/code], or give it a name with [code].equ LED_MASK, 1 << 15[/code]. Several pins at once: [code](1 << 14) | (1 << 15)[/code].

[color=#61afef][b]Three steps to drive a pin[/b][/color]
[ol type=1]​[b]Connect the pin to your program.[/b] Write 5 (function [i]SIO[/i]) to the pin's control register in IO_BANK0, at [code]0x40014004 + 8 × n[/code] (for GP15: [code]0x4001407C[/code]). Every pin starts with function [code]0x1F[/code], connected to nothing, so without this step nothing happens.
​[b]Make it an output.[/b] Write its mask to [code]GPIO_OE_SET[/code] ([code]0xD0000024[/code]).
​[b]Set its level.[/b] Write the mask to [code]GPIO_OUT_SET[/code] ([code]0xD0000014[/code]) for high, [code]GPIO_OUT_CLR[/code] ([code]0xD0000018[/code]) for low, or [code]GPIO_OUT_XOR[/code] ([code]0xD000001C[/code]) to flip it.[/ol]
The [b]Blink an LED[/b] example does exactly this. Stepping it in picosim shows:

[table=3][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Instruction[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]The board's "Last I/O write"[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]GP15 afterwards[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]str r1, [lb]r0][/code][/color]  (R0 = [code]0x4001407C[/code], R1 = 5)[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]IO_BANK0 GPIO15_CTRL ← 0x00000005[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]input, floating: connected, but nothing drives it yet[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]str r4, [lb]r0][/code][/color]  (R0 = [code]0xD0000024[/code], R4 = [code]0x8000[/code])[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]SIO GPIO_OE_SET ← 0x00008000[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]output, 0[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]str r4, [lb]r5][/code][/color]  (R5 = [code]0xD000001C[/code])[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]SIO GPIO_OUT_XOR ← 0x00008000[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]output, [color=#98c379][b]1[/b][/color] (green on the board)[/cell][/table]

[b]Why SET, CLR and XOR?[/b] Writing to [code]GPIO_OUT[/code] itself sets [i]every[/i] pin at once. Writing a mask to [code]GPIO_OUT_SET[/code] changes only the pins whose bits are 1 and leaves all the others alone, so you do not have to read the register first.

[color=#61afef][b]The registers[/b][/color]
[table=3][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Address[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Name[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]What a write (or read) does[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0xD0000004[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]GPIO_IN[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1][b]Read[/b] it: one bit per pin, 1 = that pin is high now.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0xD0000010[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]GPIO_OUT[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Every pin's output level at once.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0xD0000014[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]GPIO_OUT_SET[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Pins whose bit is 1 go high.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0xD0000018[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]GPIO_OUT_CLR[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Pins whose bit is 1 go low.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0xD000001C[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]GPIO_OUT_XOR[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Pins whose bit is 1 flip.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0xD0000020[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]GPIO_OE[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Every pin's direction at once (1 = output).[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0xD0000024[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]GPIO_OE_SET[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Pins whose bit is 1 become outputs.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0xD0000028[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]GPIO_OE_CLR[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Pins whose bit is 1 become inputs.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0xD000002C[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]GPIO_OE_XOR[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Pins whose bit is 1 change direction.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0x40014004 + 8n[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]GPIOn_CTRL[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Bits 0–4 choose what controls pin n: 5 = SIO (your program). Starts at [code]0x1F[/code] (nothing).[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0x4001C004 + 4n[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]PADS GPIOn[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Bit 3 turns on the pull-up resistor, bit 2 the pull-down. On the real chip pins start at [code]0x56[/code] (pull-down on; picosim starts them with no pull at all). [code]0x5A[/code] is the same setting with the pull-up on instead.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0x4000C000[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]RESETS[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Both picosim and the Pico SDK start with the pins' blocks already running, so you do not need it.[/cell][/table]

[color=#61afef][b]Reading an input[/b][/color]
Read [code]GPIO_IN[/code] and keep only your pin's bit with [code]ands[/code]; Z tells you whether it was 0. From the [b]Buttons and LEDs[/b] example, with the button on GP14:

[table=1][cell bg=#0e0e0e border=#474747 padding=14,10,14,10 expand=1][code]        ldr     r6, =0xD0000004 @ GPIO_IN
        ldr     r5, =1 << 14    @ the button's bit
check:
        ldr     r0, [lb]r6]        @ R0 = the level of every pin
        ands    r0, r5          @ keep only the button's bit (Z = 1 if it is 0)
        beq     pressed         @ 0: the button connects the pin to GND
        @ ... not pressed: turn the LED off ...
        b       check[/code][/cell][/table]

Checking an input over and over like this is called [b]polling[/b].

An input with nothing connected is [b]floating[/b]: on a real chip it can read 0 or 1 at random. A [b]pull-up[/b] resistor (PADS bit 3) gently holds it at 1 until a button connects it to GND; a [b]pull-down[/b] (bit 2) holds it at 0 until a button connects it to 3V3. In picosim a floating pin reads 0.

[color=#61afef][b]GP numbers and header pins[/b][/color]
GP numbers are the chip's. The board's 40 header pins are numbered separately, 1 to 40 around its edge: GP0 is header pin 1, GP14 is pin 19 and GP15 is pin 20. Hover a pin on the [url=pico][color=#61afef][u]Pico board[/u][/color][/url] to see both numbers. The GND pins are 3, 8, 13, 18, 23, 28 and 38, and 3.3 V comes out of pin 36. GP25 is not on the header: on a Raspberry Pi Pico it drives the on-board LED.

[table=1][cell bg=#2a2a2a border=#f2cc60 padding=14,9,14,9 expand=1][color=#f2cc60][b]Wiring safely[/b][/color]   Always put a resistor (220–1000 Ω) in series with an LED. The pins work at 3.3 V: never connect one to VBUS or VSYS (5 V), and never connect an output straight to GND or 3V3. Use GP0–GP22 and GP26–GP28; 23, 24, 25 and 29 are used on the board itself on some boards (such as the Pico W).[/cell][/table]
3.name: GPIO: controlling pins
3.sum:
The [b]GPIO pins[/b] (GP0–GP29) can be [b]outputs[/b], which your program drives high (1) or low (0) to light an LED, or [b]inputs[/b], which it reads to see a button. A program controls them by storing to special addresses ([b]memory-mapped I/O[/b]): write 5 to the pin's IO_BANK0 CTRL register to connect it to your program, write its bit to [code]GPIO_OE_SET[/code] to make it an output, then write its bit to [code]GPIO_OUT_SET[/code], [code]GPIO_OUT_CLR[/code] or [code]GPIO_OUT_XOR[/code] to make it high, low or flip it.

Each pin is one bit in these registers: GP15 is bit 15, so its [b]mask[/b] is [code]1 << 15[/code] = [code]0x8000[/code]. To read a button, load [code]GPIO_IN[/code] ([code]0xD0000004[/code]) and test the pin's bit with [code]ands[/code]. The [b]Blink an LED[/b] and [b]Buttons and LEDs[/b] examples do both.

3.full:
[font_size=26][b]Level 2 examples[/b][/font_size]

Open each one from [color=#e5c07b][code]Examples[/code][/color]. Every file starts with its own [i]What to watch[/i] comment. The values below are what picosim really shows.

[font_size=21][b]4 · Add up a list in memory[/b][/font_size]   [color=#8c8c8c]04_memory.s · 32 instructions[/color]
Loads four numbers with [code]ldr[/code], adds them up, and stores the total with [code]str[/code].
[ul]Open the Memory tab and Go to [code]numbers[/code]. The dump starts at the row [code]3020[/code]; its first 4 bytes are the end of the literal pool (the address of [code]total[/code]), and [code]numbers[/code] starts at [code]3024[/code]: [code]0A 00 00 00  14 00 00 00  1E 00 00 00  28 00 00 00[/code] are 10, 20, 30 and 40 as little-endian words. [code]total[/code] follows at [code]3034[/code], still 0.
Watch R1 step through [code]0x3024[/code], [code]0x3028[/code], [code]0x302C[/code], [code]0x3030[/code] and R2 grow to [code]0x64[/code] (100). [url=loadstore][color=#61afef][u]Loads and stores[/u][/color][/url] has the table.
At the [code]str[/code], the bytes at [code]3034[/code] turn yellow: [code]64 00 00 00[/code].[/ul]
[b]Try it:[/b] add a fifth number ([code].word 10, 20, 30, 40, 50[/code] and [code]movs r3, #5[/code]). The total becomes 150, [code]0x96[/code].

[font_size=21][b]5 · Blink an LED[/b][/font_size]   [color=#8c8c8c]05_blink_led.s · runs until you pause it[/color]
Flips GP15 on and off forever. [url=gpio][color=#61afef][u]GPIO: controlling pins[/u][/color][/url] explains every line.
[ul]Step the first few instructions and watch the caption under the Pico board: the CTRL write, then OE_SET, then OUT_XOR, and GP15 turns green.
Between flips, [code]subs r0, #1[/code] / [code]bne wait[/code] counts down from 20 to waste time. On a real board the program counts from 10 000 000 instead (about a quarter of a second), because the Pico build defines [code]PICOSIM_HARDWARE[/code].
Set the speed to [b]Max[/b] and press Run to see it blink; Pause to stop.[/ul]
[b]Try it:[/b] click [color=#e5c07b][code]⚙ Settings[/code][/color], change LED_PIN to 2, [color=#e5c07b][code]Apply and reload[/code][/color], and watch GP2 blink instead.

[font_size=21][b]6 · Echo what you type[/b][/font_size]   [color=#8c8c8c]06_echo.s · runs until you type q[/color]
Reads keys with [code]getchar[/code] and prints each one back.
[ul]Press Run, click in the serial console and type. While the program waits, the status text says [i]waiting for input[/i].
Each key arrives in R0 as its ASCII code; [code]cmp r0, #'q'[/code] / [code]beq done[/code] ends the program when you type q.[/ul]
[b]Try it:[/b] make it shout. Small letters are [code]0x61[/code]–[code]0x7A[/code] and capitals are 32 lower, so add before [code]bl putchar[/code]:

[table=1][cell bg=#0e0e0e border=#474747 padding=14,10,14,10 expand=1][code]        cmp     r0, #'a'
        blo     show            @ below 'a': not a small letter
        cmp     r0, #'z'
        bhi     show            @ above 'z': not a small letter
        subs    r0, #32         @ 'a' (0x61) - 32 = 'A' (0x41)
show:[/code][/cell][/table]

Typing [code]Hi, abz![/code] then prints [code]HI, ABZ![/code].

[font_size=21][b]7 · Call a function[/b][/font_size]   [color=#8c8c8c]07_function.s · 33 instructions[/color]
Calls two small functions and prints 4 and 6. [url=stack][color=#61afef][u]The stack and functions[/u][/color][/url] follows it step by step: LR, SP and the stack.
[ul]​[code]twice[/code] calls nothing, so it returns with [code]bx lr[/code] and never uses the stack.
​[code]print_digit[/code] calls putchar, so it saves LR with [code]push {lr}[/code] and returns with [code]pop {pc}[/code].[/ul]
[b]Try it:[/b] remove [code]push {lr}[/code] and change [code]pop {pc}[/code] to [code]bx lr[/code]. After printing 4 the program is stuck on that [code]bx lr[/code] forever: see why in the stack page.

[font_size=21][b]8 · Buttons and LEDs[/b][/font_size]   [color=#8c8c8c]08_button_led.s · runs until you pause it[/color]
Two jobs, chosen with [color=#e5c07b][code]⚙ Settings[/code][/color] → FIND_PINS: [i]find my pins[/i] (which pins your real LEDs and buttons are on; this is what it does at first) or [i]run it[/i] (the LED is on while you hold the button).
[ul]​[b]Run it[/b], in the simulator: in [color=#e5c07b][code]⚙ Settings[/code][/color] set FIND_PINS to [i]run it[/i] and click [color=#e5c07b][code]Apply and reload[/code][/color], then press Run. GP14 (the button, with its pull-up on) shows a blue [b]1[/b]. Click GP14 twice: it is driven to 1 and then to 0, and at 0 ("pressed": the button connects the pin to GND) GP15 turns green. Click once more to let go.
​[b]Find my pins[/b] is meant for a real board (see [url=hardware][color=#61afef][u]Running on a real Pico[/u][/color][/url]): it switches each free pin high and low and prints its number, then reports every button you press. In the simulator, type a key in the console each time it asks (twice), let part 1 run, then click pins in part 2 to see them reported.
The program is longer than the others: look for [code]ands[/code], [code]orrs[/code], [code]eors[/code], [code]tst[/code] (an AND that only sets flags) and [code]mvns[/code] (NOT), and for functions such as [code]print[/code] and [code]print_num[/code].[/ul]
3.name: Level 2 examples
3.sum: Five examples for Level 2: [b]Add up a list in memory[/b] ([code]ldr[/code] and [code]str[/code]), [b]Blink an LED[/b] (GPIO outputs), [b]Echo what you type[/b] ([code]getchar[/code]), [b]Call a function[/b] ([code]bl[/code], LR and the stack) and [b]Buttons and LEDs[/b] (GPIO inputs). Keep the Memory tab and the Pico board in view while you step: that is where these programs show what they do.

3.full:
[font_size=26][b]Explain this step[/b][/font_size]


[color=#61afef][b]Where it is[/b][/color]
At the top of the right-hand column, above the CPU diagram when it is shown. Click its title ([b]▾ Explain this step[/b]) to fold it away, and again to bring it back. Drag the bar under it to give it more room: its text grows with it.

[color=#61afef][b]What just happened[/b][/color]
After each [color=#e5c07b][code]Step instruction[/code][/color], [color=#e5c07b][code]Step over[/code][/color], [color=#e5c07b][code]Step cycle[/code][/color] or [color=#e5c07b][code]◀ Step back[/code][/color], this part names the instruction (with its line number in your file) and says in plain words what it did, with the real values: [i]Worked out R2 = R0 + R1 = 3 + 4 = 7[/i], or [i]Checked the condition “not equal” (Z = 0). The flags say Z = 0, so it jumped to loop[/i]. After [color=#e5c07b][code]Run[/code][/color] stops, it says how many instructions ran and why Run stopped (the end of the program, a breakpoint, a key to type, or Pause).

[color=#61afef][b]What happens next[/b][/color]
The instruction ▶ points at, and what it [i]will[/i] do with the values the registers hold now. picosim finds this out exactly, by running that instruction on a copy of the machine and throwing the copy away, so your program is not touched. Two lines follow:
[ul]​[b]Then[/b] — where the program goes after it: the next line, back up to the top of a loop, into a function, or back to the code that called the function.
​[b]Why[/b] — what the instruction is for: saving registers at the start of a function, setting the flags for the branch on the next line, deciding whether to go round a loop again… When the line has a comment in your file, the comment is quoted too, so good comments make better explanations.[/ul]

[color=#61afef][b]More detail[/b][/color]
Tick [b]More detail[/b] in the panel's corner for the full picture. It is remembered.

[table=2][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Detail[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]What it says[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]How this instruction works[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]One or two sentences about the instruction itself: what [code]movs[/code] does, what the S means, when a [code]bne[/code] jumps.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]What changed[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Every register and flag that changed, old → new, with what each flag means, plus memory bytes and pins, and anything printed.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]PC[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Where the PC moved: on by 2 (or 4) to the next instruction, or a jump.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]In memory[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The instruction's bits, as the Raw column of the Disassembly shows them.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Clock cycles[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]How many cycles it takes on the teaching datapath, and the FSM states in order. With [color=#e5c07b][code]Step cycle[/code][/color], each cycle is explained on its own: what the datapath does, which tri-state buffer drives the bus, the control signals and what changes at the clock edge.[/cell][/table]

[table=1][cell bg=#2a2a2a border=#61afef padding=14,9,14,9 expand=1][color=#61afef][b]Try this[/b][/color]   Before you press Step, read [b]What happens next[/b] and work out the new values yourself. Then step and check them against [b]What just happened[/b] and the yellow registers.[/cell][/table]

[color=#61afef][b]While Run is on[/b][/color]
Explanations pause: the panel says the program is running and is not updated, so Run is not slowed down. When Run stops, the panel explains where and why, and what comes next.
3.name: Explain this step
3.sum:
[b]Explain this step[/b] (top right) describes every step as you take it. [b]What just happened[/b] says in plain words what the instruction did, with the real values. [b]What happens next[/b] says what the next instruction will do, where the program goes after it ([b]Then[/b]) and what that is for ([b]Why[/b], often using the comment on that line of the program). It is exact: picosim really runs the next instruction on a copy of the machine to find out.

Tick [b]More detail[/b] for exactly what changed (registers, flags, memory and pins), how the instruction works, how it is stored in memory and its clock cycles. While [color=#e5c07b][code]Run[/code][/color] is on, the panel waits, then explains where Run stopped. Click its title to fold it away.

3.full:
[font_size=26][b]Registers panel[/b][/font_size]

Top left. The processor's 16 registers, each holding one 32-bit number. Values changed by the last step are [color=#f2cc60]yellow[/color].

[table=2][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Register[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Its job[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]R0–R7[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Your values. Almost every instruction can use these, so use them first. R0 also carries the character for [code]putchar[/code] and [code]getchar[/code].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]R8–R12[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]More storage, but most Cortex-M0+ instructions cannot use them (see [url=instructions][color=#61afef][u]Instructions[/u][/color][/url]).[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]SP[/b] (R13)[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Stack pointer: where the stack is. [code]push[/code] moves it down and [code]pop[/code] moves it back up.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]LR[/b] (R14)[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Link register: where to come back to. [code]bl[/code] puts the return address here before it jumps.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]PC[/b] (R15)[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Program counter: the address of the next instruction. It goes up by 2 (or 4) after each instruction, and jumps on a branch.[/cell][/table]

When a program is loaded, PC is [code]0x00000000[/code] (the start of the built-in OS), SP is [code]0x00010000[/code] (the top of RAM) and LR is [code]0xFFFFFFFF[/code] (nothing to return to). The others start at 0.

[color=#61afef][b]Hex, decimal or signed[/b][/color]
The menu at the panel's top right shows every register as [color=#e5c07b][code]Hex[/code][/color] ([code]0x0000002A[/code]), [color=#e5c07b][code]Decimal[/code][/color] ([code]42[/code]) or [color=#e5c07b][code]Signed[/code][/color] (decimal, where values from [code]0x80000000[/code] up are negative, so [code]0xFFFFFFFF[/code] is −1). Hover a register to see all of these at once, plus its 32 bits in binary. See [url=numbers][color=#61afef][u]Hex, binary and ASCII[/u][/color][/url].

[color=#61afef][b]Flags[/b][/color]
The four check boxes N, Z, C and V are the flags: a tick means 1. They change only after an instruction that sets them, such as [code]cmp[/code], [code]adds[/code] or [code]movs[/code]. Hover one for what it means, or read [url=branches][color=#61afef][u]Flags and branches[/u][/color][/url].

[color=#61afef][b]What changed[/b][/color]
Under the flags, a yellow line names each register the last step changed, its new value as a number (and as a character when it is one), and the line of your file that changed it, for example [code]R0 = 72 = 0x48 = 'H'   ← movs r0, #'H'   (line 22)[/code]. Hovering a yellow register says the same. The PC is left out, because every step changes it. After [color=#e5c07b][code]Run[/code][/color], [color=#e5c07b][code]◀ Step back[/code][/color] or a value you typed, the line says so instead of naming one instruction.

[color=#61afef][b]Editing[/b][/color]
Click a register, type a new value — hex like [code]0x1F[/code] or decimal like [code]31[/code] — and press [color=#e5c07b][code]Enter[/code][/color]. Click a flag to toggle it. This is a quick way to try "what if R1 were 9?" without editing the file; [color=#e5c07b][code]Reload[/code][/color] puts everything back.

[color=#61afef][b]Datapath registers[/b][/color]
The line under that shows the datapath's internal registers: MAR (memory address), MDR (memory data), IR and IR2 (the instruction being executed). They are explained in [url=components][color=#61afef][u]Datapath components[/u][/color][/url].

[color=#61afef][b]Status line[/b][/color]
[b]Next state[/b] is the FSM state the next clock cycle will run (see [url=states][color=#61afef][u]FSM states[/u][/color][/url]), and whether the CPU is between instructions or partway through one. Below it are the total instructions and clock cycles executed.

[color=#61afef][b]Bigger text[/b][/color]
Drag the bars below and beside the panel to make it larger — the text and fields scale up to fill the space.
3.name: Registers
3.sum:
The Registers panel (top left) shows the CPU's 16 registers: R0–R12 hold your values, [b]SP[/b] points at the stack, [b]LR[/b] holds a function's return address and [b]PC[/b] is the address of the next instruction. Whatever the last step changed turns [color=#f2cc60]yellow[/color], and the line under the flags says which line of your file changed it.

The four check boxes are the flags N Z C V. The menu at the top right shows the values in [color=#e5c07b][code]Hex[/code][/color], [color=#e5c07b][code]Decimal[/code][/color] or [color=#e5c07b][code]Signed[/code][/color]; hover a register to see every form at once, or click one, type a new value and press [color=#e5c07b][code]Enter[/code][/color] ([color=#e5c07b][code]Reload[/code][/color] puts everything back).

3.full:
[font_size=26][b]Disassembly and Memory[/b][/font_size]


[color=#61afef][b]Disassembly tab[/b][/color]
Below the Registers. Your program as the CPU sees it, one instruction per row. The row with ▶ is the instruction that runs next. With [color=#e5c07b][code]Follow PC[/code][/color] ticked the list scrolls to it automatically.

[table=3][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Column[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Example[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Meaning[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]●[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Breakpoint column: click it to set or clear a breakpoint (below).[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Address[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]▶3002[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Where in memory the instruction is, in hex. Each instruction is 2 bytes, so addresses go up by 2. [code]bl[/code] is 4 bytes.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Raw[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]2048[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The instruction as the CPU stores it: 16 bits in hex ([code]bl[/code] has two groups). The assembler made this from your line.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Label[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]main[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The label at this address, if there is one.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Instruction[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#56b6c2][code]movs r0, #0x48[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The instruction turned back into assembly from the raw bits, the way the CPU sees it.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Source[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]22  movs r0, #'H'  @ R0 = …[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The line of your file it came from: its line number, your code and your comment. Hover it to see the whole line.[/cell][/table]

Compare the [b]Instruction[/b] and [b]Source[/b] columns to see what the assembler did with your line:
[ul]Constants are shown in hex: [code]movs r0, #'H'[/code] becomes [code]movs r0, #0x48[/code], and [code]#10[/code] becomes [code]#0xa[/code].
Some lines are stored in a shorter form: [code]adds r4, r4, #1[/code] becomes [code]adds r4, #1[/code], which does the same thing. A few instructions have a second name: [code]bcs[/code] shows as [code]bhs[/code].
Branches and calls show the label they go to ([code]bl putchar[/code], [code]bne loop[/code]), and the Label column shows where that label is.
