The first rows, from [code]0000[/code] to [code]0016[/code], are the built-in OS ([code]_start[/code], [code]putchar[/code], [code]getchar[/code]); their Source is the OS's file, [code]os.s[/code]. Your program starts at [code]3000[/code], the [code]main[/code] row.[/ul]

[color=#61afef][b]Breakpoints[/b][/color]
Click the narrow first column of a row to put a red ● there; click again to remove it. [color=#e5c07b][code]Run[/code][/color] stops when it reaches a breakpoint, [i]before[/i] running that instruction. Use one to run straight to the part you want to study, then step from there.

[color=#61afef][b]Memory tab[/b][/color]
Memory as a place you can look around in. It has five parts, and everything in it updates after each step.

[table=2][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Part[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]What it shows[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]The map[/b] (left)[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The whole of memory from low addresses (top) to high (bottom): the built-in OS, [b]your code[/b], [b]your data[/b], [b]free RAM[/b] and the [b]stack[/b], which grows down from the top of RAM, then the [b]I/O registers[/b], which are not RAM at all. [b]PC[/b] and [b]SP[/b] tags show where they point, an [b]R[/b] or [b]W[/b] tag marks the part the last step read or wrote, and the part you are looking at has a blue outline. Click a part to go there.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]The bytes[/b] (middle)[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]256 bytes, 16 to a row; each row starts with the address of its first byte and the columns are + 0 … + F. Every byte is coloured by what it is: an instruction, a literal or string stored with the code, data, or the stack. [color=#7fd1b9]Labels[/color] sit above the bytes they name, and a register that holds an address is tagged where it points ([color=#61afef]R1 ↓[/color]): that register is a [b]pointer[/b]. The ▶ instruction is shaded, and the column on the right shows the same bytes as characters.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]Last step[/b] (above the bytes)[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]What the last instruction did to memory, in words: [i]ldr r0, [lb]r1] read a word at 3024 (numbers): the bytes 0A 00 00 00, which backwards (lowest byte first) make 0x0000000A = 10, now in R0[/i]. The bytes it read are outlined in [color=#61afef]blue[/color], the ones it wrote in [color=#f2cc60]yellow[/color]. With [b]Follow loads and stores[/b] ticked, the view moves to them by itself.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]The stack[/b] (right)[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Each word from SP up to the top of RAM as a box, the newest at the bottom with the [b]◀ SP[/b] tag. Each box says what put it there, such as [i]LR saved by push {r7, lr} (line 20)[/i], or that it looks like a return address, and boxes are grouped by the function that pushed them. A word the last step popped is shown faded just below SP, with the register it went into.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]Inspector[/b] (bottom)[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Hover a byte to see everything about it: its address and label, what kind of byte it is, its value in hex, decimal and as a character, the word it belongs to (put together lowest byte first), and which registers point to it.[/cell][/table]

[ul]​[b]Show[/b] — [color=#e5c07b][code]Bytes[/code][/color] (every byte in hex), [color=#e5c07b][code]Words[/code][/color] (4 bytes put together into one number, so [code]64 00 00 00[/code] shows as [code]00000064[/code]) or [color=#e5c07b][code]Characters[/code][/color] (each byte as the character it codes, [code]\0[/code] for the 0 that ends a string).
​[b]Go to[/b] — type an address ([code]0x3000[/code]) or any label of your program, data labels included ([code]numbers[/code]), and press [color=#e5c07b][code]Enter[/code][/color]. [color=#e5c07b][code]PC[/code][/color], [color=#e5c07b][code]SP[/code][/color] and [color=#e5c07b][code]main[/code][/color] jump straight there. The mouse wheel scrolls the bytes.
​[b]Changing memory[/b] — click a byte to select it (an orange outline), type new bytes in hex on the right ([code]2a 00 00 00[/code]) and press [color=#e5c07b][code]Enter[/code][/color]: a quick way to try your program on different data without editing the file. [color=#e5c07b][code]◀ Step back[/code][/color] and [color=#e5c07b][code]Reload[/code][/color] undo it.[/ul]
[table=1][cell bg=#2a2a2a border=#61afef padding=14,9,14,9 expand=1][color=#61afef][b]Try this[/b][/color]   Open [b]Add up a list in memory[/b], tick Follow loads and stores and step through the loop. Each [code]ldr r0, [lb]r1][/code] outlines the next number, and the [b]R1 ↓[/b] tag moves 4 bytes along each pass: R1 is a pointer walking through the list.[/cell][/table]
3.name: Disassembly & memory
3.sum:
The Disassembly lists your program one instruction per row: its address, its bits ([b]Raw[/b]), its label, the instruction as the CPU sees it and the line of your file it came from ([b]Source[/b]). The row with ▶ runs next. Click a row's first column to put a [b]breakpoint[/b] (a red ●) there: [color=#e5c07b][code]Run[/code][/color] stops just before that instruction.

The [b]Memory[/b] tab shows memory as a place: a map of where everything lives, the bytes coloured by what they are (with labels and pointer tags on them), the stack as boxes that say what put each word there, and, after each step, which bytes it read or wrote. Hover a byte to have it explained; click one to change it.

3.full:
[font_size=26][b]Raspberry Pi Pico board[/b][/font_size]

Bottom left, under Disassembly. A to-scale drawing of the Raspberry Pi Pico, lying on its side with the USB connector on the left, showing what your program does to the chip's GPIO pins. [url=gpio][color=#61afef][u]GPIO: controlling pins[/u][/color][/url] explains how a program controls them.

[color=#61afef][b]Reading the pins[/b][/color]
The 40 gold pads are the header pins, numbered 1–20 along the bottom edge and 21–40 along the top. Each GPIO pad is labelled with its GP number; a small [b]out[/b] or [color=#61afef]in[/color] under the label says which way it is set (a floating input shows neither). Power pins (GND, 3V3, VSYS, VBUS, …) are labelled in grey and red. On the pad itself:

[table=2][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]On the pad[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Means[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#98c379][b]1[/b][/color] on green[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]An output your program drives high.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]0[/b] on dark grey[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Low: an output driven low, or an input held low (by a click or a pull-down).[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#61afef][b]1[/b][/color] on blue[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]An input reading high (clicked high, or held by a pull-up).[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]nothing[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Floating: nothing drives the pin and it has no pull resistor. Your program reads it as 0.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#f2cc60]yellow ring[/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Changed by the last step.[/cell][/table]

The same key is drawn above the board. Hover any pin for its header number, GP number, direction, level and pull (for example [i]Pin 20: GP15 — output, high (1)[/i]).

[color=#61afef][b]Under the board[/b][/color]
[ul]​[b]Last I/O write[/b] — the last I/O register the current instruction wrote, decoded: [code]SIO GPIO_OUT_XOR ← 0x00008000[/code] or [code]IO_BANK0 GPIO15_CTRL ← 0x00000005[/code].
​[b]Changed by the last step[/b] — which pins changed, for example [code]GP15 → 1[/code].[/ul]

[color=#61afef][b]The on-board LED[/b][/color]
The drawing's LED lights when GP25 is high, as on a Raspberry Pi Pico. Real boards differ (on a Pico W that LED is wired to the Wi-Fi chip, not to GP25), so for programs that should work on any board, wire your own LED to a GPIO pin: see the [b]Blink an LED[/b] example.

[color=#61afef][b]Driving inputs[/b][/color]
Click an [i]input[/i] pin to drive it like a switch: floating (Z) → 1 → 0 → floating. Your program sees it when it reads [code]GPIO_IN[/code]. A pin with a pull-up already reads 1, so for a button to GND click it [i]twice[/i] (1, then 0) to "press" it. Output pins cannot be clicked: your program controls them.

[color=#61afef][b]Live from your board[/b][/color]
In [color=#e5c07b][code]Pico (USB serial)[/code][/color] mode, while a board you flashed from picosim is connected, the drawing shows your [i]real[/i] board's pins instead: the subtitle turns green and says LIVE. The pins update as your program runs (about 50 times a second), and pins that just changed get a yellow ring. You cannot click pins in this mode; use your real buttons. An input with nothing connected reads 0.

[color=#61afef][b]Full window[/b][/color]
Click [color=#e5c07b][code]⛶ Enlarge[/code][/color] in the board's corner to fill the window with it; [color=#e5c07b][code]✕ Close[/code][/color] or [color=#e5c07b][code]Esc[/code][/color] returns.
3.name: Raspberry Pi Pico board
3.sum:
The drawing of the Raspberry Pi Pico (bottom left) shows what your program does to the chip's pins. A pin your program drives high shows a green [b]1[/b], one driven low a dark [b]0[/b], and an input reading high a blue [b]1[/b]; a [color=#f2cc60]yellow[/color] ring marks a pin the last step changed. Hover a pin for its numbers and state.

Click an [i]input[/i] pin to drive it like a switch: floating → 1 → 0 → floating. In [b]Pico (USB serial)[/b] mode, with a board you flashed connected, the drawing shows your real board's pins instead.

3.full:
[font_size=26][b]USB Serial console[/b][/font_size]

Bottom right. Shows what your program prints with [code]putchar[/code].

[color=#61afef][b]Typing input[/b][/color]
[ul]Click in the output area and type: each key is sent immediately (what [code]getchar[/code] expects).
Or type a whole line in the box below and press [color=#e5c07b][code]Enter[/code][/color] — it is sent followed by a carriage return.[/ul]
When the program is waiting in [code]getchar[/code], the console header says so. [color=#e5c07b][code]Clear[/code][/color] empties the output.
3.name: Serial console
3.sum: The serial console (bottom right) shows what your program prints with [code]putchar[/code]. When the program calls [code]getchar[/code] it waits for a key: click in the console and type (each key is sent at once), or type a line in the box underneath and press [color=#e5c07b][code]Enter[/code][/color]. [color=#e5c07b][code]Clear[/code][/color] empties it.

3.full:
[font_size=26][b]Layout and zoom[/b][/font_size]

[ul]​[b]Resize panels[/b] by dragging the bars between them. The registers panel's text grows with it.
​[b]Zoom[/b] the whole window with [color=#e5c07b][code]−[/code][/color] / [color=#e5c07b][code]+[/code][/color] in the toolbar, [color=#e5c07b][code]Ctrl/Cmd +[/code][/color] / [color=#e5c07b][code]Ctrl/Cmd −[/code][/color], or [color=#e5c07b][code]Ctrl/Cmd[/code][/color] + mouse wheel. Click the percentage (or [color=#e5c07b][code]Ctrl/Cmd 0[/code][/color]) to reset. The zoom is remembered.
​[b]Colours:[/b] [color=#e5c07b][code]View[/code][/color] in the toolbar picks System, Blue, Dark or Light. It is remembered too.
Zoom stops at the largest size where the whole toolbar still fits, so no button is ever cut off.
​[color=#e5c07b][code]Show / Hide CPU Diagram[/code][/color] toggles the diagram and the panel under it.
The Pico board can fill the window — see [url=pico][color=#61afef][u]Raspberry Pi Pico board[/u][/color][/url].[/ul]

Where each panel is, and what every toolbar button does, is in [url=tour][color=#61afef][u]The screen at a glance[/u][/color][/url]. Which panels and buttons you see depends on the [color=#e5c07b][code]Level[/code][/color] menu.
3.name: Layout and zoom
3.sum: Drag the bars between the panels to resize them; a panel you make bigger also gets bigger text. Zoom the whole window with [color=#e5c07b][code]−[/code][/color] / [color=#e5c07b][code]+[/code][/color] in the toolbar, [color=#e5c07b][code]Ctrl/Cmd +[/code][/color] / [color=#e5c07b][code]Ctrl/Cmd −[/code][/color] or [color=#e5c07b][code]Ctrl/Cmd[/code][/color] + mouse wheel, and click the percentage to fit the window again. [color=#e5c07b][code]View[/code][/color] picks the colours (System, Blue, Dark or Light). picosim remembers all of these.

3.full:
[font_size=26][b]Running on a real Pico[/b][/font_size]

The same [code].s[/code] file that runs in the simulator can run on a real Raspberry Pi Pico (or any RP2040 board) plugged into your computer by USB. picosim turns it into a [code].uf2[/code] file, the format the Pico loads programs from, and copies it to the board. This is called [b]flashing[/b], because the program is stored in the board's flash memory and stays there after you unplug it.

[color=#61afef][b]What you need[/b][/color]
[ul]The board and a USB cable that carries data (some cables only charge).
The tools from [code]installation.md[/code]: the ARM compiler, git and, ideally, [code]picotool[/code]. Your teacher has probably installed them already.[/ul]

[color=#61afef][b]Steps[/b][/color]
[ol type=1]Load your program in picosim and check it in the Simulator first.
Choose [b]Pico (USB serial)[/b] in the toolbar's mode menu (it says [b]Simulator[/b] until you change it). The port menu, [color=#e5c07b][code]⟳[/code][/color], [color=#e5c07b][code]Connect[/code][/color] and [color=#e5c07b][code]Flash[/code][/color] appear.
Click [color=#e5c07b][code]Flash[/code][/color]. picosim builds the program with the Pico SDK and uploads it; the console shows each step. The very first build downloads the SDK and takes a few minutes; later ones take seconds. It uploads with [code]picotool[/code] if that is installed; otherwise it copies the file to the board's [code]RPI-RP2[/code] drive, which appears when you [b]hold the BOOTSEL button while plugging the board in[/b].
When the upload finishes, picosim connects to the board by itself and the console talks to it: what the board prints appears in green, and keys you type go to the board. The board waits up to 5 seconds for this connection before your program starts, so nothing it prints is lost. If it does not connect, pick the port marked [i](Pico)[/i] ([color=#e5c07b][code]⟳[/code][/color] refreshes the list) and click [color=#e5c07b][code]Connect[/code][/color].
The [url=pico][color=#61afef][u]Pico board[/u][/color][/url] drawing turns LIVE and shows your real board's pins.[/ol]

[color=#61afef][b]What is different on the board[/b][/color]
[ul]The build defines [code]PICOSIM_HARDWARE[/code], so a program can use bigger delays on the board ([code].ifdef PICOSIM_HARDWARE[/code], as the LED examples do): the real chip runs millions of instructions a second.
Your [color=#e5c07b][code]⚙ Settings[/code][/color] values (pins and wiring) are built in.
Your [code]main:[/code] is renamed [code]asm_main[/code] and called by the Pico SDK after it has started USB. When [code]main[/code] returns, the board does not halt: it waits, with USB still running, so its last output stays in the console and the next Flash works.
Stepping, the registers, the Memory tab and the CPU diagram work only in [b]Simulator[/b] mode. Switch back to it to debug.[/ul]

[color=#61afef][b]If Flash fails[/b][/color]
The status text says [i]Flash failed — see console[/i]; the console shows why:

[table=2][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]The console says[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]What to do[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]picotool could not find or access the Pico[/code] or [code]Put the Pico in BOOTSEL mode[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Unplug the board, hold BOOTSEL, plug it back in, let go, and click Flash again.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]'picotool' was not found and no RPI-RP2 volume is mounted[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]No picotool: put the board in BOOTSEL mode as above, so its drive appears.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]git is not on PATH[/code], [code]ARM GNU C/C++ compiler was not found[/code] or [code]has no C library (newlib)[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]A tool is missing: see [code]installation.md[/code] or ask your teacher.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]an assembler error[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Your program does not assemble: fix it in the Simulator first.[/cell][/table]
3.name: Running on a real Pico
3.sum:
The same [code].s[/code] file can run on a real Raspberry Pi Pico plugged in by USB. Choose [b]Pico (USB serial)[/b] in the mode menu and click [color=#e5c07b][code]Flash[/code][/color]: picosim builds your program, copies it to the board and connects the console, so you see what the board prints. If picotool is not installed, hold the board's [b]BOOTSEL[/b] button while you plug it in, so it appears as a drive.

The first build takes a few minutes because it downloads the Pico SDK; later ones take seconds. If Flash fails the console says why, and the details list what to do. Stepping, the registers and the CPU diagram work only in Simulator mode.

3.full:
[font_size=26][b]Inside the CPU: the big picture[/b][/font_size]

Until now, [color=#e5c07b][code]Step instruction[/code][/color] did a whole instruction at once. Inside the processor, every instruction is really a short series of smaller steps, one per tick of the processor's clock. Level 3 lets you watch those steps on a drawing of the hardware.

[color=#61afef][b]The clock[/b][/color]
The processor is driven by a [b]clock[/b]: a signal that ticks at a steady rate (the Pico's RP2040 normally ticks 125 million times a second). The time from one tick to the next is one [b]clock cycle[/b]. During a cycle, values flow through wires and are worked on; at the tick that ends it — the [b]clock edge[/b] — storage boxes called [b]registers[/b] capture their new values all at once. Then the next cycle begins.

[color=#61afef][b]Datapath and control[/b][/color]
A processor has two halves:
[ul]The [b]datapath[/b] holds, moves and computes data: registers, a shared [b]bus[/b] (wires that carry one value at a time), the [b]ALU[/b] that does arithmetic, adders for addresses, and the connection to memory.
The [b]control unit[/b] decides, every cycle, what each part of the datapath does, by turning [b]control signals[/b] on and off: "put the PC on the bus", "MAR, load the bus", "ALU, add". In this processor it is a [b]finite-state machine[/b] (FSM): in each cycle it is in one [b]state[/b], and each state turns on its own set of signals.[/ul]
[url=blocks][color=#61afef][u]Building blocks[/u][/color][/url] describes each kind of part.

[color=#61afef][b]Why several cycles per instruction?[/b][/color]
This teaching processor has [b]one[/b] bus and [b]one[/b] memory. Only one value can travel on the bus in a cycle, and memory does one read or write per cycle. So an instruction has to be done in steps. Just reading the instruction from memory (the [i]fetch[/i]) takes 3 cycles: send the address, read memory, copy the result into the instruction register. Most instructions take 5 to 7 cycles in all.

[color=#61afef][b]The six phases[/b][/color]
Every instruction goes through some of these phases, in this order. The [url=cycles][color=#61afef][u]cycle inspector[/u][/color][/url]'s chips light up for the phase of the cycle you are looking at.

[table=4][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Phase[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Chip[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]What happens[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]FSM states[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]Fetch[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#e5c07b][code]F[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Read the instruction from memory into IR (and IR2).[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#8c8c8c]FETCH_ADDR, FETCH_MEMORY, FETCH_IR, FETCH2_ADDR, FETCH2_MEMORY, FETCH2_IR[/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]Decode[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#e5c07b][code]D[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Work out what the instruction is and which states come next.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#8c8c8c]DECODE[/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]Evaluate Address[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#e5c07b][code]EA[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Compute a memory address with the address adder.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#8c8c8c]EVALUATE_ADDRESS[/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]Fetch Operands[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#e5c07b][code]FO[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Get the values the instruction works on: registers into the ALU, or memory into MDR.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#8c8c8c]FETCH_OPERANDS[/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]Execute[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#e5c07b][code]EX[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Do the work: the ALU computes, or the PC changes, or the OS is called.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#8c8c8c]EXECUTE_COMMIT, EXECUTE_PC, SVC_CALL, HALT[/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]Store Result[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#e5c07b][code]SR[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Put the result where it belongs: a register, memory, LR or the base register.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#8c8c8c]STORE_RESULT, LINK, WRITEBACK[/color][/cell][/table]

An ADDS, for example, uses Fetch (3 cycles), Decode, Fetch operands and Execute: 6 cycles. [url=tutorial][color=#61afef][u]Tutorial: one ADDS[/u][/color][/url] goes through all six with real values.

[color=#61afef][b]Getting started[/b][/color]
[ol type=1]Load a program, for example [b]Add two numbers[/b].
Click [color=#e5c07b][code]Show CPU Diagram[/code][/color] in the toolbar. The diagram appears on the right with the cycle inspector under it.
Press [color=#e5c07b][code]Step cycle[/code][/color] ([color=#e5c07b][code]F11[/code][/color]). One clock cycle runs: the parts it used light up, and the inspector explains it.
Keep pressing F11. After three cycles of fetch and a few more, the instruction is done and the next one starts with FETCH_ADDR.[/ol]
[color=#e5c07b][code]Step instruction[/code][/color] still works: it runs the rest of the current instruction's cycles at once. The status text now counts both instructions and clock cycles.

[table=1][cell bg=#2a2a2a border=#61afef padding=14,9,14,9 expand=1][color=#61afef][b]Model[/b][/color]   This datapath is the course's teaching processor (textbook Chapter 7), not a picture of the real Cortex-M0+'s insides. It runs exactly the same programs with exactly the same results; only the way it is built and its cycle counts differ. Level 4 shows the real chip's own design, a pipeline.[/cell][/table]
3.name: The big picture
3.sum:
Inside the processor, every instruction is a short series of [b]clock cycles[/b]. In each cycle the [b]control unit[/b] (a finite-state machine, or FSM) turns on [b]control signals[/b] that tell the [b]datapath[/b] (the registers, a shared bus, the ALU, adders and memory) what to do; at the [b]clock edge[/b] that ends the cycle, the registers take their new values.

This teaching processor has one bus and one memory, so every instruction first spends 3 cycles fetching itself from memory, and most take 5 to 7 cycles in all. [color=#e5c07b][code]Show CPU Diagram[/code][/color] draws it, and [color=#e5c07b][code]Step cycle[/code][/color] ([color=#e5c07b][code]C[/code][/color] or [color=#e5c07b][code]F11[/code][/color]) runs one cycle at a time.

3.full:
[font_size=26][b]Building blocks[/b][/font_size]

The CPU diagram is made of a few kinds of part, used again and again. Learn these and you can read the whole drawing. Click any block on the diagram for a card about that particular one, or see [url=components][color=#61afef][u]Datapath components[/u][/color][/url].

[table=4][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Part[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]What it does[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]On the diagram[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Examples[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]Register[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Stores one number. It takes a new value only at the clock edge, and only when its load signal ([code]LD.X[/code]) is on; otherwise it keeps what it has.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]A box showing its value.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]PC, IR, MAR, MDR, the register file (R0–R12, SP, LR), the N Z C V flags[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]Bus[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Shared wires that carry one 32-bit value from one part to any others that want it.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]The long line across the middle; its value is printed above it.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]the bus[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]Tri-state buffer[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]A switch between a part and the bus. When its [code]Gate[/code] signal is on, the part drives the bus; when off, the part is disconnected ("high impedance"). Only one may be on in a cycle.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]A small triangle on the bus; the lit one is driving.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]gatePC, GateMDR, GateALU, GateADDR, gateVector[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]Multiplexer[/b] (mux)[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Picks one of its inputs and passes it through. Its [b]select[/b] signal says which.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]A trapezoid: inputs on the long side, output from the short side, select on a slanted side.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]PCMUX, ADDR1MUX, ADDR2MUX, SR2MUX[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]Adder[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Adds two numbers, all the time.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]A trapezoid.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]the +2 PC incrementer, the address adder, the +4 MAR incrementer[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]ALU[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Arithmetic Logic Unit: adds, subtracts, ANDs, shifts…, picked by the [code]ALUK[/code] signal. It also works out the N Z C V flags of its result.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]A trapezoid labelled ALU. It also shows the values held in its two input latches, A and B.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]the ALU[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]Memory[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Reads or writes the byte, halfword or word at the address in MAR when [code]MEM.EN[/code] is on; [code]R/W[/code] says which.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]The box labelled MEMORY / I-O.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]RAM and the I/O registers[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]Control unit[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The FSM. Each cycle, its current state turns on a set of control signals and chooses the next state.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]The FSM box; its control signals are the purple dashed stubs.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]the FSM[/cell][/table]

[color=#61afef][b]Two kinds of logic[/b][/color]
[ul]​[b]Combinational[/b] parts (muxes, adders, the ALU) have no memory: their output follows their inputs straight away, within the cycle.
​[b]Sequential[/b] parts (registers, and memory being written) change only at the clock edge.[/ul]
So during a cycle, data flows from registers, through combinational parts, to the inputs of other registers, and at the clock edge those registers capture it. That is why the diagram writes a register's new value as a yellow [code]old → new[/code] caption: the box itself changes only when the next cycle starts.

[color=#61afef][b]Why a bus with switches?[/b][/color]
Connecting every part to every other part would need a huge number of wires. With one shared bus, any part can send a value to any other, but only one at a time. If two tri-state buffers were on together, two parts would try to drive the same wires to different values and fight; the FSM never lets that happen.
3.name: Building blocks
3.sum:
The CPU diagram is built from a few kinds of part. [b]Registers[/b] store a value and change only at the clock edge. The [b]bus[/b] carries one value at a time between parts, and [b]tri-state buffers[/b] decide which part drives it. [b]Multiplexers[/b] (muxes) pick one of their inputs, [b]adders[/b] and the [b]ALU[/b] compute, [b]memory[/b] reads or writes at the address in MAR, and the [b]FSM[/b] controls them all.

Muxes, adders and the ALU have no memory: their output follows their inputs straight away. Registers remember, which is why the diagram shows a register's new value as a [color=#f2cc60]yellow[/color] [code]old → new[/code] caption until the next cycle starts.

3.full:
[font_size=26][b]Datapath diagram[/b][/font_size]

New to this? Read [url=cpuintro][color=#61afef][u]The big picture[/u][/color][/url] and [url=blocks][color=#61afef][u]Building blocks[/u][/color][/url] first.

Click [color=#e5c07b][code]Show CPU Diagram[/code][/color] in the toolbar, with the machine menu next to it on [color=#e5c07b][code]Multi-cycle[/code][/color]. The diagram is the multi-cycle datapath from the course text: one shared 32-bit bus, MAR/MDR, IR/IR2, a separate address adder, the ALU, the register file and the FSM that controls them.

[color=#61afef][b]Values during a cycle, and the clock edge[/b][/color]
The diagram shows the cycle [i]while it happens[/i]. Every register (PC, IR, MAR, MDR, the register file, the flags) keeps showing the value it holds during the cycle. A register that loads a new value at the clock edge which ends the cycle turns [color=#f2cc60]yellow[/color] and gets a caption [code]old → new[/code] underneath; the box itself only shows the new value once you step to the next cycle. For example in FETCH_ADDR the PC still reads [code]0x00003000[/code] with [code]0x00003000 → 0x00003002[/code] below it, and in FETCH_MEMORY it reads [code]0x00003002[/code]. (The Registers panel on the left always shows the machine after the last clock edge.)

[color=#61afef][b]What the colors mean[/b][/color]
[ul]​[color=#61afef]Bright blue wires and boxes[/color] carry data in the cycle being shown.
​[color=#c678dd]Purple dashed arrows[/color] are control inputs from the FSM: the short stubs into the muxes (select), the ALU (ALUK), the +2 incrementer (PCINC) and each tri-state buffer (GatePC, GateADDR, …), plus BranchTaken. A bright stub is asserted this cycle and is labelled with the value it selects.
​[color=#f2cc60]Yellow[/color] marks a value loaded at the clock edge that ends this cycle (old → new).
The triangles on the bus are tri-state buffers, each named after the control signal that turns it on: GatePC, GateADDR, GateMDR, GateALU and GateVEC. The lit one is driving the bus; the others are off (high impedance). The bus value is printed above the bus.
Every mux, the ALU and the adders take their inputs on the long side and send their result out of the short side; control comes in on a slanted side.
The [b]heat tint[/b] behind each box, from cool to hot, shows how much of the run so far that part has been used, and its small label gives its share of all clock cycles. It is on from Level 3; [color=#e5c07b][code]View[/code][/color] ▸ [b]Heat overlay on the CPU diagram[/b] turns it off and on.[/ul]
When you step, a glowing pulse travels along the active wires in the order the data flows; a register's yellow caption appears when the pulse reaches it. Its speed follows the speed slider; at high speeds animation is skipped.

[color=#61afef][b]Learning the components[/b][/color]
Hover a block for a one-line summary. [b]Click a block[/b], a tri-state buffer (▲ / ▼) or the bus to open a card explaining what it does, how it works, what it connects to and when it is used; the block and its wires are outlined in [color=#ffb86c]orange[/color]. Click it again, click empty space, press ✕ or [color=#e5c07b][code]Esc[/code][/color] to close. The same descriptions are in [url=components][color=#61afef][u]Datapath components[/u][/color][/url].
3.name: Datapath diagram
3.sum:
The CPU diagram shows the multi-cycle datapath during the cycle that just ran. [color=#61afef]Bright blue[/color] wires and boxes carry data in this cycle, [color=#c678dd]purple dashed[/color] stubs are control signals from the FSM (bright means on), and a [color=#f2cc60]yellow[/color] [code]old → new[/code] caption marks a register that takes a new value at the clock edge. When you step, a glowing pulse follows the data along the wires.

The [b]heat tint[/b] behind each box shows how much of the run that part has been used so far ([color=#e5c07b][code]View[/code][/color] ▸ [b]Heat overlay[/b] turns it off). Hover a block for a one-line summary, or click it for a card that explains what it does and when it is used.

3.full:
[font_size=26][b]Cycle-by-cycle inspector[/b][/font_size]

Shown below the CPU diagram. It follows the instruction being executed one clock cycle at a time. [url=tutorial][color=#61afef][u]Tutorial: one ADDS[/u][/color][/url] walks through it with an example.

[color=#61afef][b]Left side[/b][/color]
[ul]The instruction's address and text, and how far through it the CPU is.
The phase chips — [color=#e5c07b][code]F[/code][/color] Fetch, [color=#e5c07b][code]D[/code][/color] Decode, [color=#e5c07b][code]EA[/code][/color] Evaluate address, [color=#e5c07b][code]FO[/code][/color] Fetch operands, [color=#e5c07b][code]EX[/code][/color] Execute, [color=#e5c07b][code]SR[/code][/color] Store result — light up for the selected cycle. Hover one for its name.
The list of this instruction's cycles: number, FSM state and phase. Click a row to look at an earlier cycle again; the diagram shows that cycle.
​[color=#e5c07b][code]◀ Prev[/code][/color] and [color=#e5c07b][code]Next ▶[/code][/color] move through the cycles. At the latest cycle, Next clocks the CPU (the same as Step cycle).[/ul]

[color=#61afef][b]Right side[/b][/color]
[ul]The state name and a plain-language description of what the cycle does, including the value on the bus.
​[b]Control signals asserted[/b] — what the FSM turns on. [code]GateX[/code] puts X on the bus, [code]LD.X[/code] makes X load at the clock edge, [code]XMUX=…[/code] picks a multiplexer input, [code]ALUK=…[/code] picks the ALU operation.
​[b]What changes at the clock edge[/b] — every register, flag, memory byte or I/O register the cycle loads at the edge that ends it, old → new. On the diagram these are the yellow captions.[/ul]

[color=#61afef][b]How many cycles?[/b][/color]
Every instruction starts with the same 3 fetch cycles (FETCH_ADDR → FETCH_MEMORY → FETCH_IR). Typical totals: B 5, ADDS, MOVS and CMP 6, LDR and STR 7, BL 9, and PUSH or POP of 2 registers 10. [url=states][color=#61afef][u]FSM states[/u][/color][/url] explains every state and lists each instruction's sequence; the full table is also in [code]docs/cycles.md[/code].
3.name: Cycle by cycle
3.sum:
The cycle inspector under the diagram follows the current instruction one clock cycle at a time. The left side lists its cycles (click one to look at it again) with the phase chips F, D, EA, FO, EX and SR; the right side says what the cycle does, which control signals it turns on and what changes at the clock edge.

Every instruction starts with the same 3 fetch cycles. Typical totals: B 5, ADDS, MOVS and CMP 6, LDR and STR 7, BL 9, and PUSH or POP of 2 registers 10.

3.full:
[font_size=26][b]Tutorial: one instruction, cycle by cycle[/b][/font_size]

Follow one ADDS through the CPU, with the real values picosim shows. It is the instruction [code]adds r2, r0, r1[/code] at address [code]3006[/code] in the [b]Add two numbers[/b] example, where R0 = 3 and R1 = 4.

[color=#61afef][b]Set it up[/b][/color]
[ol type=1]Open [b]Add two numbers[/b] from [color=#e5c07b][code]Examples[/code][/color] and click [color=#e5c07b][code]Show CPU Diagram[/code][/color].
In the Disassembly, click the first column of the row [code]3006  adds r2, r0, r1[/code] to set a breakpoint (a red ●).
Press [color=#e5c07b][code]Run[/code][/color]. It stops just before that instruction.
Press [color=#e5c07b][code]Step cycle[/code][/color] ([color=#e5c07b][code]F11[/code][/color]) once for each row of the table, and compare the diagram and the inspector with it.[/ol]

[color=#61afef][b]The six cycles[/b][/color]
[table=5][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]#[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]State[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Control signals[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]What happens[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]At the clock edge[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]1[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]FETCH_ADDR[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#c678dd][code]GatePC LD.MAR PCINC=+2 PCMUX=PC+2 LD.PC[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The PC drives the bus ([code]0x00003006[/code]) so MAR can take it. The +2 incrementer and PCMUX prepare PC + 2.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]MAR ← [code]0x00003006[/code]
PC → [code]0x00003008[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]2[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]FETCH_MEMORY[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#c678dd][code]MEM.EN R/W=READ LD.MDR[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Memory reads the halfword at MAR. Nothing is on the bus: memory's output goes straight to MDR.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]MDR ← [code]0x00001842[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]3[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]FETCH_IR[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#c678dd][code]GateMDR LD.IR[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]MDR drives the bus ([code]0x00001842[/code]) and IR takes it: the instruction is now where the FSM can read it.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]IR ← [code]0x1842[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]4[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]DECODE[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#c678dd][code]DR=R2 SR1=R0 SR2=R1 ALUK=ADD[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The FSM reads IR: an ADDS, result to R2, inputs R0 and R1. It sets up register numbers and the ALU operation for the next cycles.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]nothing is stored[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]5[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]FETCH_OPERANDS[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#c678dd][code]SR1=R0 SR2=R1 LD.ALUA LD.ALUB[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The register file reads R0 and R1 into the ALU's input latches. The bus is not needed: the register file has its own read ports.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]ALU A ← [code]0x00000003[/code]
ALU B ← [code]0x00000004[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]6[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]EXECUTE_COMMIT[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#c678dd][code]ALUK=ADD GateALU DR=R2 LD.REG LD.CC[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The ALU adds; GateALU puts the result, [code]0x00000007[/code], on the bus; R2 and the flags load it.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]R2 → [code]0x00000007[/code]
N Z C V ← 0 0 0 0[/cell][/table]

(ALU B already held 4 from the instruction before, so picosim lists only ALU A as changed in cycle 5.)

[color=#61afef][b]Decoding 0x1842[/b][/color]
How does the FSM know, from [code]0x1842[/code], that this is ADDS R2, R0, R1? It looks at groups of bits ([b]fields[/b]). The Thumb encoding of ADDS with three registers is:

[table=5][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Bits[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]15 – 9[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]8 – 6[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]5 – 3[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]2 – 0[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Field[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]opcode: ADDS (registers)[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Rm[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Rn[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Rd[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]0x1842[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]0001100[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]001[/code] = R1[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]000[/code] = R0[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]010[/code] = R2[/cell][/table]

Write [code]0x1842[/code] in binary ([code]0001 1000 0100 0010[/code]) and split it at those places to check. Each register field is 3 bits, which is why these instructions can only name R0–R7.

[color=#61afef][b]What to notice[/b][/color]
[ul]The first three cycles are the same for every instruction: that is the fetch.
The PC already points at the [i]next[/i] instruction ([code]0x3008[/code]) after the first cycle.
The bus carries at most one value per cycle, and in cycles 2, 4 and 5 it carries nothing.
R2 changes only at the very last clock edge. Until then the Registers panel still shows the old value.[/ul]

[color=#61afef][b]Check yourself[/b][/color]
[ol type=1]How many cycles does [code]subs r3, r1, r0[/code] take, and what changes?
In which cycle does the PC change, and why so early?
Why does FETCH_MEMORY not use the bus?[/ol]
[color=#8c8c8c]Answers: 1. Six, the same states; DECODE sets ALUK=SUB, DR=R3, SR1=R1, SR2=R0. 2. At the end of FETCH_ADDR: the +2 incrementer works in the same cycle that the PC is sent to MAR, so the PC is ready for the next fetch. 3. Memory's data output is wired straight to MDR; only MDR's [i]output[/i] goes through a tri-state buffer onto the bus.[/color]

Next: [url=kinds][color=#61afef][u]Other instructions[/u][/color][/url] shows the other kinds of instruction the same way.
3.name: Tutorial: one ADDS
3.sum: This tutorial follows one instruction, [code]adds r2, r0, r1[/code] from [b]Add two numbers[/b], through its six clock cycles with the real values: three fetch cycles, DECODE, FETCH_OPERANDS (R0 and R1 go into the ALU) and EXECUTE_COMMIT (the sum goes into R2 and the flags). Set a breakpoint on it, press [color=#e5c07b][code]Run[/code][/color], then press [color=#e5c07b][code]Step cycle[/code][/color] once for each row of the table.

3.full:
[font_size=26][b]Loads, stores, branches and calls[/b][/font_size]

Every instruction starts with the same 3-cycle fetch (see the [url=tutorial][color=#61afef][u]tutorial[/u][/color][/url]). What follows depends on the kind of instruction. These are the cycles after the fetch, with the values picosim really shows. Set a breakpoint on the instruction, Run to it, and press [color=#e5c07b][code]Step cycle[/code][/color] to follow along.

[color=#61afef][b]Load: ldr r0, [lb]r1]  —  7 cycles[/b][/color]
From [b]Add up a list in memory[/b], address [code]3008[/code], first pass (R1 = [code]0x3024[/code]):

[table=3][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]State[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]What happens[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]At the clock edge[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]DECODE[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]A word load into R0; the address will be R1 + 0. [color=#c678dd][code]DR=R0 ADDR1MUX=SR1 ADDR2MUX=ZEXT(IR[lb]10:6])x4 SIZE=word[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]nothing[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]EVALUATE_ADDRESS[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The address adder adds R1 and the offset (0) and drives the sum onto the bus through GateADDR. [color=#c678dd][code]GateADDR LD.MAR[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]MAR ← [code]0x00003024[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]FETCH_OPERANDS[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Memory reads the word at MAR. [color=#c678dd][code]MEM.EN R/W=READ LD.MDR[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]MDR ← [code]0x0000000A[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]STORE_RESULT[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]MDR drives the bus through LOAD EXT (which would fill in the top bits for ldrb or ldrh) and R0 loads it. [color=#c678dd][code]GateMDR DR=R0 LD.REG[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]R0 → [code]0x0000000A[/code][/cell][/table]

[color=#61afef][b]Store: str r2, [lb]r1]  —  7 cycles[/b][/color]
Same example, address [code]3014[/code] (R1 = [code]0x3034[/code], R2 = [code]0x64[/code]):

[table=3][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]State[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]What happens[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]At the clock edge[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]EVALUATE_ADDRESS[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]As for the load: MAR gets the address.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]MAR ← [code]0x00003034[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]FETCH_OPERANDS[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The data to store must get into MDR. R2 goes through the ALU unchanged ([code]ALUK=PASS[/code]) and onto the bus. [color=#c678dd][code]SR1=R2 ALUK=PASS GateALU LD.MDR[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]MDR ← [code]0x00000064[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]STORE_RESULT[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Memory writes MDR at the address in MAR. [color=#c678dd][code]MEM.EN R/W=WRITE[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]memory [code]3034[/code]–[code]3037[/code] ← [code]64 00 00 00[/code][/cell][/table]

[color=#61afef][b]Branch: bne loop  —  5 cycles[/b][/color]
Same example, address [code]3010[/code], when Z = 0 (taken):

[table=3][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]State[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]What happens[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]At the clock edge[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]DECODE[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]A conditional branch: condition NE; the target will be PC + offset. [color=#c678dd][code]COND=NE ADDR1MUX=PC ADDR2MUX=SEXT(offset)x2[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]nothing[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]EXECUTE_PC[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]COND EVAL checks the flags: Z = 0, so [code]BranchTaken=1[/code]. The address adder works out the target, [code]0x00003014 + (−12) = 0x00003008[/code], and PCMUX passes it to the PC. [color=#c678dd][code]BranchTaken=1 PCMUX=ADDER LD.PC[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]PC → [code]0x00003008[/code][/cell][/table]

When the branch is [i]not[/i] taken (on the last pass), BranchTaken = 0 and LD.PC stays off, so the PC keeps [code]0x3012[/code], the next instruction, which the fetch already put there. Either way it takes 5 cycles.

[table=1][cell bg=#2a2a2a border=#61afef padding=14,9,14,9 expand=1][color=#61afef][b]PC + 4[/b][/color]   Why [code]0x3014[/code] and not [code]0x3010[/code]? On ARM, an instruction that uses the PC as a value always sees its own address + 4. The assembler knows this and works out the offset (−12) to match.[/cell][/table]

[color=#61afef][b]Call: bl twice  —  9 cycles[/b][/color]
From [b]Call a function[/b], address [code]3004[/code]. BL is 32 bits long, so it is fetched in two halves:

[table=3][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]State[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]What happens[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]At the clock edge[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]FETCH_IR[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]IR's top bits ([code]0xF000[/code]) say this is a 32-bit instruction, so…[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]IR ← [code]0xF000[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]FETCH2_ADDR, FETCH2_MEMORY, FETCH2_IR[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]…the fetch runs again for the second halfword, into IR2.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]IR2 ← [code]0xF80C[/code], PC → [code]0x00003008[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]DECODE[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]BL: the offset (24) comes from bits of both IR and IR2. [color=#c678dd][code]DR=LR ADDR1MUX=PC ADDR2MUX=SEXT(offset)x2[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]nothing[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]LINK[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The PC (already the address of the next instruction) goes onto the bus with bit 0 set by SET THUMB, into LR. [color=#c678dd][code]GatePC SET THUMB BIT LD.LR[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]LR → [code]0x00003009[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]EXECUTE_PC[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]PC ← [code]0x00003008 + 24[/code]. [color=#c678dd][code]PCMUX=ADDER LD.PC[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]PC → [code]0x00003020[/code] ([code]twice[/code])[/cell][/table]

[color=#61afef][b]Push and pop: 6 + 2 cycles per register[/b][/color]
[code]push {lr}[/code] in print_digit ([code]3024[/code], SP = [code]0xFFF8[/code]), 8 cycles:

[table=3][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]State[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]What happens[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]At the clock edge[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]EVALUATE_ADDRESS[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The address adder works out SP − 4 × (number of registers). [color=#c678dd][code]ADDR1MUX=SP ADDR2MUX=-4n GateADDR LD.MAR[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]MAR ← [code]0x0000FFF4[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]FETCH_OPERANDS[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]LR passes through the ALU into MDR. [color=#c678dd][code]SR1=LR ALUK=PASS GateALU LD.MDR[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]MDR ← [code]0x0000300D[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]STORE_RESULT[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Memory writes it; MAR steps on by 4 for the next register. [color=#c678dd][code]MEM.EN R/W=WRITE MAR+4[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]memory [code]FFF4[/code] ← [code]0x0000300D[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]WRITEBACK[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]SP is lowered by the same amount. [color=#c678dd][code]ADDR1MUX=SP ADDR2MUX=-4n GateADDR LD.SP[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]SP → [code]0x0000FFF4[/code][/cell][/table]

[code]pop {pc}[/code] at [code]302C[/code] mirrors it: MAR ← SP ([code]0xFFF4[/code]); memory → MDR ([code]0x0000300D[/code]); then, because the register is the PC, [b]EXECUTE_PC[/b] loads PC ← MDR with bit 0 cleared by CLR THUMB ([code]0x0000300C[/code]); WRITEBACK raises SP to [code]0xFFF8[/code]. With 2 registers ([code]push {r7, lr}[/code]) the FETCH_OPERANDS / STORE_RESULT pair runs twice: 10 cycles.

[color=#61afef][b]All the counts[/b][/color]
Operate (ADDS, MOVS, CMP …) 6 · load and store 7 · B and B<cond> 5 · BX 6 · BL 9 · PUSH and POP 6 + 2 per register · SVC and BKPT 5. [url=states][color=#61afef][u]FSM states[/u][/color][/url] lists every sequence, and the full table is in [code]docs/cycles.md[/code].
3.name: Other instructions
3.sum: After the 3-cycle fetch, each kind of instruction uses its own states. A load or store works out its address (EVALUATE_ADDRESS) and then reads or writes memory: 7 cycles. A branch decides and changes the PC: 5 cycles. BL saves the return address in LR and jumps: 9 cycles, because it is 32 bits long and is fetched in two halves. PUSH and POP move one register every two cycles: 6 + 2 per register.

3.full:
[font_size=26][b]Control signals[/b][/font_size]

Each cycle, the FSM turns on a few [b]control signals[/b]. The cycle inspector lists them under [b]Control signals asserted[/b], and on the diagram they are the purple dashed stubs (a bright one is on). Most names follow a pattern:

[table=3][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Signal[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Meaning[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Examples[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#c678dd][code]GateX[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Turn on X's tri-state buffer: X drives the bus this cycle. At most one at a time.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#c678dd][code]GatePC GateMDR GateALU GateADDR GateVEC[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#c678dd][code]LD.X[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]X loads a new value at the clock edge. Without it, X keeps its value.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#c678dd][code]LD.PC LD.MAR LD.MDR LD.IR LD.IR2 LD.REG LD.CC LD.LR LD.SP LD.ALUA LD.ALUB[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#c678dd][code]DR=Rn[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Destination register: which register LD.REG writes.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#c678dd][code]DR=R2[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#c678dd][code]SR1=Rn SR2=Rn[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Source registers: which registers the register file reads.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#c678dd][code]SR1=R0 SR2=R1[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#c678dd][code]PCMUX=…[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Where the PC's next value comes from: the +2 incrementer, the address adder, or the bus.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#c678dd][code]PCMUX=PC+2 PCMUX=ADDER PCMUX=BUS[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#c678dd][code]PCINC=+2[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The incrementer adds 2 to the PC (one halfword).[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#c678dd][code]ADDR1MUX=…[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The address adder's base: the PC, a register (SR1) or SP.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#c678dd][code]ADDR1MUX=SR1[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#c678dd][code]ADDR2MUX=…[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The address adder's offset: an immediate from IR (scaled), a register, or ±4 × the number of registers.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#c678dd][code]ADDR2MUX=ZEXT(IR[lb]10:6])x4 ADDR2MUX=-4n[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#c678dd][code]SR2MUX=IMM[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The ALU's B input takes the immediate from the instruction instead of a register.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#c678dd][code]ALUK=…[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The ALU's operation, named after the instruction (ADD, SUB, AND, LSL, MUL …). PASS lets input A through unchanged.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#c678dd][code]ALUK=ADD ALUK=PASS[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#c678dd][code]MEM.EN R/W=…[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Memory does an access this cycle; READ or WRITE says which way.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#c678dd][code]MEM.EN R/W=READ[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#c678dd][code]SIZE=…[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The access size: word, halfword or byte.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#c678dd][code]SIZE=word[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#c678dd][code]LOAD EXT=…[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]How LOAD EXT widens a loaded byte or halfword to 32 bits: with zeros (Z…) or copies of its sign bit (S…).[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#c678dd][code]LOAD EXT=Zword[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#c678dd][code]STORE ALIGN[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Keeps only the byte or halfword a STRB or STRH writes.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#c678dd][code]IOSEL=IO[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The access goes to an I/O register (address 0x10000 and up) instead of RAM.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#c678dd][code]COND=… BranchTaken=…[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The branch condition from DECODE, and COND EVAL's answer (1 = jump).[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#c678dd][code]COND=NE BranchTaken=1[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#c678dd][code]SET THUMB BIT[/code][/color] / [color=#c678dd][code]CLR THUMB BIT[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Set bit 0 of a return address going into LR; clear it on an address going into the PC.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#c678dd][code]MAR+4[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The +4 incrementer moves MAR on to the next word (PUSH, POP, LDM, STM).[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#c678dd][code]EXCEPTION[/code][/color] / [color=#c678dd][code]HALT[/code][/color][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]An SVC call into the OS, and BKPT stopping the CPU.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][/cell][/table]

Signals listed in DECODE are [i]prepared[/i] there (register numbers, mux selects, the ALU operation) for the cycles that follow; nothing is stored in DECODE itself.
3.name: Control signals
3.sum: Control signals are how the FSM runs the datapath. Most follow a pattern: [code]GateX[/code] puts X on the bus, [code]LD.X[/code] makes X load a new value at the clock edge, [code]XMUX=…[/code] picks a mux input, [code]ALUK=…[/code] picks the ALU's operation, and [code]MEM.EN[/code] with [code]R/W=READ[/code] or [code]WRITE[/code] makes memory do an access. The details list every signal.

3.full:
[font_size=26][b]FSM states[/b][/font_size]

The control unit of the multi-cycle datapath is a finite-state machine (FSM). In every clock cycle it is in exactly one [b]state[/b], and the state decides which control signals are on: which tri-state buffer drives the bus, which registers load at the clock edge, what the muxes select and what the ALU does. Stepping one clock cycle runs one state.

You see the state in the FSM box on the [url=diagram][color=#61afef][u]datapath diagram[/u][/color][/url], in the list of the [url=cycles][color=#61afef][u]cycle-by-cycle inspector[/u][/color][/url] (hover a row for a summary) and as [b]Next state[/b] in the Registers panel.

[color=#61afef][b]The six phases[/b][/color]
Each state belongs to one phase of the instruction cycle. The inspector's chips light up for the phase of the cycle shown.

[table=3][cell padding=0,3,14,3][color=#e5c07b][b]F[/b][/color][/cell][cell padding=0,3,14,3][b]Fetch[/b][/cell][cell padding=0,3,0,3]Read the instruction from memory into IR (and IR2). [color=#8c8c8c]FETCH_ADDR, FETCH_MEMORY, FETCH_IR, FETCH2_ADDR, FETCH2_MEMORY, FETCH2_IR[/color][/cell][cell padding=0,3,14,3][color=#e5c07b][b]D[/b][/color][/cell][cell padding=0,3,14,3][b]Decode[/b][/cell][cell padding=0,3,0,3]Work out what the instruction is and which states come next. [color=#8c8c8c]DECODE[/color][/cell][cell padding=0,3,14,3][color=#e5c07b][b]EA[/b][/color][/cell][cell padding=0,3,14,3][b]Evaluate Address[/b][/cell][cell padding=0,3,0,3]Compute a memory address with the address adder. [color=#8c8c8c]EVALUATE_ADDRESS[/color][/cell][cell padding=0,3,14,3][color=#e5c07b][b]FO[/b][/color][/cell][cell padding=0,3,14,3][b]Fetch Operands[/b][/cell][cell padding=0,3,0,3]Get the values the instruction works on: registers into the ALU, or memory into MDR. [color=#8c8c8c]FETCH_OPERANDS[/color][/cell][cell padding=0,3,14,3][color=#e5c07b][b]EX[/b][/color][/cell][cell padding=0,3,14,3][b]Execute[/b][/cell][cell padding=0,3,0,3]Do the work: the ALU computes, or the PC changes, or the OS is called. [color=#8c8c8c]EXECUTE_COMMIT, EXECUTE_PC, SVC_CALL, HALT[/color][/cell][cell padding=0,3,14,3][color=#e5c07b][b]SR[/b][/color][/cell][cell padding=0,3,14,3][b]Store Result[/b][/cell][cell padding=0,3,0,3]Put the result where it belongs: a register, memory, LR or the base register. [color=#8c8c8c]STORE_RESULT, LINK, WRITEBACK[/color][/cell][/table]

[color=#61afef][b]Which states each instruction uses[/b][/color]
Every instruction starts with the same fetch, [code]FETCH_ADDR → FETCH_MEMORY → FETCH_IR[/code] (3 cycles). After that:
