Some states appear in several kinds of instruction and do a different job in each (FETCH_OPERANDS reads memory for a load but feeds the ALU for an ADDS); each state below lists what it does for which instructions.

[color=#61afef][b]Other words you may see[/b][/color]
[ul]​[b]HALTED[/b] — shown as Next state after BKPT (or a CPU fault): the CPU is stopped. [color=#e5c07b][code]Reload[/code][/color] starts again.
​[b](next)[/b] — the inspector's row for the cycle that has not run yet; between instructions it is always FETCH_ADDR.
​[b]IOSEL=IO[/b] — a memory access to an address of 0x10000 or above goes to the Pico's I/O registers instead of RAM.[/ul]

[hr color=#474747 height=1]
[font_size=20][b]FETCH_ADDR[/b][/font_size]
[color=#8c8c8c]Fetch phase[/color]

MAR ← PC, and the PC steps on to the next halfword.

[color=#61afef][b]At the clock edge[/b][/color]
[code]MAR ← PC
PC ← PC + 2[/code]

[color=#61afef][b]Control signals[/b][/color]
[color=#c678dd][code]GatePC  LD.MAR  PCINC=+2  PCMUX=PC+2  LD.PC[/code][/color]

[color=#61afef][b]Used by[/b][/color]
[ul]​[b]every instruction[/b]  [color=#ababab]— its first clock cycle[/color][/ul]

The PC drives the bus through GatePC so MAR can capture the address. In the same cycle the +2 incrementer feeds PC + 2 through PCMUX, so after this cycle the PC already points past the halfword being fetched.


[hr color=#474747 height=1]
[font_size=20][b]FETCH_MEMORY[/b][/font_size]
[color=#8c8c8c]Fetch phase[/color]

Memory is read at MAR: the instruction halfword goes into MDR.

[color=#61afef][b]At the clock edge[/b][/color]
[code]MDR ← M[MAR]   (16 bits)[/code]

[color=#61afef][b]Control signals[/b][/color]
[color=#c678dd][code]MEM.EN  R/W=READ  LD.MDR[/code][/color]

[color=#61afef][b]Used by[/b][/color]
[ul]​[b]every instruction[/b]  [color=#ababab]— its second clock cycle[/color][/ul]

Nothing drives the bus: memory's data output goes straight into MDR.


[hr color=#474747 height=1]
[font_size=20][b]FETCH_IR[/b][/font_size]
[color=#8c8c8c]Fetch phase[/color]

IR ← MDR: the instruction is now where the FSM can read it.

[color=#61afef][b]At the clock edge[/b][/color]
[code]IR ← MDR[/code]

[color=#61afef][b]Control signals[/b][/color]
[color=#c678dd][code]GateMDR  LD.IR[/code][/color]

[color=#61afef][b]Used by[/b][/color]
[ul]​[b]every instruction[/b]  [color=#ababab]— its third clock cycle[/color][/ul]

If IR's top five bits are 11101, 11110 or 11111 the instruction is 32 bits long, so the FSM goes on to FETCH2_ADDR for its second halfword; otherwise the next state is DECODE.


[hr color=#474747 height=1]
[font_size=20][b]FETCH2_ADDR[/b][/font_size]
[color=#8c8c8c]Fetch phase[/color]

Second fetch of a 32-bit instruction: MAR ← PC, PC ← PC + 2.

[color=#61afef][b]At the clock edge[/b][/color]
[code]MAR ← PC
PC ← PC + 2[/code]

[color=#61afef][b]Control signals[/b][/color]
[color=#c678dd][code]GatePC  LD.MAR  PCINC=+2  PCMUX=PC+2  LD.PC[/code][/color]

[color=#61afef][b]Used by[/b][/color]
[ul]​[b]BL, DMB, DSB, ISB, MRS, MSR[/b]  [color=#ababab]— the 32-bit instructions of the Cortex-M0+[/color][/ul]

The same as FETCH_ADDR, for the instruction's second halfword.


[hr color=#474747 height=1]
[font_size=20][b]FETCH2_MEMORY[/b][/font_size]
[color=#8c8c8c]Fetch phase[/color]

Memory is read at MAR: the second halfword goes into MDR.

[color=#61afef][b]At the clock edge[/b][/color]
[code]MDR ← M[MAR]   (16 bits)[/code]

[color=#61afef][b]Control signals[/b][/color]
[color=#c678dd][code]MEM.EN  R/W=READ  LD.MDR[/code][/color]

[color=#61afef][b]Used by[/b][/color]
[ul]​[b]BL, DMB, DSB, ISB, MRS, MSR[/b][/ul]


[hr color=#474747 height=1]
[font_size=20][b]FETCH2_IR[/b][/font_size]
[color=#8c8c8c]Fetch phase[/color]

IR2 ← MDR: IR and IR2 now hold the whole 32-bit instruction.

[color=#61afef][b]At the clock edge[/b][/color]
[code]IR2 ← MDR[/code]

[color=#61afef][b]Control signals[/b][/color]
[color=#c678dd][code]GateMDR  LD.IR2[/code][/color]

[color=#61afef][b]Used by[/b][/color]
[ul]​[b]BL, DMB, DSB, ISB, MRS, MSR[/b][/ul]

The next state is DECODE.


[hr color=#474747 height=1]
[font_size=20][b]DECODE[/b][/font_size]
[color=#8c8c8c]Decode phase[/color]

The FSM reads IR (and IR2) and sets up the states and selects that follow; nothing is stored.

[color=#61afef][b]At the clock edge[/b][/color]
[code](no register is loaded)[/code]

[color=#61afef][b]Control signals[/b][/color]
[color=#c678dd][code]the selects for the rest of the instruction, for example DR=R2  SR1=R0  SR2=R1  ALUK=ADD  SIZE=word  COND=EQ[/code][/color]

[color=#61afef][b]Used by[/b][/color]
[ul]​[b]every instruction[/b]  [color=#ababab]— its fourth cycle (seventh for a 32-bit one)[/color]
​[b]NOP, YIELD, WFE, WFI, SEV, DMB, DSB, ISB[/b]  [color=#ababab]— the last state: there is nothing more to do (picosim has no interrupts or events, so WFI and WFE do not wait)[/color]
​[b]CPSID i, CPSIE i[/b]  [color=#ababab]— the last state: PRIMASK is set or cleared here (it is not part of the datapath)[/color]
​[b]an undefined instruction[/b]  [color=#ababab]— the CPU stops here with a fault, as the Pico would[/color][/ul]

The signals listed in DECODE are what the FSM [i]prepares[/i]: register numbers (DR destination, SR1 / SR2 sources), mux selects, the ALU operation and the access size. It holds DR and SIZE for the rest of the instruction. No tri-state buffer is on, so the bus is idle.


[hr color=#474747 height=1]
[font_size=20][b]EVALUATE_ADDRESS[/b][/font_size]
[color=#8c8c8c]Evaluate Address phase[/color]

The address adder computes base + offset; MAR ← the address.

[color=#61afef][b]At the clock edge[/b][/color]
[code]MAR ← ADDR1MUX + ADDR2MUX[/code]

[color=#61afef][b]Control signals[/b][/color]
[color=#c678dd][code]ADDR1MUX=…  ADDR2MUX=…  GateADDR  LD.MAR  (SR1=… SR2=…)[/code][/color]

[color=#61afef][b]Used by[/b][/color]
[ul]​[b]LDR, STR, LDRB, STRB, LDRH, STRH, LDRSB, LDRSH[/b]  [color=#ababab]— base register (ADDR1MUX=SR1) or SP (ADDR1MUX=SP) plus an immediate (ZEXT(IR[…])×4, ×2 or ×1) or a second register (ADDR2MUX=SR2)[/color]
​[b]LDR Rd, =constant (literal)[/b]  [color=#ababab]— Align(PC,4) + ZEXT(IR[7:0])×4: the literal pool word[/color]
​[b]ADR[/b]  [color=#ababab]— Align(PC,4) + ZEXT(IR[7:0])×4; the sum is not loaded into MAR yet, it goes to the register in STORE_RESULT[/color]
​[b]PUSH[/b]  [color=#ababab]— SP − 4 × (number of registers): the lowest address written (ADDR2MUX=-4n)[/color]
​[b]POP, LDM, STM[/b]  [color=#ababab]— the base register itself (ADDR2MUX=0)[/color][/ul]

The address adder is separate from the ALU, so computing an address never disturbs the ALU's inputs.


[hr color=#474747 height=1]
[font_size=20][b]FETCH_OPERANDS[/b][/font_size]
[color=#8c8c8c]Fetch Operands phase[/color]

The instruction's operands are fetched: registers into the ALU's A / B latches, memory into MDR, or store data into MDR.

[color=#61afef][b]At the clock edge[/b][/color]
[code]ALU_A ← SR1;  ALU_B ← SR2 or immediate
— or —  MDR ← M[MAR]
— or —  MDR ← register (through the ALU)[/code]

[color=#61afef][b]Control signals[/b][/color]
[color=#c678dd][code]depends on the instruction (below)[/code][/color]

[color=#61afef][b]Used by[/b][/color]
[ul]​[b]ADDS, SUBS, MOVS, CMP, ANDS, LSLS, MULS, MOV, ADD SP … (operate)[/b]  [color=#ababab]— ALU_A ← SR1 and ALU_B ← SR2, or the immediate through SR2MUX (SR2MUX=IMM): LD.ALUA LD.ALUB. MOV, MVN, NEG, SXTB … use only B[/color]
​[b]LDR … (loads), and POP / LDM once per register[/b]  [color=#ababab]— MDR ← M[MAR] in the access size: MEM.EN R/W=READ LD.MDR (and IOSEL=IO for an I/O register at 0x10000 and up)[/color]
​[b]STR … (stores), and PUSH / STM once per register[/b]  [color=#ababab]— MDR ← the register being stored, passed through the ALU: SR1=… ALUK=PASS GateALU LD.MDR (STORE ALIGN keeps only the byte or halfword for STRB / STRH)[/color]
​[b]BX, BLX[/b]  [color=#ababab]— ALU_A ← the register holding the target address: SR1=… LD.ALUA[/color][/ul]


[hr color=#474747 height=1]
[font_size=20][b]EXECUTE_COMMIT[/b][/font_size]
[color=#8c8c8c]Execute phase[/color]

The ALU computes, and the result is committed: DR ← result, flags ← N Z C V.

[color=#61afef][b]At the clock edge[/b][/color]
[code]DR ← ALU(ALU_A, ALU_B)
NZCV ← the ALU's flags   (if the instruction sets them)[/code]

[color=#61afef][b]Control signals[/b][/color]
[color=#c678dd][code]ALUK=…  GateALU  DR=…  LD.REG  LD.CC[/code][/color]

[color=#61afef][b]Used by[/b][/color]
[ul]​[b]ADDS, SUBS, ANDS, LSLS, MOVS … (operate)[/b]  [color=#ababab]— the result goes over the bus into the destination register, and LD.CC loads the flags for the S forms[/color]
​[b]CMP, CMN, TST[/b]  [color=#ababab]— only the flags change (LD.CC): no GateALU, no register is written[/color]
​[b]MOV, ADD (high registers), ADD SP, SXTB, REV …[/b]  [color=#ababab]— the register is written; the flags are not[/color]
​[b]MOV PC, Rm / ADD PC, Rm[/b]  [color=#ababab]— the result goes to the PC instead (CLR THUMB BIT, PCMUX=BUS, LD.PC): a branch[/color]
​[b]MRS Rd, <special register>[/b]  [color=#ababab]— GateSYS puts APSR, PRIMASK, CONTROL, MSP or PSP on the bus and Rd loads it. These registers are not drawn on the diagram[/color]
​[b]MSR <special register>, Rn[/b]  [color=#ababab]— Rn passes through the ALU onto the bus and the special register loads it (LD.SYS); MSR APSR sets the flags[/color][/ul]

This is where an operate instruction does its real work, in a single cycle: compute and write back together.


[hr color=#474747 height=1]
[font_size=20][b]EXECUTE_PC[/b][/font_size]
[color=#8c8c8c]Execute phase[/color]

The PC changes: a branch, call or return goes to its target (or a branch not taken leaves the PC alone).

[color=#61afef][b]At the clock edge[/b][/color]
[code]PC ← target[/code]

[color=#61afef][b]Control signals[/b][/color]
[color=#c678dd][code]PCMUX=ADDER or PCMUX=BUS, LD.PC (BranchTaken=0/1 for B<cond>)[/code][/color]

[color=#61afef][b]Used by[/b][/color]
[ul]​[b]B label[/b]  [color=#ababab]— PC ← PC + offset: the address adder (ADDR1MUX=PC, ADDR2MUX=SEXT(offset)×2) feeds PCMUX=ADDER. Here PC means the branch's own address + 4[/color]
​[b]B<cond> label (BEQ, BNE, BLT …)[/b]  [color=#ababab]— COND EVAL compares the flags with the condition and tells the FSM BranchTaken. 1: as B. 0: no LD.PC, so the PC keeps the address of the next instruction[/color]
​[b]BL label[/b]  [color=#ababab]— PC ← PC + offset, after LINK has saved the return address[/color]
​[b]BX Rm, BLX Rm[/b]  [color=#ababab]— PC ← ALU_A (passed through the ALU) with bit 0 cleared by CLR THUMB (PCMUX=BUS). Bit 0 must be 1 (Thumb), or the CPU faults as the Pico would[/color]
​[b]POP {…, PC}[/b]  [color=#ababab]— PC ← MDR (the popped return address) with bit 0 cleared; MAR ← MAR + 4[/color][/ul]


[hr color=#474747 height=1]
[font_size=20][b]STORE_RESULT[/b][/font_size]
[color=#8c8c8c]Store Result phase[/color]

The result is stored: a loaded value into its register, or store data into memory.

[color=#61afef][b]At the clock edge[/b][/color]
[code]DR ← LOAD EXT(MDR)
— or —  M[MAR] ← MDR[/code]

[color=#61afef][b]Control signals[/b][/color]
[color=#c678dd][code]depends on the instruction (below)[/code][/color]

[color=#61afef][b]Used by[/b][/color]
[ul]​[b]LDR, LDRB, LDRH, LDRSB, LDRSH, LDR =constant[/b]  [color=#ababab]— DR ← MDR through LOAD EXT, which zero- or sign-extends a byte or halfword to 32 bits: LOAD EXT=… GateMDR DR=… LD.REG[/color]
​[b]STR, STRB, STRH[/b]  [color=#ababab]— M[MAR] ← MDR: MEM.EN R/W=WRITE (IOSEL=IO for an I/O register)[/color]
​[b]ADR[/b]  [color=#ababab]— DR ← the address adder's sum: GateADDR LD.REG[/color]
​[b]POP, LDM (once per register)[/b]  [color=#ababab]— the register ← MDR, and MAR ← MAR + 4 for the next word[/color]
​[b]PUSH, STM (once per register)[/b]  [color=#ababab]— M[MAR] ← MDR, and MAR ← MAR + 4 for the next word[/color][/ul]


[hr color=#474747 height=1]
[font_size=20][b]LINK[/b][/font_size]
[color=#8c8c8c]Store Result phase[/color]

LR ← the return address with bit 0 set, so the called function can come back.

[color=#61afef][b]At the clock edge[/b][/color]
[code]LR ← PC | 1[/code]

[color=#61afef][b]Control signals[/b][/color]
[color=#c678dd][code]GatePC  SET THUMB BIT  LD.LR[/code][/color]

[color=#61afef][b]Used by[/b][/color]
[ul]​[b]BL, BLX[/b]  [color=#ababab]— before EXECUTE_PC changes the PC[/color][/ul]

The PC already points at the instruction after the call (it stepped on during fetch), which is exactly where the function must return to. Bit 0 = 1 marks it as Thumb code, so BX LR and POP {PC} can use it.


[hr color=#474747 height=1]
[font_size=20][b]WRITEBACK[/b][/font_size]
[color=#8c8c8c]Store Result phase[/color]

The base register moves past the words transferred: SP ← SP ∓ 4n (PUSH / POP) or Rn ← Rn + 4n (STM / LDM).

[color=#61afef][b]At the clock edge[/b][/color]
[code]SP ← SP − 4n   (PUSH)
SP ← SP + 4n   (POP)
Rn ← Rn + 4n   (STM, LDM)[/code]

[color=#61afef][b]Control signals[/b][/color]
[color=#c678dd][code]ADDR1MUX=SP or SR1  ADDR2MUX=-4n or +4n  GateADDR  LD.SP or LD.REG[/code][/color]

[color=#61afef][b]Used by[/b][/color]
[ul]​[b]PUSH, POP, STM, LDM[/b]  [color=#ababab]— the last state. LDM skips it when the base register is in the list (it was just loaded)[/color][/ul]

n is the number of registers in the list. The address adder computes the new value, so the ALU is not needed.


[hr color=#474747 height=1]
[font_size=20][b]SVC_CALL[/b][/font_size]
[color=#8c8c8c]Execute phase[/color]

Supervisor call: GateVEC drives the SVCall vector address 0x0000002C, and picosim performs the OS service.

[color=#61afef][b]At the clock edge[/b][/color]
[code]bus ← 0x0000002C (SVCall vector)
the OS service runs[/code]

[color=#61afef][b]Control signals[/b][/color]
[color=#c678dd][code]GateVEC  EXCEPTION[/code][/color]

[color=#61afef][b]Used by[/b][/color]
[ul]​[b]SVC #n[/b]  [color=#ababab]— #2 putchar, #3 getchar, #1 exit, #0 write[/color][/ul]

On a real Cortex-M0+ an SVC starts exception entry: the CPU saves registers on the stack and jumps to the handler whose address is in the vector table at 0x2C (exception 11 × 4). picosim shows the first step, then runs the service directly instead of simulating a handler. A getchar with no key typed waits in this state.


[hr color=#474747 height=1]
[font_size=20][b]HALT[/b][/font_size]
[color=#8c8c8c]Execute phase[/color]

BKPT: the processor stops.

[color=#61afef][b]At the clock edge[/b][/color]
[code](the CPU halts)[/code]

[color=#61afef][b]Control signals[/b][/color]
[color=#c678dd][code]HALT[/code][/color]

[color=#61afef][b]Used by[/b][/color]
[ul]​[b]BKPT[/b]  [color=#ababab]— the built-in OS runs BKPT when your main returns, so this is how every program ends[/color][/ul]

After this the Registers panel shows Next state: HALTED. Press Reload to start again. On a real Pico, BKPT stops the CPU only when a debugger is attached; without one it causes a HardFault.
4.name: FSM states
4.sum: The FSM is always in exactly one [b]state[/b], and each state is one clock cycle that turns on its own control signals. Every instruction starts with [code]FETCH_ADDR → FETCH_MEMORY → FETCH_IR[/code], then DECODE, then the states its kind needs: for example FETCH_OPERANDS → EXECUTE_COMMIT for an ADDS. The details list every state, what it does and which instructions use it.

4.full:
[font_size=26][b]Datapath components[/b][/font_size]

Every block on the multi-cycle [url=diagram][color=#61afef][u]datapath diagram[/u][/color][/url], in the order data usually flows. Click a block on the diagram to see the same text next to it.

[hr color=#474747 height=1]
[font_size=20][b]PC — Program Counter[/b][/font_size]
[color=#8c8c8c]Register (loads at the clock edge)[/color]

[color=#61afef][b]What it does[/b][/color]
Holds the address of the next instruction halfword to fetch. Every instruction starts by copying the PC to MAR.

[color=#61afef][b]How it works[/b][/color]
In FETCH_ADDR the PC drives the bus through GatePC so MAR can capture it; in the same cycle the +2 incrementer and PCMUX feed PC + 2 back and LD.PC loads it at the clock edge — so the box still shows the old PC during FETCH_ADDR and the new one from FETCH_MEMORY on. Later in the instruction a branch can load a new value through PCMUX. Because the PC register is stepped during fetch, it holds A + 2 after a 16-bit instruction at address A (A + 4 after BL); an instruction that reads the PC as an operand always gets A + 4, as ARMv6-M defines.

[color=#61afef][b]Connects to[/b][/color]
[color=#8c8c8c]receives from[/color]
[ul]​[b]PCMUX[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]LD.PC[/code][/color]  [color=#ababab]— the next PC value[/color][/ul]
[color=#8c8c8c]sends to[/color]
[ul]​[b]GatePC[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]GatePC[/code][/color]  [color=#ababab]— to the bus, then MAR[/color]
​[b]+2[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]PCINC=+2[/code][/color]  [color=#ababab]— the +2 incrementer reads it[/color]
​[b]PC / Align(PC,4)[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]ADDR1MUX=PC / Align[/code][/color]  [color=#ababab]— PC-relative base for branches and literal loads[/color][/ul]

[color=#61afef][b]When it is used[/b][/color]
Every FETCH_ADDR cycle; EXECUTE_PC for B, BL, BX, BLX, POP {PC}.

[hr color=#474747 height=1]
[font_size=20][b]+2 — PC incrementer[/b][/font_size]
[color=#8c8c8c]Combinational adder[/color]

[color=#61afef][b]What it does[/b][/color]
Computes PC + 2, the address of the next sequential halfword (Thumb instructions are 2 bytes).

[color=#61afef][b]How it works[/b][/color]
It is an adder drawn sideways: the PC enters its long side and PC + 2 leaves its short side. PCINC (its control input, from the FSM) selects the increment; this model fetches one halfword at a time, so it is always +2 and BL simply fetches twice. The result only matters when PCMUX selects it (PCMUX=PC+2) and LD.PC is asserted, which happens in every fetch cycle FETCH_ADDR / FETCH2_ADDR.

[color=#61afef][b]Connects to[/b][/color]
[color=#8c8c8c]receives from[/color]
[ul]​[b]PC[/b]  [color=#ababab]— current PC[/color][/ul]
[color=#8c8c8c]sends to[/color]
[ul]​[b]PCMUX[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]PCMUX=PC+2[/code][/color]  [color=#ababab]— sequential next PC[/color][/ul]
[color=#8c8c8c]controlled by[/color]
[ul]​[b]FSM[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]PCINC[/code][/color]  [color=#ababab]— selects +2[/color][/ul]

[color=#61afef][b]When it is used[/b][/color]
FETCH_ADDR and FETCH2_ADDR.

[hr color=#474747 height=1]
[font_size=20][b]PCMUX — next-PC selector[/b][/font_size]
[color=#8c8c8c]Multiplexer (select lines from the FSM)[/color]

[color=#61afef][b]What it does[/b][/color]
Chooses which value the PC loads next.

[color=#61afef][b]How it works[/b][/color]
It chooses between three inputs: PC+2 (sequential fetch), ADDER (a branch target computed by the address adder) and BUS through CLR THUMB (an address held in a register: BX, BLX, POP {PC}, MOV/ADD PC). The FSM sets the select and asserts LD.PC in the same cycle. For a conditional branch that is not taken the FSM simply does not assert LD.PC, so the PC keeps the sequential value it loaded during fetch.

[color=#61afef][b]Connects to[/b][/color]
[color=#8c8c8c]receives from[/color]
[ul]​[b]+2[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]PCMUX=PC+2[/code][/color]
​[b]ADDRESS ADDER[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]PCMUX=ADDER[/code][/color]  [color=#ababab]— branch target[/color]
​[b]CLR THUMB[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]PCMUX=BUS[/code][/color]  [color=#ababab]— register target[/color][/ul]
[color=#8c8c8c]sends to[/color]
[ul]​[b]PC[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]LD.PC[/code][/color][/ul]
[color=#8c8c8c]controlled by[/color]
[ul]​[b]FSM[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]PCMUX[/code][/color]  [color=#ababab]— select: PC+2 / ADDER / BUS[/color][/ul]

[color=#61afef][b]When it is used[/b][/color]
Fetch (PC+2); EXECUTE_PC of branches.

[hr color=#474747 height=1]
[font_size=20][b]CLR THUMB — clear bit 0[/b][/font_size]
[color=#8c8c8c]Combinational logic[/color]

[color=#61afef][b]What it does[/b][/color]
Clears the Thumb bit (bit 0) of a jump address, so the next fetch uses an even, halfword-aligned address.

[color=#61afef][b]How it works[/b][/color]
Addresses stored in LR or used by BX have bit 0 set to mean 'Thumb state'. When such a value goes from the bus into the PC, this block forces bit 0 to 0 (value & ~1) before it reaches PCMUX. The bus itself still carries the value with bit 0 set.

[color=#61afef][b]Connects to[/b][/color]
[color=#8c8c8c]receives from[/color]
[ul]​[b]BUS[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]CLR THUMB BIT[/code][/color]  [color=#ababab]— target address from a register[/color][/ul]
[color=#8c8c8c]sends to[/color]
[ul]​[b]PCMUX[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]PCMUX=BUS[/code][/color][/ul]

[color=#61afef][b]When it is used[/b][/color]
EXECUTE_PC of BX, BLX, POP {PC}, MOV PC / ADD PC.

[hr color=#474747 height=1]
[font_size=20][b]PC / Align(PC,4)[/b][/font_size]
[color=#8c8c8c]Combinational logic[/color]

[color=#61afef][b]What it does[/b][/color]
Supplies the PC-relative base for the address adder.

[color=#61afef][b]How it works[/b][/color]
Thumb defines the PC read value as A + 4, where A is the address of the instruction being executed. After fetch the PC register already points past the instruction (A + 2 for a 16-bit instruction, A + 4 after BL's two halfwords), so this block forms A + 4 from it. With ADDR1MUX=PC it passes A + 4 on unchanged (B, B<cond>, BL). With ADDR1MUX=Align(PC,4) it rounds A + 4 down to a multiple of 4 (clears bits 1:0) for LDR Rd, =literal / LDR Rd, [PC, #imm] and ADR, whose offsets count words from a word-aligned base.

[color=#61afef][b]Connects to[/b][/color]
[color=#8c8c8c]receives from[/color]
[ul]​[b]PC[/b][/ul]
[color=#8c8c8c]sends to[/color]
[ul]​[b]ADDR1MUX[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]ADDR1MUX=PC / Align(PC,4)[/code][/color][/ul]

[color=#61afef][b]When it is used[/b][/color]
B, B<cond>, BL (PC); LDR literal and ADR (Align).

[hr color=#474747 height=1]
[font_size=20][b]ADDR1MUX — address base selector[/b][/font_size]
[color=#8c8c8c]Multiplexer[/color]

[color=#61afef][b]What it does[/b][/color]
Chooses the base (left) input of the address adder.

[color=#61afef][b]How it works[/b][/color]
It chooses the base address for the address adder: PC or Align(PC,4) for PC-relative addressing, a register from the register file's SR1 port (LDR R2, [R0, #4]) or SP (LDR R2, [SP, #4], PUSH, POP). The FSM sets the select in DECODE and holds it through the cycle that uses the adder.

[color=#61afef][b]Connects to[/b][/color]
[color=#8c8c8c]receives from[/color]
[ul]​[b]PC / Align(PC,4)[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]ADDR1MUX=PC / Align[/code][/color]
​[b]REGISTER FILE[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]ADDR1MUX=SR1 / SP[/code][/color]  [color=#ababab]— shown as the 'SR1 / SP' stub[/color][/ul]
[color=#8c8c8c]sends to[/color]
[ul]​[b]ADDRESS ADDER[/b]  [color=#ababab]— base[/color][/ul]
[color=#8c8c8c]controlled by[/color]
[ul]​[b]FSM[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]ADDR1MUX[/code][/color]  [color=#ababab]— select[/color][/ul]

[color=#61afef][b]When it is used[/b][/color]
EVALUATE_ADDRESS of loads/stores; branches.

[hr color=#474747 height=1]
[font_size=20][b]ADDR2MUX — address offset selector[/b][/font_size]
[color=#8c8c8c]Multiplexer[/color]

[color=#61afef][b]What it does[/b][/color]
Chooses the offset (right) input of the address adder.

[color=#61afef][b]How it works[/b][/color]
It chooses the offset for the address adder: an immediate scaled by the access size (for LDR R2, [R0, #8] the instruction holds 2, and ×4 gives 8), a branch offset ×2 (sign-extended, so it can be negative), a second register (SR2) for [Rn, Rm] addressing, −4n or +4n for PUSH, POP, LDM and STM (n = how many registers), or zero. The immediates come from IMM / OFFSET.

[color=#61afef][b]Connects to[/b][/color]
[color=#8c8c8c]receives from[/color]
[ul]​[b]IMM / OFFSET[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]ADDR2MUX=ZEXT / SEXT[/code][/color]  [color=#ababab]— immediate or branch offset[/color]
​[b]REGISTER FILE[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]ADDR2MUX=SR2[/code][/color]  [color=#ababab]— index register[/color][/ul]
[color=#8c8c8c]sends to[/color]
[ul]​[b]ADDRESS ADDER[/b]  [color=#ababab]— offset[/color][/ul]
[color=#8c8c8c]controlled by[/color]
[ul]​[b]FSM[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]ADDR2MUX[/code][/color]  [color=#ababab]— select[/color][/ul]

[color=#61afef][b]When it is used[/b][/color]
Same cycles as ADDR1MUX; −4n / +4n in EVALUATE_ADDRESS and WRITEBACK of PUSH, POP, LDM, STM.

[hr color=#474747 height=1]
[font_size=20][b]ADDRESS ADDER[/b][/font_size]
[color=#8c8c8c]Combinational adder (separate from the ALU)[/color]

[color=#61afef][b]What it does[/b][/color]
Adds base + offset to form an effective memory address or a branch target.

[color=#61afef][b]How it works[/b][/color]
It adds the base from ADDR1MUX and the offset from ADDR2MUX. It has no control input: it always adds, and the FSM decides who uses the sum. Because it is its own adder, address arithmetic never occupies the ALU. The sum either drives the bus through GateADDR so MAR — or a register, for ADR and the SP update of PUSH/POP — can capture it, or goes straight to PCMUX as a branch target.

[color=#61afef][b]Connects to[/b][/color]
[color=#8c8c8c]receives from[/color]
[ul]​[b]ADDR1MUX[/b]  [color=#ababab]— base[/color]
​[b]ADDR2MUX[/b]  [color=#ababab]— offset[/color][/ul]
[color=#8c8c8c]sends to[/color]
[ul]​[b]GateADDR[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]GateADDR[/code][/color]  [color=#ababab]— to the bus: MAR or a register[/color]
​[b]PCMUX[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]PCMUX=ADDER[/code][/color]  [color=#ababab]— branch target[/color][/ul]

[color=#61afef][b]When it is used[/b][/color]
EVALUATE_ADDRESS (loads, stores, PUSH/POP); EXECUTE_PC (B, BL); STORE_RESULT of ADR; WRITEBACK of PUSH/POP/LDM/STM (new SP or base register).

[hr color=#474747 height=1]
[font_size=20][b]IR — Instruction Register[/b][/font_size]
[color=#8c8c8c]Register (16 bits)[/color]

[color=#61afef][b]What it does[/b][/color]
Holds the instruction being executed (or the first half of a 32-bit one) for the whole instruction.

[color=#61afef][b]How it works[/b][/color]
Loaded from the bus at the clock edge that ends FETCH_IR (GateMDR + LD.IR), so it shows the new instruction from DECODE on. Its bits are wired to the FSM, which decodes the opcode, and to IMM / OFFSET, which pulls out immediates and register numbers. It does not change again until the next fetch.

[color=#61afef][b]Connects to[/b][/color]
[color=#8c8c8c]receives from[/color]
[ul]​[b]BUS[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]LD.IR[/code][/color]  [color=#ababab]— the fetched halfword (via MDR)[/color][/ul]
[color=#8c8c8c]sends to[/color]
[ul]​[b]FSM[/b]  [color=#ababab]— opcode bits for decoding[/color]
​[b]IMM / OFFSET[/b]  [color=#ababab]— immediate and offset fields[/color][/ul]

[color=#61afef][b]When it is used[/b][/color]
Loaded every FETCH_IR; read in DECODE.

[hr color=#474747 height=1]
[font_size=20][b]IR2 — second instruction halfword[/b][/font_size]
[color=#8c8c8c]Register (16 bits)[/color]

[color=#61afef][b]What it does[/b][/color]
Holds the second halfword of a 32-bit encoding: BL, or the rarer MRS, MSR, DMB, DSB and ISB.

[color=#61afef][b]How it works[/b][/color]
When DECODE finds a 32-bit prefix in IR, the FSM runs a second fetch (FETCH2_ADDR → FETCH2_MEMORY → FETCH2_IR) that loads IR2. For BL its bits complete the branch offset in IMM / OFFSET; for MRS, MSR and the barriers (DMB, DSB, ISB) they name the special register or option.

[color=#61afef][b]Connects to[/b][/color]
[color=#8c8c8c]receives from[/color]
[ul]​[b]BUS[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]LD.IR2[/code][/color][/ul]
[color=#8c8c8c]sends to[/color]
[ul]​[b]IMM / OFFSET[/b]  [color=#ababab]— rest of the offset[/color][/ul]

[color=#61afef][b]When it is used[/b][/color]
BL (the only common 32-bit instruction).

[hr color=#474747 height=1]
[font_size=20][b]FSM — control unit[/b][/font_size]
[color=#8c8c8c]Finite state machine[/color]

[color=#61afef][b]What it does[/b][/color]
Runs the datapath. Each clock cycle it is in one state, asserts that state's control signals, and chooses the next state.

[color=#61afef][b]How it works[/b][/color]
Every instruction begins FETCH_ADDR → FETCH_MEMORY → FETCH_IR. In DECODE it reads IR and picks the path for this instruction (e.g. EVALUATE_ADDRESS → FETCH_OPERANDS → STORE_RESULT for a load). The signals it asserts — gates (GateX puts X on the bus), loads (LD.X makes X capture its input at the clock edge), mux selects and the ALU function (ALUK) — are listed in the cycle panel. For conditional branches it uses BranchTaken from COND EVAL.

[color=#61afef][b]Connects to[/b][/color]
[color=#8c8c8c]receives from[/color]
[ul]​[b]IR[/b]  [color=#ababab]— opcode[/color]
​[b]COND EVAL[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]BranchTaken[/code][/color]  [color=#ababab]— take the branch or not[/color][/ul]
[color=#8c8c8c]sends to[/color]
[ul] [color=#ababab]— control signals to every block: drawn as the short purple stubs into the muxes, the ALU, the +2 incrementer and the tri-state buffers; the load enables (LD.x) are not drawn[/color][/ul]

[color=#61afef][b]When it is used[/b][/color]
Every cycle — the box shows the state of the cycle on display.

[hr color=#474747 height=1]
[font_size=20][b]IMM / OFFSET — immediate extractor[/b][/font_size]
[color=#8c8c8c]Combinational logic[/color]

[color=#61afef][b]What it does[/b][/color]
Extracts constants from the instruction bits and widens them to 32 bits.

[color=#61afef][b]How it works[/b][/color]
Depending on the instruction it takes a field from IR (and IR2), then zero-extends it (ZEXT) or sign-extends it (SEXT) and scales it: ×4 for word offsets, ×2 for halfword offsets and branch offsets, ×1 for bytes. The result goes to ADDR2MUX (addresses, branches) or SR2MUX (ALU immediates like ADDS R0, #5).

[color=#61afef][b]Connects to[/b][/color]
[color=#8c8c8c]receives from[/color]
[ul]​[b]IR[/b]
​[b]IR2[/b]  [color=#ababab]— 32-bit encodings[/color][/ul]
[color=#8c8c8c]sends to[/color]
[ul]​[b]ADDR2MUX[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]ADDR2MUX=ZEXT / SEXT[/code][/color]
​[b]SR2MUX[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]SR2MUX=IMM[/code][/color][/ul]

[color=#61afef][b]When it is used[/b][/color]
DECODE onward, whenever an instruction has an immediate.

[hr color=#474747 height=1]
[font_size=20][b]COND EVAL — branch condition[/b][/font_size]
[color=#8c8c8c]Combinational logic[/color]

[color=#61afef][b]What it does[/b][/color]
Decides whether a conditional branch (BEQ, BNE, BLT, …) is taken.

[color=#61afef][b]How it works[/b][/color]
It compares the condition field IR[11:8] against the N, Z, C and V flags (e.g. EQ is Z = 1, LT is N ≠ V) and sends BranchTaken to the FSM. If it is 1 the FSM selects PCMUX=ADDER and asserts LD.PC; if 0 the PC keeps its sequential value.

[color=#61afef][b]Connects to[/b][/color]
[color=#8c8c8c]receives from[/color]
[ul]​[b]N Z C V[/b]  [color=#ababab]— N Z C V[/color][/ul]
[color=#8c8c8c]sends to[/color]
[ul]​[b]FSM[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]BranchTaken[/code][/color]  [color=#ababab]— control (purple dashed)[/color][/ul]

[color=#61afef][b]When it is used[/b][/color]
EXECUTE_PC of B<cond>.

[hr color=#474747 height=1]
[font_size=20][b]VECTOR ADDR[/b][/font_size]
[color=#8c8c8c]Constant source[/color]

[color=#61afef][b]What it does[/b][/color]
Provides the exception vector address for a supervisor call.

[color=#61afef][b]How it works[/b][/color]
On SVC entry it supplies the SVCall vector address, 0x0000002C (SVCall is exception number 11, and each vector-table entry is 4 bytes), and GateVEC puts it on the bus. A complete exception entry would read the handler's address from that vector and save a stack frame (Chapter 13). picosim simplifies this: it performs the call directly — for example putchar (SVC #2) and getchar (SVC #3) — and continues with the next instruction.

[color=#61afef][b]Connects to[/b][/color]
[color=#8c8c8c]sends to[/color]
[ul]​[b]GateVEC[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]GateVEC[/code][/color]  [color=#ababab]— to the bus[/color][/ul]

[color=#61afef][b]When it is used[/b][/color]
SVC_CALL (putchar, getchar).

[hr color=#474747 height=1]
[font_size=20][b]BUS — shared 32-bit bus[/b][/font_size]
[color=#8c8c8c]Shared wires with tri-state gates[/color]

[color=#61afef][b]What it does[/b][/color]
The single path most values take between blocks.

[color=#61afef][b]How it works[/b][/color]
Five tri-state buffers (the triangles) can drive it: GatePC, GateADDR, GateALU, GateMDR and GateVEC. A tri-state buffer has a data input, a data output and one control input. While its control signal is 1 the output copies the input; while it is 0 the output is high impedance (Z): electrically disconnected, driving the wires neither high nor low. The FSM turns on at most one Gate signal per cycle, because two enabled buffers would fight over the same wires. A buffer stores nothing: the bus carries a value only during the cycle. Every block whose load signal is asserted (LD.MAR, LD.IR, LD.REG, …) captures the bus value at the clock edge. Because there is only one bus, moving two values needs two cycles — which is why instructions take several cycles. The value on the bus is shown above it.

[color=#61afef][b]Connects to[/b][/color]
[color=#8c8c8c]receives from[/color]
[ul]​[b]GatePC[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]GatePC[/code][/color]  [color=#ababab]— the PC[/color]
​[b]GateADDR[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]GateADDR[/code][/color]  [color=#ababab]— address adder[/color]
​[b]GateALU[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]GateALU[/code][/color]  [color=#ababab]— ALU result[/color]
​[b]GateMDR[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]GateMDR[/code][/color]  [color=#ababab]— memory data[/color]
​[b]GateVEC[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]GateVEC[/code][/color]  [color=#ababab]— exception vector[/color][/ul]
[color=#8c8c8c]sends to[/color]
[ul]​[b]MAR[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]LD.MAR[/code][/color]
​[b]IR[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]LD.IR[/code][/color]
​[b]IR2[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]LD.IR2[/code][/color]
​[b]REGISTER FILE[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]LD.REG[/code][/color]
​[b]STORE ALIGN[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]LD.MDR[/code][/color]  [color=#ababab]— store data[/color]
​[b]CLR THUMB[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]PCMUX=BUS[/code][/color]
​[b]SET THUMB[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]SET THUMB BIT[/code][/color][/ul]

[color=#61afef][b]When it is used[/b][/color]
Almost every cycle.

[hr color=#474747 height=1]
[font_size=20][b]GatePC — PC tri-state buffer[/b][/font_size]
[color=#8c8c8c]Tri-state buffer (control: GatePC)[/color]

[color=#61afef][b]What it does[/b][/color]
Connects the PC to the bus when GatePC is asserted, so the current fetch address (or a return address) can reach other registers.

[color=#61afef][b]How it works[/b][/color]
While GatePC is 1 the buffer copies the PC's value onto the bus; while it is 0 it is disconnected (high impedance, Z). The BUS card explains how the five buffers share the bus. In FETCH_ADDR the bus carries the PC to MAR; in the LINK state of BL / BLX it carries the return address to SET THUMB and LR.

[color=#61afef][b]Connects to[/b][/color]
[color=#8c8c8c]receives from[/color]
[ul]​[b]PC[/b]  [color=#ababab]— the PC's value[/color][/ul]
[color=#8c8c8c]sends to[/color]
[ul]​[b]BUS[/b]  [color=#ababab]— drives the shared bus[/color][/ul]
[color=#8c8c8c]controlled by[/color]
[ul]​[b]FSM[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]GatePC[/code][/color]  [color=#ababab]— 1 = drive the bus, 0 = off (Z)[/color][/ul]

[color=#61afef][b]When it is used[/b][/color]
FETCH_ADDR and FETCH2_ADDR of every instruction; LINK of BL and BLX.

[hr color=#474747 height=1]
[font_size=20][b]GateADDR — address-adder tri-state buffer[/b][/font_size]
[color=#8c8c8c]Tri-state buffer (control: GateADDR)[/color]

[color=#61afef][b]What it does[/b][/color]
Connects the address adder's sum to the bus when GateADDR is asserted, so an effective address can be loaded into MAR or a computed address into a register.

[color=#61afef][b]How it works[/b][/color]
While GateADDR is 1 the buffer copies the address adder's value onto the bus; while it is 0 it is disconnected (high impedance, Z). The BUS card explains how the five buffers share the bus. A branch target does not need it: it reaches PCMUX on its own wire.

[color=#61afef][b]Connects to[/b][/color]
[color=#8c8c8c]receives from[/color]
[ul]​[b]ADDRESS ADDER[/b]  [color=#ababab]— base + offset[/color][/ul]
[color=#8c8c8c]sends to[/color]
[ul]​[b]BUS[/b]  [color=#ababab]— to MAR (loads, stores) or a register (ADR, SP update)[/color][/ul]
[color=#8c8c8c]controlled by[/color]
[ul]​[b]FSM[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]GateADDR[/code][/color]  [color=#ababab]— 1 = drive the bus, 0 = off (Z)[/color][/ul]

[color=#61afef][b]When it is used[/b][/color]
EVALUATE_ADDRESS of loads, stores, PUSH, POP, LDM, STM; STORE_RESULT of ADR; WRITEBACK of PUSH, POP, LDM, STM.

[hr color=#474747 height=1]
[font_size=20][b]GateMDR — memory-data tri-state buffer[/b][/font_size]
[color=#8c8c8c]Tri-state buffer (control: GateMDR)[/color]

[color=#61afef][b]What it does[/b][/color]
Connects the memory data (MDR, after LOAD EXT has selected and extended the right bytes) to the bus when GateMDR is asserted.

[color=#61afef][b]How it works[/b][/color]
While GateMDR is 1 the buffer copies LOAD EXT's value onto the bus; while it is 0 it is disconnected (high impedance, Z). The BUS card explains how the five buffers share the bus. It is how a fetched instruction reaches IR, and how loaded data reaches a register or the PC.

[color=#61afef][b]Connects to[/b][/color]
[color=#8c8c8c]receives from[/color]
[ul]​[b]LOAD EXT[/b]  [color=#ababab]— MDR, extended to 32 bits[/color][/ul]
[color=#8c8c8c]sends to[/color]
[ul]​[b]BUS[/b]  [color=#ababab]— to IR, IR2, a register or the PC[/color][/ul]
[color=#8c8c8c]controlled by[/color]
[ul]​[b]FSM[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]GateMDR[/code][/color]  [color=#ababab]— 1 = drive the bus, 0 = off (Z)[/color][/ul]

[color=#61afef][b]When it is used[/b][/color]
FETCH_IR / FETCH2_IR of every instruction; STORE_RESULT of loads; each register of POP and LDM.

[hr color=#474747 height=1]
[font_size=20][b]GateALU — ALU tri-state buffer[/b][/font_size]
[color=#8c8c8c]Tri-state buffer (control: GateALU)[/color]

[color=#61afef][b]What it does[/b][/color]
Connects the ALU's result to the bus when GateALU is asserted.

[color=#61afef][b]How it works[/b][/color]
While GateALU is 1 the buffer copies the ALU's value onto the bus; while it is 0 it is disconnected (high impedance, Z). The BUS card explains how the five buffers share the bus. The ALU's flag outputs do not use it: they go straight to the N Z C V register, which loads them when LD.CC is asserted.

[color=#61afef][b]Connects to[/b][/color]
[color=#8c8c8c]receives from[/color]
[ul]​[b]ALU[/b]  [color=#ababab]— the ALU result[/color][/ul]
[color=#8c8c8c]sends to[/color]
[ul]​[b]BUS[/b]  [color=#ababab]— to a register, MDR (store data) or the PC (BX)[/color][/ul]
[color=#8c8c8c]controlled by[/color]
[ul]​[b]FSM[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]GateALU[/code][/color]  [color=#ababab]— 1 = drive the bus, 0 = off (Z)[/color][/ul]

[color=#61afef][b]When it is used[/b][/color]
EXECUTE_COMMIT of data-processing instructions that write a register; FETCH_OPERANDS of stores and PUSH/STM (ALU PASS); EXECUTE_PC of BX and BLX.

[hr color=#474747 height=1]
[font_size=20][b]GateVEC — exception-vector tri-state buffer[/b][/font_size]
[color=#8c8c8c]Tri-state buffer (control: GateVEC)[/color]

[color=#61afef][b]What it does[/b][/color]
Connects VECTOR ADDR to the bus when GateVEC is asserted, at the start of exception entry.

[color=#61afef][b]How it works[/b][/color]
While GateVEC is 1 the buffer copies VECTOR ADDR's value onto the bus; while it is 0 it is disconnected (high impedance, Z). The BUS card explains how the five buffers share the bus. For SVC it drives the SVCall vector address 0x0000002C.

[color=#61afef][b]Connects to[/b][/color]
[color=#8c8c8c]receives from[/color]
[ul]​[b]VECTOR ADDR[/b]  [color=#ababab]— vector address[/color][/ul]
[color=#8c8c8c]sends to[/color]
[ul]​[b]BUS[/b]  [color=#ababab]— drives the shared bus[/color][/ul]
[color=#8c8c8c]controlled by[/color]
[ul]​[b]FSM[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]GateVEC[/code][/color]  [color=#ababab]— 1 = drive the bus, 0 = off (Z)[/color][/ul]

[color=#61afef][b]When it is used[/b][/color]
SVC_CALL (putchar, getchar).

[hr color=#474747 height=1]
[font_size=20][b]MAR — Memory Address Register[/b][/font_size]
[color=#8c8c8c]Register[/color]

[color=#61afef][b]What it does[/b][/color]
Holds the address for the next memory or I/O access.

[color=#61afef][b]How it works[/b][/color]
Loaded from the bus (LD.MAR): with the PC during fetch, or with the address adder's result in EVALUATE_ADDRESS. Memory reads and writes always use MAR's address. For PUSH/POP/LDM/STM its +4 incrementer steps it to the next word between transfers.

[color=#61afef][b]Connects to[/b][/color]
[color=#8c8c8c]receives from[/color]
[ul]​[b]BUS[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]LD.MAR[/code][/color]
​[b]+4[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]MAR+4[/code][/color][/ul]
[color=#8c8c8c]sends to[/color]
[ul]​[b]MEMORY / I-O[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]MEM.EN[/code][/color]  [color=#ababab]— address[/color][/ul]

[color=#61afef][b]When it is used[/b][/color]
FETCH_ADDR; EVALUATE_ADDRESS of every load and store.

[hr color=#474747 height=1]
[font_size=20][b]+4 — MAR incrementer[/b][/font_size]
[color=#8c8c8c]Combinational adder[/color]

[color=#61afef][b]What it does[/b][/color]
Adds 4 to MAR so a multi-register transfer can move to the next word.

[color=#61afef][b]How it works[/b][/color]
It is an adder drawn sideways: MAR's value enters its long side and MAR + 4 leaves its short side, back into MAR. In the same cycle as each word transfer of PUSH, POP, LDM and STM, the FSM also asserts MAR+4: at the clock edge MAR loads its own value + 4, ready for the next word, without using the bus or the address adder. The memory access in that cycle still uses the old MAR, because MAR only changes at the edge.

[color=#61afef][b]Connects to[/b][/color]
[color=#8c8c8c]receives from[/color]
[ul]​[b]MAR[/b][/ul]
[color=#8c8c8c]sends to[/color]
[ul]​[b]MAR[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]MAR+4[/code][/color][/ul]

[color=#61afef][b]When it is used[/b][/color]
PUSH, POP, LDMIA, STMIA with more than one register.

[hr color=#474747 height=1]
[font_size=20][b]MEMORY / I-O[/b][/font_size]
[color=#8c8c8c]Memory (64 KB RAM + memory-mapped I/O)[/color]

[color=#61afef][b]What it does[/b][/color]
Stores the program and its data, and connects to the Pico's GPIO peripherals.

[color=#61afef][b]How it works[/b][/color]
RAM covers 0x0000–0xFFFF: the OS at 0x0000, your code from 0x3000, the stack growing down from the top. (This is picosim's simplified map: on a real RP2040, flash starts at 0x10000000 and SRAM at 0x20000000.) Addresses 0x10000 and up are I/O registers (SIO at 0xD0000000, IO_BANK0 at 0x40014000, PADS_BANK0 at 0x4001C000); writing them changes the pins on the Pico board. An access takes a cycle of its own: with MEM.EN asserted, a read (R/W=READ, LD.MDR) puts M[MAR] into MDR at the clock edge, and a write (R/W=WRITE) stores MDR at M[MAR] at the clock edge.

[color=#61afef][b]Connects to[/b][/color]
[color=#8c8c8c]receives from[/color]
[ul]​[b]MAR[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]MEM.EN[/code][/color]  [color=#ababab]— address[/color]
​[b]MDR[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]R/W=WRITE[/code][/color]  [color=#ababab]— write data[/color][/ul]
[color=#8c8c8c]sends to[/color]
[ul]​[b]MDR[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]R/W=READ[/code][/color]  [color=#ababab]— read data[/color][/ul]

[color=#61afef][b]When it is used[/b][/color]
FETCH_MEMORY every instruction; FETCH_OPERANDS of loads; STORE_RESULT of stores.

[hr color=#474747 height=1]
[font_size=20][b]MDR — Memory Data Register[/b][/font_size]
[color=#8c8c8c]Register[/color]

[color=#61afef][b]What it does[/b][/color]
Buffers every value going to or coming from memory.

[color=#61afef][b]How it works[/b][/color]
On a read, memory loads MDR at the clock edge (LD.MDR); the next cycle LOAD EXT and GateMDR put it on the bus for IR or a register. On a write, the store data is first loaded into MDR from the bus (through STORE ALIGN), then memory copies it at M[MAR].

[color=#61afef][b]Connects to[/b][/color]
[color=#8c8c8c]receives from[/color]
[ul]​[b]MEMORY / I-O[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]R/W=READ[/code][/color]
​[b]STORE ALIGN[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]LD.MDR[/code][/color][/ul]
[color=#8c8c8c]sends to[/color]
[ul]​[b]MEMORY / I-O[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]R/W=WRITE[/code][/color]
​[b]LOAD EXT[/b][/ul]

[color=#61afef][b]When it is used[/b][/color]
Every fetch (instruction halfword); every load and store.

[hr color=#474747 height=1]
[font_size=20][b]LOAD EXT — load extender[/b][/font_size]
[color=#8c8c8c]Combinational logic[/color]

[color=#61afef][b]What it does[/b][/color]
Turns a byte or halfword read from memory into a full 32-bit value.

[color=#61afef][b]How it works[/b][/color]
It selects the right byte lanes from MDR and zero-extends (LDRB, LDRH, and the instruction halfword in FETCH_IR) or sign-extends (LDRSB, LDRSH) them. Words pass through unchanged. Its output reaches the bus through the GateMDR buffer when GateMDR is asserted.

[color=#61afef][b]Connects to[/b][/color]
[color=#8c8c8c]receives from[/color]
[ul]​[b]MDR[/b][/ul]
[color=#8c8c8c]sends to[/color]
[ul]​[b]GateMDR[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]GateMDR[/code][/color]  [color=#ababab]— to the bus[/color][/ul]
[color=#8c8c8c]controlled by[/color]
[ul]​[b]FSM[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]LOAD EXT[/code][/color]  [color=#ababab]— Z/S + size[/color][/ul]

[color=#61afef][b]When it is used[/b][/color]
FETCH_IR; STORE_RESULT of loads.

[hr color=#474747 height=1]
[font_size=20][b]STORE ALIGN[/b][/font_size]
[color=#8c8c8c]Combinational logic[/color]

[color=#61afef][b]What it does[/b][/color]
Prepares store data for memory.

[color=#61afef][b]How it works[/b][/color]
It places the byte or halfword being stored into the correct byte lanes and sets the byte enables, so STRB / STRH only change the bytes they should. Data arrives from the register via the ALU (ALUK=PASS), GateALU and the bus, and goes into MDR (LD.MDR) at the clock edge.

[color=#61afef][b]Connects to[/b][/color]
[color=#8c8c8c]receives from[/color]
[ul]​[b]BUS[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]STORE ALIGN[/code][/color]  [color=#ababab]— value from the ALU[/color][/ul]
[color=#8c8c8c]sends to[/color]
[ul]​[b]MDR[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]LD.MDR[/code][/color][/ul]

[color=#61afef][b]When it is used[/b][/color]
FETCH_OPERANDS of STR, STRB, STRH, PUSH, STMIA.

[hr color=#474747 height=1]
[font_size=20][b]REGISTER FILE[/b][/font_size]
[color=#8c8c8c]Register array (R0–R12, SP, LR)[/color]

[color=#61afef][b]What it does[/b][/color]
The registers your program uses.

[color=#61afef][b]How it works[/b][/color]
Two read ports, SR1 and SR2, can read any two registers at once; they are combinational, so the selected values are available during the cycle and feed ALU A, SR2MUX and the address muxes. One write port, DR, loads the bus value into a register at the clock edge when LD.REG is asserted (LD.SP / LD.LR for SP and LR) — the new value appears from the next cycle on. The register numbers come from the instruction fields selected by the FSM. The PC is kept separately.

[color=#61afef][b]Connects to[/b][/color]
[color=#8c8c8c]receives from[/color]
[ul]​[b]BUS[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]LD.REG[/code][/color]  [color=#ababab]— result to DR[/color]
​[b]SET THUMB[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]LD.LR[/code][/color]  [color=#ababab]— return address into LR[/color][/ul]
[color=#8c8c8c]sends to[/color]
[ul]​[b]ALU[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]SR1[/code][/color]  [color=#ababab]— ALU A input[/color]
​[b]SR2MUX[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]SR2[/code][/color]
​[b]ADDR1MUX[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]ADDR1MUX=SR1 / SP[/code][/color][/ul]

[color=#61afef][b]When it is used[/b][/color]
Most instructions read it in FETCH_OPERANDS and write it in EXECUTE_COMMIT or STORE_RESULT.

[hr color=#474747 height=1]
[font_size=20][b]SET THUMB — set bit 0[/b][/font_size]
[color=#8c8c8c]Combinational logic[/color]

[color=#61afef][b]What it does[/b][/color]
Marks a return address as Thumb code before it is saved in LR.

[color=#61afef][b]How it works[/b][/color]
In the LINK state of BL and BLX the PC (already pointing at the next instruction) goes onto the bus through GatePC, this block sets bit 0 (value | 1) and LD.LR saves it in LR at the clock edge. The bus carries the PC itself; only LR gets the bit. Later BX LR or POP {PC} returns there, and CLR THUMB removes the bit again.

[color=#61afef][b]Connects to[/b][/color]
[color=#8c8c8c]receives from[/color]
[ul]​[b]BUS[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]SET THUMB BIT[/code][/color]  [color=#ababab]— return address[/color][/ul]
[color=#8c8c8c]sends to[/color]
[ul]​[b]REGISTER FILE[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]LD.LR[/code][/color]  [color=#ababab]— into LR[/color][/ul]

[color=#61afef][b]When it is used[/b][/color]
LINK state of BL and BLX.

[hr color=#474747 height=1]
[font_size=20][b]SR2MUX — ALU B selector[/b][/font_size]
[color=#8c8c8c]Multiplexer[/color]

[color=#61afef][b]What it does[/b][/color]
Chooses the ALU's second (B) operand.

[color=#61afef][b]How it works[/b][/color]
It chooses the ALU's B input: the register from read port SR2 (ADDS R2, R0, R1) or an immediate from IMM / OFFSET (ADDS R2, R0, #5). The FSM's select picks REG or IMM.

[color=#61afef][b]Connects to[/b][/color]
[color=#8c8c8c]receives from[/color]
[ul]​[b]REGISTER FILE[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]SR2[/code][/color]
​[b]IMM / OFFSET[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]SR2MUX=IMM[/code][/color][/ul]
[color=#8c8c8c]sends to[/color]
[ul]​[b]ALU[/b]  [color=#ababab]— B input[/color][/ul]
[color=#8c8c8c]controlled by[/color]
[ul]​[b]FSM[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]SR2MUX[/code][/color]  [color=#ababab]— select: REG / IMM[/color][/ul]

[color=#61afef][b]When it is used[/b][/color]
FETCH_OPERANDS of data-processing instructions.

[hr color=#474747 height=1]
[font_size=20][b]ALU — Arithmetic Logic Unit[/b][/font_size]
[color=#8c8c8c]Combinational unit with latched inputs[/color]

[color=#61afef][b]What it does[/b][/color]
Does the arithmetic and logic: ADD, SUB, ADC, SBC, RSB, AND, ORR, EOR, BIC, MVN, shifts (LSL, LSR, ASR, ROR), MUL, extends (SXTB, UXTH…), byte reverses (REV…), compare (CMP, CMN, TST) and PASS.

[color=#61afef][b]How it works[/b][/color]
Its inputs are A (from SR1) and B (from SR2MUX); ALUK, the operation select, says what to do with them. In FETCH_OPERANDS the inputs are loaded into the ALU A / ALU B latches at the clock edge (LD.ALUA, LD.ALUB); in the next cycle (EXECUTE_COMMIT) the ALU computes the ALUK function from them. GateALU puts the result on the bus for the register file (or MDR, or the PC); LD.CC loads the N Z C V flags from it. PASS just forwards a register's value straight onto the bus (store data); for BX it forwards the latched target in A. CMP / CMN / TST set flags without writing a register.

[color=#61afef][b]Connects to[/b][/color]
[color=#8c8c8c]receives from[/color]
[ul]​[b]REGISTER FILE[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]SR1[/code][/color]  [color=#ababab]— A input[/color]
​[b]SR2MUX[/b]  [color=#ababab]— B input[/color][/ul]
[color=#8c8c8c]sends to[/color]
[ul]​[b]GateALU[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]GateALU[/code][/color]  [color=#ababab]— result to the bus[/color]
​[b]N Z C V[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]LD.CC[/code][/color][/ul]
[color=#8c8c8c]controlled by[/color]
[ul]​[b]FSM[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]ALUK[/code][/color]  [color=#ababab]— operation select[/color][/ul]

[color=#61afef][b]When it is used[/b][/color]
EXECUTE_COMMIT of data-processing; FETCH_OPERANDS of stores (PASS); EXECUTE_PC of BX.

[hr color=#474747 height=1]
[font_size=20][b]N Z C V — condition flags[/b][/font_size]
[color=#8c8c8c]Register (4 bits)[/color]

[color=#61afef][b]What it does[/b][/color]
Record facts about the last flag-setting result.

[color=#61afef][b]How it works[/b][/color]
N = result negative (bit 31), Z = result zero, C = carry out of an add (1 = no borrow on a subtract or compare) or the last bit shifted out by a shift, V = signed overflow of an add or subtract. Logical operations (ANDS, ORRS, EORS, BICS, MVNS, MOVS #imm, MULS) change only N and Z. The flags are loaded from the ALU at the clock edge only when LD.CC is asserted — instructions ending in S and CMP, CMN, TST — so a following B<cond> sees them in its own cycles. Conditional branches read them through COND EVAL.

[color=#61afef][b]Connects to[/b][/color]
[color=#8c8c8c]receives from[/color]
[ul]​[b]ALU[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]LD.CC[/code][/color][/ul]
[color=#8c8c8c]sends to[/color]
[ul]​[b]COND EVAL[/b][/ul]

[color=#61afef][b]When it is used[/b][/color]
EXECUTE_COMMIT of flag-setting instructions.

4.full:
[font_size=26][b]Pipelining: the big idea[/b][/font_size]

[i]Beyond the textbook: the course text stops at the multi-cycle datapath. This level is for going further.[/i]

On the multi-cycle datapath, one instruction has the whole CPU to itself until it is finished, and most parts sit idle most of the time. The real Pico's processor, the [b]Cortex-M0+[/b], does better by working on two instructions at once.

[color=#61afef][b]The laundry idea[/b][/color]
Washing and drying two loads of laundry one after the other takes wash + dry + wash + dry. But while the first load is drying, the washer is free: start the second load then. Each load still takes as long as before, but a load comes out of the dryer every [i]one[/i] step instead of every two. That is a [b]pipeline[/b].

[color=#61afef][b]The Cortex-M0+'s two stages[/b][/color]
The M0+ splits each instruction into two [b]stages[/b] that work at the same time, each on a different instruction:
[ul]​[color=#3987e5][b]Fetch[/b][/color] reads the [i]next[/i] instruction from memory.
​[color=#199e70][b]Decode + Execute[/b][/color] decodes and runs the [i]current[/i] one.[/ul]
Between them sits a [b]pipeline register[/b] (IF/EX) that hands the fetched instruction on. When nothing gets in the way, one instruction finishes every cycle: [b]CPI = 1[/b] (cycles per instruction).

[color=#61afef][b]Latency and throughput[/b][/color]
[ul]​[b]Latency[/b]: how long one instruction takes from start to finish. Pipelining does not shorten it.
​[b]Throughput[/b]: how many instructions finish per cycle. Pipelining raises it.[/ul]

[color=#61afef][b]A real example[/b][/color]
One pass round the loop of [b]Add up a list in memory[/b], as the Performance window lays it out on the RP2040 (F = fetch, E = execute, R = a taken branch refilling, ✕ = fetched but thrown away):
