bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][color=#3987e5][b]F[/b][/color][/cell][/table]

[ul]The load needs Execute for 2 cycles (one more to reach memory over the bus), so the [code]adds[/code] behind it can only execute in cycle 3.
The staircase from cycle 2 to 5: one instruction fetched while the one before executes.
​[code]bne[/code] is taken. Fetch had already guessed "not taken" and fetched the next instruction in memory; that one is thrown away (✕, a [b]flush[/b]), and the branch spends one more cycle (R) while the right instruction is fetched.[/ul]
So a pass takes [b]7 cycles[/b] for 5 instructions on the RP2040. On the multi-cycle datapath the same pass takes 7 + 6 + 6 + 6 + 5 = [b]30 cycles[/b].

[color=#61afef][b]What breaks the pattern[/b][/color]
A perfect pipeline would reach CPI = 1. Two things cost extra cycles on the M0+:
[ul]Instructions that need Execute for several cycles: loads and stores (2), PUSH and POP (1 + one per register; 3 + one per register for a POP that loads the PC), BL (3).
Taken branches, calls and returns: the instruction fetched behind them is flushed and the target must be fetched (1 extra cycle).[/ul]
Problems like these are called [b]hazards[/b]. A third kind, the [i]data hazard[/i] (an instruction needing a result that is not ready yet), cannot happen with only one Execute stage. [url=pipecycles][color=#61afef][u]Pipeline cycle by cycle[/u][/color][/url] has the details.

[color=#61afef][b]Deeper pipelines[/b][/color]
Splitting the work into more stages lets each stage be simpler, so a real chip could tick faster. But a taken branch then throws more away. The Performance window compares a 3-stage design (fetch, decode, execute), which loses 2 cycles per taken branch instead of 1. picosim times all machines at the same clock, so you see only the cycle counts change.

[table=1][cell bg=#2a2a2a border=#61afef padding=14,9,14,9 expand=1][color=#61afef][b]Same results[/b][/color]   Pipelining changes only [i]when[/i] things happen. The same program gives exactly the same register values, memory and output on every machine.[/cell][/table]

Next: [url=pipeline][color=#61afef][u]Pipeline diagram[/u][/color][/url] shows how to watch it in picosim.
4.name: Pipelining: the big idea
4.sum:
The real Pico's processor, the Cortex-M0+, overlaps instructions in a [b]2-stage pipeline[/b]: while one instruction is decoded and executed, the next one is already being fetched. When nothing gets in the way, an instruction finishes every clock cycle (CPI = 1), instead of every 5 to 7 cycles as on the multi-cycle datapath.

Two things cost extra cycles: instructions that need Execute for more than one cycle (loads, stores, PUSH, POP and BL), and taken branches, where the instruction fetched behind the branch is thrown away ([b]flushed[/b]). Pipelining changes only [i]when[/i] things happen, never the results.

4.full:
[font_size=26][b]Pipeline diagram[/b][/font_size]

New to pipelines? Read [url=pipeintro][color=#61afef][u]Pipelining: the big idea[/u][/color][/url] first.

Pick [color=#e5c07b][code]2-stage pipeline[/code][/color] in the toolbar's machine menu, next to [color=#e5c07b][code]Show CPU Diagram[/code][/color]. The diagram turns into the Raspberry Pi Pico's own processor, the Cortex-M0+, which overlaps instructions in a [b]2-stage pipeline[/b]. Pick [color=#e5c07b][code]Multi-cycle[/code][/color] to go back to the [url=diagram][color=#61afef][u]datapath diagram[/u][/color][/url].

[color=#61afef][b]Two instructions at once[/b][/color]
On the multi-cycle datapath one instruction uses the whole CPU until it is finished. The M0+ splits the work into two stages that run at the same time:
[ul]​[color=#3987e5][b]FETCH[/b][/color] (left) — reads the next instruction from memory at the address in the PC.
​[color=#199e70][b]DECODE + EXECUTE[/b][/color] (right) — decodes the instruction fetched in the previous cycle, reads its registers, uses the ALU or memory, and writes the result back.
​[b]IF/EX[/b] — the pipeline register between them. It holds the fetched instruction until Execute is free.[/ul]
So while one instruction executes, the one after it is already being fetched. When nothing gets in the way, an instruction finishes every cycle.

[color=#61afef][b]Instruction tokens[/b][/color]
Every instruction in flight is a coloured token labelled with its address and assembly, for example [code]3022  ldr r2, [lb]pc, #0x20][/code]. The token keeps its colour as it moves, so you can follow one instruction. The line under the label says what it is doing:
[ul]​[b]fetching[/b] — it is being read from memory this cycle.
​[b]waiting in IF/EX: Execute is busy[/b] — it has been fetched, but the instruction ahead of it still needs Execute.
​[b]cycle k of n[/b] — it is executing; n is its cycle count from RP2040 datasheet Table 81.
​[b]· refilling from the target[/b] — added to a taken branch's last cycle, while its target is fetched.
​[b]fetched (sequential: predicted not-taken)[/b] — the instruction after a branch, fetched before anyone knows whether the branch is taken.
​[color=#e06c75][b]✕ wrong path: flushed[/b][/color] — that instruction, once the branch turns out to be taken: it is discarded and never executes.[/ul]
When you step, each token slides to its next position: from Fetch across IF/EX into Execute, and out to the right when it finishes. A new instruction drops into Fetch. The slide follows the speed slider.

[color=#61afef][b]What the colours mean[/b][/color]
The diagram follows the same rules as the datapath diagram:
[ul]​[color=#61afef]Bright blue wires and boxes[/color] carry data in the cycle shown, and a glowing pulse runs along them when you step.
​[color=#c678dd]Purple dashed stubs[/color] are control inputs. Each enters a mux or the ALU on a [i]slanted[/i] side and is labelled with what it selects this cycle: the PC MUX's select ([code]PC+2[/code] or [code]target[/code]) and the ALU's operation ([code]ALUK[/code]).
Every mux and the ALU take their inputs on the long side and send their result out of the short side. The +2 adder is drawn sideways: the PC enters its long left side and PC + 2 leaves its short right side.
​[color=#e06c75]FLUSH[/color] is a control line from BRANCH RESOLVE to IF/EX. It is dashed, and turns red when a taken branch discards the instruction in Fetch. IF/EX then shows ✕.
​[color=#f2cc60]Yellow[/color] registers and flags changed in the last step.[/ul]

[color=#61afef][b]Registers[/b][/color]
The simulator executes each instruction as a whole, so the register file, the flags and the Registers panel show the state [i]after[/i] the instruction in Execute has finished. The datapath diagram is different: it shows values during the cycle.

[color=#61afef][b]Learning the components[/b][/color]
Hover a block for a one-line summary, or click it for a card explaining what it does, how it works and what it connects to. The same descriptions are in [url=pipecomponents][color=#61afef][u]Pipeline components[/u][/color][/url]. [url=pipecycles][color=#61afef][u]Pipeline cycle by cycle[/u][/color][/url] explains stepping, the instruction strip and where the pipeline loses cycles.
4.name: Pipeline diagram
4.sum: Pick [b]2-stage pipeline[/b] in the machine menu to see the Pico's own processor. The left stage is [color=#3987e5]Fetch[/color] and the right one [color=#199e70]Decode + Execute[/color], joined by the IF/EX pipeline register. Each instruction in flight is a coloured token that moves across as you step, and FLUSH turns red when a taken branch throws away the wrong instruction. The registers show the state after the instruction in Execute has finished.

4.full:
[font_size=26][b]Pipeline cycle by cycle[/b][/font_size]


[color=#61afef][b]Stepping[/b][/color]
[ul]​[color=#e5c07b][code]Step cycle[/code][/color] ([color=#e5c07b][code]F11[/code][/color]) — one pipeline clock cycle: every token moves on one stage.
​[color=#e5c07b][code]Step instruction[/code][/color] ([color=#e5c07b][code]F10[/code][/color]) — jump to the next instruction's first Execute cycle.
​[color=#e5c07b][code]Run[/code][/color] ([color=#e5c07b][code]F5[/code][/color]) — run at the speed slider's rate in pipeline cycles per second. At high speeds the animation is skipped.
Breakpoints stop the run when the instruction is in Fetch, just before it executes.[/ul]
The status bar and the diagram's title show the pipeline cycle, the instructions finished so far, and the CPI (cycles per instruction).

[color=#61afef][b]The instruction strip[/b][/color]
Under the stages are the last 8 cycles: one row per instruction, one column per cycle, with the current cycle highlighted. Blue cells are [color=#3987e5]Fetch[/color] and green cells are [color=#199e70]Execute[/color]. An outlined cell means [i]waiting[/i] in IF/EX, or a branch [i]refilling[/i]. A ✕ cell is a flushed instruction. When nothing stalls, every row starts one column after the one above it. This is the staircase pattern of a pipeline: each instruction is one step behind the one before.

[color=#61afef][b]The explanation panel[/b][/color]
In pipeline mode, the cycle inspector under the diagram is replaced by a panel that explains the cycle shown. It says what each stage holds, its Table 81 row and cycle count, and why it waits, refills or is flushed.

[color=#61afef][b]Where the pipeline loses cycles[/b][/color]
A perfect 2-stage pipeline finishes one instruction per cycle (CPI = 1). Two things break the pattern:
[ul]​[b]Instructions that need Execute for more than one cycle.[/b] Loads and stores take 2 cycles over the AHB-Lite bus (1 to the SIO), PUSH and POP take 1 + the number of registers, and BL takes 3. The next instruction waits in IF/EX meanwhile.
​[b]Taken branches.[/b] The M0+ has no branch predictor. Fetch always assumes the instruction it just fetched will not branch, and fetches the next address ("predict not-taken"). When a branch in Execute turns out to be taken, BRANCH RESOLVE sends the target to the PC MUX and FLUSHes the wrong instruction from IF/EX. The branch then spends one more cycle while the target is fetched. That is why a B<cond> costs 1 cycle when it is not taken and 2 when it is taken, and B and BX always cost 2.[/ul]
There are no [b]data hazards[/b]: with only one Execute stage, an instruction's result is written back before the next instruction reads its registers. So the M0+ needs no forwarding and no stalls for data.

[color=#61afef][b]Example: the bottom of a loop[/b][/color]
[code]cmp  r3, r2      @ 1 cycle
bls  loop        @ taken: 2 cycles[/code]
[ul]Cycle 1: [code]cmp[/code] executes, [code]bls[/code] is fetched.
Cycle 2: [code]bls[/code] executes and the condition is true. The instruction after it (fetched by predict-not-taken) is flushed ✕, and the PC MUX selects the target.
Cycle 3: [code]bls[/code] refills: the first instruction of [code]loop[/code] is fetched.
Cycle 4: that instruction executes.[/ul]
Each pass round the loop pays one extra cycle for the taken branch. The [url=performance][color=#61afef][u]Performance window[/u][/color][/url] totals these costs and compares them with a 3-stage pipeline, which loses 2 cycles per taken branch.
4.name: Pipeline cycle by cycle
4.sum:
[color=#e5c07b][code]Step cycle[/code][/color] ([color=#e5c07b][code]C[/code][/color] or [color=#e5c07b][code]F11[/code][/color]) moves the pipeline one clock cycle; [color=#e5c07b][code]Step instruction[/code][/color] ([color=#e5c07b][code]S[/code][/color] or [color=#e5c07b][code]F10[/code][/color]) jumps to the next instruction's first Execute cycle. Under the stages, the instruction strip shows the last 8 cycles as a staircase, and the panel under the diagram explains what each stage holds and why it waits, refills or is flushed.

A perfect 2-stage pipeline gets CPI = 1. Instructions that take several Execute cycles, and taken branches (1 extra cycle each on the M0+), are where cycles are lost. With only one Execute stage there are no data hazards.

4.full:
[font_size=26][b]Pipeline components[/b][/font_size]

Every block on the [url=pipeline][color=#61afef][u]pipeline diagram[/u][/color][/url], Fetch stage first, in the order an instruction meets them. Click a block on the diagram to see the same text next to it.

[hr color=#474747 height=1]
[font_size=20][b]PC — fetch address[/b][/font_size]
[color=#8c8c8c]Register (Fetch stage)[/color]

[color=#61afef][b]What it does[/b][/color]
The address of the instruction being fetched this cycle.

[color=#61afef][b]How it works[/b][/color]
Loaded from the PC MUX at every clock edge where Fetch moves on. When Execute is busy with a multi-cycle instruction, Fetch stalls and the PC holds its value. An instruction that reads PC as an operand still sees its own address + 4, as ARMv6-M defines.

[color=#61afef][b]Connects to[/b][/color]
[color=#8c8c8c]receives from[/color]
[ul]​[b]PC MUX[/b]  [color=#ababab]— next PC[/color][/ul]
[color=#8c8c8c]sends to[/color]
[ul]​[b]Instruction fetch[/b]  [color=#ababab]— fetch address[/color]
​[b]+2[/b]  [color=#ababab]— for PC + 2[/color][/ul]

[color=#61afef][b]When it is used[/b][/color]
Every fetch.

[hr color=#474747 height=1]
[font_size=20][b]+2 — sequential next address[/b][/font_size]
[color=#8c8c8c]Adder (Fetch stage)[/color]

[color=#61afef][b]What it does[/b][/color]
Computes PC + 2, the next Thumb halfword.

[color=#61afef][b]How it works[/b][/color]
This is the "prediction": whatever the instruction just fetched is, the next fetch comes from here unless a taken branch overrides it. A 32-bit BL is fetched as two halfwords.

[color=#61afef][b]Connects to[/b][/color]
[color=#8c8c8c]receives from[/color]
[ul]​[b]PC[/b][/ul]
[color=#8c8c8c]sends to[/color]
[ul]​[b]PC MUX[/b]  [color=#ababab]— PC + 2[/color][/ul]

[color=#61afef][b]When it is used[/b][/color]
Every fetch.

[hr color=#474747 height=1]
[font_size=20][b]PC MUX — next fetch address[/b][/font_size]
[color=#8c8c8c]Multiplexer (Fetch stage)[/color]

[color=#61afef][b]What it does[/b][/color]
Chooses the address the next cycle fetches from: the next sequential halfword (PC + 2) or a branch target.

[color=#61afef][b]How it works[/b][/color]
The Cortex-M0+ has no branch predictor. Fetch always assumes the instruction it just fetched will not branch and selects PC + 2 ("predict not-taken"). Only when BRANCH RESOLVE finds a taken branch in Execute does it select the target instead, and the instruction already fetched from PC + 2 is flushed.

[color=#61afef][b]Connects to[/b][/color]
[color=#8c8c8c]receives from[/color]
[ul]​[b]+2[/b]  [color=#ababab]— PC + 2 (sequential)[/color]
​[b]Branch resolve[/b]  [color=#ababab]— branch target[/color][/ul]
[color=#8c8c8c]sends to[/color]
[ul]​[b]PC[/b]  [color=#ababab]— next PC[/color][/ul]
[color=#8c8c8c]controlled by[/color]
[ul]​[b]Branch resolve[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]select[/code][/color]  [color=#ababab]— PC+2, or target when a branch is taken (dashed stub on its slanted side)[/color][/ul]

[color=#61afef][b]When it is used[/b][/color]
Every cycle; it picks the branch target in the cycle a taken branch resolves.

[hr color=#474747 height=1]
[font_size=20][b]Instruction fetch[/b][/font_size]
[color=#8c8c8c]Bus read (Fetch stage)[/color]

[color=#61afef][b]What it does[/b][/color]
Reads the instruction at PC and places it in the IF/EX register.

[color=#61afef][b]How it works[/b][/color]
The fetch goes over the AHB-Lite bus to flash (through the XIP cache) or SRAM. The real M0+ fetches 32 bits at a time and can run up to a halfword ahead. This model fetches the instruction in the cycle before it executes, which gives the same cycle counts as datasheet Table 81.

[color=#61afef][b]Connects to[/b][/color]
[color=#8c8c8c]receives from[/color]
[ul]​[b]PC[/b]  [color=#ababab]— address[/color][/ul]
[color=#8c8c8c]sends to[/color]
[ul]​[b]IF/EX[/b]  [color=#ababab]— instruction[/color][/ul]

[color=#61afef][b]When it is used[/b][/color]
Every cycle in which Fetch is not stalled.

[hr color=#474747 height=1]
[font_size=20][b]IF/EX — pipeline register[/b][/font_size]
[color=#8c8c8c]Register between the stages[/color]

[color=#61afef][b]What it does[/b][/color]
Holds the fetched instruction while Execute works on the one before it. This register is what lets two instructions be in flight at once.

[color=#61afef][b]How it works[/b][/color]
At each clock edge where Execute takes a new instruction, IF/EX passes its instruction on and captures the next fetch. While a multi-cycle instruction (LDR, STR, PUSH, BL…) occupies Execute, IF/EX keeps its instruction, which waits. A FLUSH from BRANCH RESOLVE throws its contents away and turns them into a bubble.

[color=#61afef][b]Connects to[/b][/color]
[color=#8c8c8c]receives from[/color]
[ul]​[b]Instruction fetch[/b]  [color=#ababab]— fetched instruction[/color][/ul]
[color=#8c8c8c]sends to[/color]
[ul]​[b]Decode[/b]  [color=#ababab]— to Execute[/color][/ul]
[color=#8c8c8c]controlled by[/color]
[ul]​[b]Branch resolve[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]FLUSH[/code][/color]  [color=#ababab]— discard on a taken branch[/color][/ul]

[color=#61afef][b]When it is used[/b][/color]
Every cycle.

[hr color=#474747 height=1]
[font_size=20][b]Decode[/b][/font_size]
[color=#8c8c8c]Combinational logic (Execute stage)[/color]

[color=#61afef][b]What it does[/b][/color]
Works out what the instruction in IF/EX does: its operation, the registers it reads and writes, and whether it can change the PC.

[color=#61afef][b]How it works[/b][/color]
In this model the M0+ decodes in the first cycle of the Execute stage (ARM describes the first stage as fetch plus a pre-decode; this simplifies that). That is why it has 2 stages and not 3: there is no separate Decode stage, so a taken branch only wastes the one instruction fetched behind it. The label under the box is the instruction's row in datasheet Table 81.

[color=#61afef][b]Connects to[/b][/color]
[color=#8c8c8c]receives from[/color]
[ul]​[b]IF/EX[/b]  [color=#ababab]— instruction[/color][/ul]
[color=#8c8c8c]sends to[/color]
[ul]​[b]Register file[/b]  [color=#ababab]— register numbers[/color]
​[b]Branch resolve[/b]  [color=#ababab]— branch? condition, target[/color][/ul]

[color=#61afef][b]When it is used[/b][/color]
The first cycle of every instruction.

[hr color=#474747 height=1]
[font_size=20][b]Register file[/b][/font_size]
[color=#8c8c8c]Registers (Execute stage)[/color]

[color=#61afef][b]What it does[/b][/color]
R0–R12, SP and LR, shown after the instruction in Execute has finished.

[color=#61afef][b]How it works[/b][/color]
Operands are read in Execute and the result is written back at its end. With only one Execute stage, an instruction's result is ready for the very next instruction, so this pipeline never has data hazards or forwarding.

[color=#61afef][b]Connects to[/b][/color]
[color=#8c8c8c]receives from[/color]
[ul]​[b]Decode[/b]  [color=#ababab]— register numbers[/color]
​[b]ALU[/b]  [color=#ababab]— result[/color]
​[b]Data access[/b]  [color=#ababab]— loaded data[/color][/ul]
[color=#8c8c8c]sends to[/color]
[ul]​[b]ALU[/b]  [color=#ababab]— operands[/color][/ul]

[color=#61afef][b]When it is used[/b][/color]
Most instructions.

[hr color=#474747 height=1]
[font_size=20][b]ALU[/b][/font_size]
[color=#8c8c8c]Combinational (Execute stage)[/color]

[color=#61afef][b]What it does[/b][/color]
Arithmetic and logic operations, and the address of a load or store.

[color=#61afef][b]How it works[/b][/color]
Its operands from the register file enter its long top side and the result leaves its short bottom side, to the register file, the flags and (as an address) the data access. ALUK, its control input from Decode, enters a slanted side and selects the operation; for loads and stores it adds to form the address. One ALU operation per cycle; MULS takes 1 cycle with the RP2040's fast multiplier.

[color=#61afef][b]Connects to[/b][/color]
[color=#8c8c8c]receives from[/color]
[ul]​[b]Register file[/b]  [color=#ababab]— operands[/color][/ul]
[color=#8c8c8c]sends to[/color]
[ul]​[b]Register file[/b]  [color=#ababab]— result[/color]
​[b]N Z C V flags[/b]  [color=#ababab]— N Z C V[/color]
​[b]Data access[/b]  [color=#ababab]— address[/color][/ul]
[color=#8c8c8c]controlled by[/color]
[ul]​[b]Decode[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]ALUK[/code][/color]  [color=#ababab]— the operation (dashed stub on its slanted side)[/color][/ul]

[color=#61afef][b]When it is used[/b][/color]
ALU instructions, loads and stores.

[hr color=#474747 height=1]
[font_size=20][b]N Z C V flags[/b][/font_size]
[color=#8c8c8c]Register (Execute stage)[/color]

[color=#61afef][b]What it does[/b][/color]
The condition flags.

[color=#61afef][b]How it works[/b][/color]
Set by CMP, CMN, TST and instructions ending in S. A conditional branch reads them in BRANCH RESOLVE.

[color=#61afef][b]Connects to[/b][/color]
[color=#8c8c8c]receives from[/color]
[ul]​[b]ALU[/b][/ul]
[color=#8c8c8c]sends to[/color]
[ul]​[b]Branch resolve[/b]  [color=#ababab]— for B<cond>[/color][/ul]

[color=#61afef][b]When it is used[/b][/color]
Flag-setting instructions, and B<cond>.

[hr color=#474747 height=1]
[font_size=20][b]Data access[/b][/font_size]
[color=#8c8c8c]Bus access (Execute stage)[/color]

[color=#61afef][b]What it does[/b][/color]
The data transfer of a load, store, PUSH or POP.

[color=#61afef][b]How it works[/b][/color]
Over AHB-Lite a transfer takes 2 cycles (address, then data), so Execute is busy and the instruction behind it waits in IF/EX. The SIO, which includes the GPIO registers, sits on the single-cycle IOPORT, so loads and stores there take 1 cycle. APB peripherals add bus wait states that Table 81 does not include.

[color=#61afef][b]Connects to[/b][/color]
[color=#8c8c8c]receives from[/color]
[ul]​[b]ALU[/b]  [color=#ababab]— address[/color][/ul]
[color=#8c8c8c]sends to[/color]
[ul]​[b]Register file[/b]  [color=#ababab]— loaded data[/color][/ul]

[color=#61afef][b]When it is used[/b][/color]
LDR, STR, PUSH, POP, LDM, STM.

[hr color=#474747 height=1]
[font_size=20][b]Branch resolve[/b][/font_size]
[color=#8c8c8c]Control (Execute stage)[/color]

[color=#61afef][b]What it does[/b][/color]
Decides whether a branch is taken and, if so, fixes up the pipeline.

[color=#61afef][b]How it works[/b][/color]
Fetch has already fetched the next sequential instruction (predict not-taken). If the branch is not taken (B<cond> with a false condition), that guess was right and nothing is lost: 1 cycle. If it is taken (B, BL, BX, BLX, POP {PC}, MOV/ADD PC, or B<cond> with a true condition), it sends the target to the PC MUX and asserts FLUSH so IF/EX discards the wrong instruction. Execute then spends one more cycle while the target is fetched (the refill). That is why Table 81 gives a taken B<cond> 2 cycles and a not-taken one 1.

[color=#61afef][b]Connects to[/b][/color]
[color=#8c8c8c]receives from[/color]
[ul]​[b]Decode[/b]  [color=#ababab]— branch, condition[/color]
​[b]N Z C V flags[/b]  [color=#ababab]— for B<cond>[/color][/ul]
[color=#8c8c8c]sends to[/color]
[ul]​[b]PC MUX[/b]  [color=#ababab]— target address[/color]
​[b]PC MUX[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]select[/code][/color]  [color=#ababab]— picks the target when taken[/color]
​[b]IF/EX[/b]  [color=#c678dd][code]FLUSH[/code][/color]  [color=#ababab]— discard the wrong-path instruction[/color][/ul]

[color=#61afef][b]When it is used[/b][/color]
Branches, calls and returns.
4.name: Pipeline components
4.sum: Every block on the pipeline diagram, Fetch stage first, with what it does and how it connects. The same card opens when you click a block on the diagram.

4.full:
[font_size=26][b]Performance: the formulas[/b][/font_size]

How long does a program take? Three numbers decide it:

[table=3][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Number[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Meaning[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Depends on[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]N[/b], instruction count[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]How many instructions the program runs (loops count every pass).[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]the program and its data[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]CPI[/b], cycles per instruction[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The average number of clock cycles each instruction takes.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]the processor's design, and the mix of instructions[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][b]f[/b], clock frequency[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Clock cycles per second. 125 MHz = 125 000 000 per second.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]the chip (and its settings)[/cell][/table]

They combine like this:

[table=1][cell bg=#0e0e0e border=#474747 padding=14,10,14,10 expand=1][code]cycles = N × CPI
time   = cycles ÷ f   = N × CPI ÷ f[/code][/cell][/table]

One cycle at 125 MHz lasts 1 ÷ 125 000 000 s = 8 ns (nanoseconds), so 125 cycles take 1 µs (a microsecond, a millionth of a second).

[color=#61afef][b]Worked example[/b][/color]
[b]Add up a list in memory[/b], run to the end (32 instructions, counting the OS's). The Performance window's Metrics tab shows:

[table=4][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Machine[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Cycles[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]CPI[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Time at 125 MHz[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Multi-cycle (teaching datapath)[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]205[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]6.41[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]1.64 µs[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]2-stage pipeline (RP2040)[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]50[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]1.61[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]0.40 µs[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]3-stage pipeline (teaching)[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]55[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]1.77[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]0.44 µs[/cell][/table]

Check the first row: CPI = 205 ÷ 32 = 6.41, and time = 205 ÷ 125 MHz = 1.64 µs. For the pipelines, the final BKPT is not timed (the datasheet gives no fixed count for it), so their CPI is over 31 instructions: 50 ÷ 31 = 1.61.

[color=#61afef][b]Speed-up[/b][/color]
[b]Speed-up[/b] = old time ÷ new time. At the same clock that is old cycles ÷ new cycles: 205 ÷ 50 = [b]4.1×[/b]. The RP2040's pipeline runs this program 4.1 times as fast as the teaching datapath. The Compare tab prints this ratio for you.

[color=#61afef][b]Where the cycles go[/b][/color]
Improving the part that takes most of the time helps most. In the example, the multi-cycle machine spends 96 of its 205 cycles (47 %) just fetching instructions, which is exactly the work a pipeline overlaps with executing. The Metrics tab shows this breakdown by phase and by kind of instruction.

[color=#61afef][b]Check yourself[/b][/color]
[ol type=1]A program runs 1 000 instructions with CPI 1.5 at 125 MHz. How many cycles, and how long?
The same program on the multi-cycle machine has CPI 6.3. What is the speed-up of the pipeline?
A loop runs 5 instructions in 7 cycles per pass. What is its CPI?[/ol]
[color=#8c8c8c]Answers: 1. 1 500 cycles; 1 500 ÷ 125 000 000 s = 12 µs. 2. 6.3 ÷ 1.5 = 4.2× (same N and f, so only CPI matters). 3. 7 ÷ 5 = 1.4.[/color]

Try it on your own programs with the [url=performance][color=#61afef][u]Performance window[/u][/color][/url].
4.name: Performance formulas
4.sum: A program's run time is [b]N × CPI ÷ f[/b]: N is how many instructions it runs, CPI the average number of clock cycles per instruction, and f the clock frequency (the RP2040 runs at 125 MHz, so one cycle lasts 8 ns). For the [b]Add up a list in memory[/b] example the multi-cycle datapath takes 205 cycles (CPI 6.41) and the RP2040's pipeline 50, so the pipeline is 205 ÷ 50 = 4.1 times as fast.

4.full:
[font_size=26][b]Performance window[/b][/font_size]

Click [color=#e5c07b][code]Performance[/code][/color] in the toolbar ([color=#e5c07b][code]F2[/code][/color]). The window counts every instruction your program has completed since it was loaded and updates while it runs. The same run is timed on three machines; they execute the same instructions with the same results, so only the number of clock cycles differs.
[ul]​[b]Multi-cycle[/b] — the teaching datapath on the CPU diagram: one instruction at a time, 4 or more cycles each (most take 5–7).
​[b]2-stage pipeline (RP2040)[/b] — the Raspberry Pi Pico's Cortex-M0+: the next instruction is fetched while the current one decodes and executes. To watch it run, see [url=pipeline][color=#61afef][u]Pipeline diagram[/u][/color][/url].
​[b]3-stage pipeline[/b] — a teaching design with separate fetch, decode and execute stages.[/ul]

[color=#61afef][b]How to use it[/b][/color]
[ol type=1]Load a program and run it (to the end, or as far as you like). The window measures only what has run so far.
Press [color=#e5c07b][code]F2[/code][/color]. Read the [b]Metrics[/b] tab first, then try options on [b]Compare[/b], then look at the [b]Pipeline[/b] tab.
Keep it open while you step: it updates as the program runs.[/ol]
If the formulas are new to you, read [url=perfmath][color=#61afef][u]Performance formulas[/u][/color][/url] first.

[color=#61afef][b]Metrics tab[/b][/color]
Cycles, CPI (cycles per instruction) and time at the RP2040's default 125 MHz for each machine; for the multi-cycle machine, the cycles spent in each phase and how often the bus, the ALU and memory are busy; the instruction mix; where data accesses went (RAM, the SIO, APB peripherals); branch statistics; and the instructions that cost the most cycles.

[color=#61afef][b]Heat map tab[/b][/color]
How much each part of the CPU, each register and each flag was used: totals, a timeline down to single clock cycles, per program line, and before/after comparisons. See [url=heat][color=#61afef][u]Heat map[/u][/color][/url].

[color=#61afef][b]Compare tab[/b][/color]
Change the design and see the new cycle counts next to the stock ones: the [b]multiplier[/b] (the Cortex-M0+ can be built with a fast 1-cycle or a small 32-cycle multiplier; the RP2040 has the fast one) and [b]memory wait states[/b] for the multi-cycle machine (every memory access takes longer).

[color=#61afef][b]Pipeline tab[/b][/color]
Pick the 2-stage or 3-stage design and how many recent instructions to show. The chart lays out the last instructions on that pipeline, one row per instruction and one column per clock cycle: [color=#e5c07b][code]F[/code][/color] fetch, [color=#e5c07b][code]D[/code][/color] decode, [color=#e5c07b][code]E[/code][/color] execute, [color=#e5c07b][code]R[/code][/color] a branch's refill cycle, [color=#e5c07b][code]✕[/code][/color] an instruction fetched from the wrong path and discarded after a taken branch. Click a column (or use [color=#e5c07b][code]◀ Cycle[/code][/color] / [color=#e5c07b][code]Cycle ▶[/code][/color]) to see what each stage holds in that cycle and why it takes the cycles it does.

[color=#61afef][b]Where the numbers come from[/b][/color]
[ul]RP2040 cycle counts are the [b]RP2040 datasheet, Table 81[/b] (Cortex-M0+ instruction summary), which assumes zero wait states — code and data in SRAM, or the flash cache hitting. For example ADDS = 1, LDR/STR = 2 (or 1 to the SIO's single-cycle I/O port), B<cond> = 1 not taken / 2 taken, B = 2, BL = 3, PUSH = 1 + N, POP {…, PC} = 3 + N.
The 3-stage design uses the same execute cycles, but a taken branch costs one cycle more than on the 2-stage (2 refill cycles instead of 1), because it has one more stage to refill.
Not timed, and listed separately instead of guessed: SVC and BKPT (the datasheet gives no fixed count), and the extra bus cycles of APB peripheral accesses (datasheet §2.1.3) — the window tells you how many there were.
The exact cycle in which the real Cortex-M0+ fetches is not published (it fetches up to 32 bits ahead), so the chart's F marks when an instruction is in this model's fetch stage; the execute-stage counts are the datasheet's.[/ul]
4.name: Performance window
4.sum: The Performance window ([color=#e5c07b][code]F2[/code][/color]) times the run so far on three machines that give exactly the same results: the multi-cycle teaching datapath, the RP2040's 2-stage pipeline and a 3-stage teaching pipeline. [b]Metrics[/b] shows cycles, CPI and time; [b]Compare[/b] tries a slower multiplier or slower memory; [b]Pipeline[/b] draws a cycle-by-cycle chart; [b]Heat map[/b] shows which parts were busy. The RP2040's numbers come from its datasheet (Table 81).

4.full:
[font_size=26][b]Heat map[/b][/font_size]

A [b]heat map[/b] is a grid of coloured cells where the colour shows how much: here, how much each part of the CPU was used while your program ran. Rows are the parts (the datapath's registers, muxes, adder, ALU, memory and bus; then every register's reads and writes; then the flags). The stronger the colour, the more that part was used. It answers questions a cycle count alone cannot: [i]which part is the bottleneck? which register does my loop lean on? which line of my program keeps the memory busy?[/i]
Open it with [color=#e5c07b][code]Performance[/code][/color] ([color=#e5c07b][code]F2[/code][/color]) ▸ [b]Heat map[/b]. Like the rest of the window it measures what has run so far, and updates while the program runs.

[color=#61afef][b]What "used" means[/b][/color]
On the [b]multi-cycle datapath[/b] a part is used in a clock cycle when the FSM asserts a control signal that makes it work — the same signals the [url=diagram][color=#61afef][u]CPU diagram[/u][/color][/url] lights up — so these counts are [b]exact[/b]:

[table=2][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Part[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Used in a cycle when[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]MAR, MDR, IR, IR2, PC[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]it is loaded ([code]LD.MAR[/code], [code]LD.MDR[/code], [code]LD.IR[/code], [code]LD.PC[/code]…) or drives what it holds (MAR addressing memory, MDR through GateMDR, PC through GatePC)[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Bus and its buffers[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]a tri-state buffer drives the bus ([code]GatePC[/code], [code]GateADDR[/code], [code]GateMDR[/code], [code]GateALU[/code], [code]GateVEC[/code]); the Bus row counts cycles with any driver[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]ALU, its A / B latches[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1][code]ALUK[/code] selects an operation outside DECODE; the latches when [code]LD.ALUA[/code] / [code]LD.ALUB[/code] load them[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Muxes, adder, incrementers[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]their select signal is set ([code]ADDR1MUX[/code], [code]ADDR2MUX[/code], [code]SR2MUX[/code], [code]PCMUX[/code], [code]PCINC[/code], [code]MAR+4[/code])[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Memory / I-O[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1][code]MEM.EN[/code]. In Totals and Per line it is also split into instruction fetches and data accesses to RAM, the SIO (GPIO) and APB peripherals[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]FSM[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]every cycle (it is the clock's own row, a reference for 100%)[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Register reads / writes[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]one use of a register-file read port ([code]SR1[/code], [code]SR2[/code]) or the write port ([code]DR[/code] with [code]LD.REG[/code], [code]LD.SP[/code], [code]LD.LR[/code]). [code]adds r0, r0, r0[/code] reads R0 twice. The PC is read by every fetch and PC-relative address, and written by every fetch and branch[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Flag reads / writes[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]an instruction ending in S (or CMP, CMN, TST) writes the flags it sets; a conditional branch reads the flags its condition tests (BNE reads Z; BGT reads Z, N and V)[/cell][/table]

The [b]2-stage pipeline[/b] (the RP2040's Cortex-M0+) has no control signals in picosim, so its rows are an [b]estimate[/b] built from the datasheet's cycle counts: the fetch blocks once per halfword fetched (and again after a branch), decode once per instruction, the ALU for ALU instructions and load/store addresses, data memory once per data access, branch resolve for every PC change, and [i]Refill[/i] for the cycle a taken branch wastes. Its registers and flags are counted the same way as on the multi-cycle machine. SVC and BKPT, which the datasheet does not time, count as one cycle.

[color=#61afef][b]Views[/b][/color]
[ul]​[b]Totals[/b] — one row per part: how many cycles it was used and what share of all cycles that is (its [i]utilisation[/i]). Start here.
​[b]Timeline[/b] — one column per [i]bucket[/i] of clock cycles, from 1 cycle (every cycle of every instruction: you can see the fetch–decode–execute pattern) to thousands. Drag across the grid to zoom into those cycles; [color=#e5c07b][code]Zoom out[/code][/color], [color=#e5c07b][code]Whole run[/code][/color] and [color=#e5c07b][code]Fit to width[/code][/color] move back out. It includes the built-in OS.
​[b]Per line[/b] — one column per line of your program (and of the OS), with the uses that line caused over the whole run: a loop body shows up as the hot columns. Hover a column for the line's text and how many times it ran.
​[b]Compare[/b] — this run against a saved [b]baseline[/b]: blue = used less than before, red = used more, grey = no change. See [i]Before and after[/i] below.[/ul]
Beside the grid, [b]Register reads[/b] and [b]Register writes[/b] show R0–R15 as tiles, so you can see at a glance which registers your code relies on. Click a row's name to show that part on the CPU diagram.

[color=#61afef][b]Making small differences visible[/b][/color]
[ul]​[b]Scale[/b]: [i]Linear[/i] colours in proportion to the value; [i]Log[/i] spreads out small values, so a part used a few times still shows next to one used thousands of times; [i]Percentile[/i] colours by rank, so every shade holds the same number of cells and even tiny differences separate.
Untick [b]Auto range[/b] and set [b]Min[/b] and [b]Max[/b] to stretch the colours over just the range you care about (values outside are clamped).
​[b]Threshold[/b] draws cells below that share of the colour range as unused, so only the busy parts stand out.
​[b]Cell width[/b] and [b]Row height[/b] go down to 2 pixels, to fit thousands of cycles on screen (or [color=#e5c07b][code]Ctrl/Cmd[/code][/color] + mouse wheel on the grid). [b]Value[/b] switches between counts and % of cycles; [b]Your code only[/b] leaves out the OS (Totals and Per line).[/ul]

[color=#61afef][b]Before and after: finding what to optimise[/b][/color]
[ol type=1]Run your program to the end and open [b]Totals[/b] or [b]Per line[/b]: the strongest cells are the parts and lines doing the most work.
Press [color=#e5c07b][code]Save baseline[/code][/color]. picosim keeps the counts in a file next to your program ([code]<name>.heat-baseline.json[/code]).
Change the program (keep a register instead of reloading it from memory, unroll a loop, use a cheaper instruction…), save it — picosim reloads it — and run it again.
Choose View ▸ [b]Compare[/b]. Each row shows the baseline, the new count, the change and the change in %. [i]Per 1000 cycles[/i] compares the share of time instead of raw counts, which is fairer when the two runs have different lengths.[/ol]
[table=1][cell bg=#2a2a2a border=#61afef padding=14,9,14,9 expand=1][color=#61afef][b]Tip[/b][/color]   On the multi-cycle machine the busiest parts are nearly always the bus (about half of all cycles in the examples) and MAR and MDR (about 40%), because every instruction is fetched through them and the bus is shared by everything. Fewer instructions and fewer memory accesses (loads, stores, PUSH and POP) lower them most; compare the Per line view before and after to see which lines changed.[/cell][/table]

[color=#61afef][b]Exporting for analysis[/b][/color]
[color=#e5c07b][code]Export CSV…[/code][/color] and [color=#e5c07b][code]Export JSON…[/code][/color] save exactly what the grid shows. A CSV starts with [code]#[/code] lines describing the run (program, model, exact or estimate, cycles, instructions, date), then: Totals — one row per part with its count and % of cycles; Per line — one row per line with a column per part; Timeline — one row per bucket with its first and last cycle; Compare — before, after, change and change %. In Python, [code]pandas.read_csv(path, comment='#')[/code] reads it. [color=#e5c07b][code]Save PNG…[/code][/color] saves a picture of the grid.

[color=#61afef][b]On the CPU diagram[/b][/color]
View ▸ [b]Heat overlay on the CPU diagram[/b] tints every box of the [url=diagram][color=#61afef][u]CPU diagram[/u][/color][/url] (or the [url=pipeline][color=#61afef][u]pipeline diagram[/u][/color][/url]) by how much of the run it was used, with a small label giving its share of all cycles; the register file tints each register by its reads + writes. It updates while the program runs, alongside the usual animation.

[color=#61afef][b]Limits[/b][/color]
[ul]The timeline keeps every instruction for the first 20 million instructions (about 100 million cycles). After that its columns are samples every few thousand cycles; Totals and Per line stay exact for the whole run.
The multi-cycle counts are exact for picosim's teaching datapath, which is not how the real RP2040 is built; the pipeline counts are a model of the real chip, not a measurement of it.
Step back rewinds the counts too: they always describe the run up to the instruction shown.[/ul]
4.name: Heat map
4.sum:
The heat map (Performance ▸ [b]Heat map[/b]) colours each part of the CPU, each register and each flag by how much your program used it: the stronger the colour, the busier the part. [b]Totals[/b] gives each part's share of all cycles, [b]Timeline[/b] shows the use cycle by cycle, and [b]Per line[/b] shows which lines of your program cause it.

To see what a change saves: [color=#e5c07b][code]Save baseline[/code][/color], change the program, run it again and choose [b]Compare[/b]. The multi-cycle counts are exact; the pipeline's are an estimate from the datasheet's cycle counts.

4.full:
[font_size=26][b]Keyboard shortcuts[/b][/font_size]

[table=2][cell][color=#e5c07b][code]S  or  F10[/code][/color]    [/cell][cell]Step instruction: run one instruction (hold to repeat)[/cell][cell][color=#e5c07b][code]B[/code][/color]    [/cell][cell]Step back: undo the last step (hold to repeat)[/cell][cell][color=#e5c07b][code]O[/code][/color]    [/cell][cell]Step over: run a whole bl call, stop on the line after it[/cell][cell][color=#e5c07b][code]C  or  F11[/code][/color]    [/cell][cell]Step cycle: one clock cycle (hold to repeat)[/cell][cell][color=#e5c07b][code]Space  or  F5[/code][/color]    [/cell][cell]Run / Pause[/cell][cell][color=#e5c07b][code]F2[/code][/color]    [/cell][cell]open the Performance window[/cell][cell][color=#e5c07b][code]F1[/code][/color]    [/cell][cell]open this guide[/cell][cell][color=#e5c07b][code]?[/code][/color]    [/cell][cell]open Ask picosim, the help chat[/cell][cell][color=#e5c07b][code]Ctrl/Cmd+O[/code][/color]    [/cell][cell]open a .s file[/cell][cell][color=#e5c07b][code]Ctrl/Cmd+R[/code][/color]    [/cell][cell]reload (start the program over)[/cell][cell][color=#e5c07b][code]Ctrl/Cmd + / −[/code][/color]    [/cell][cell]zoom in / out[/cell][cell][color=#e5c07b][code]Ctrl/Cmd 0[/code][/color]    [/cell][cell]reset zoom[/cell][cell][color=#e5c07b][code]Esc[/code][/color]    [/cell][cell]close this guide, the enlarged Pico board or a component card[/cell][/table]

On the 2-stage pipeline, C / F11 steps one pipeline cycle, S / F10 jumps to the next instruction's first Execute cycle and B goes back a whole instruction. The letter keys work on every keyboard: on a Mac, F11 shows the desktop and the F keys need Fn, so use S, B, C and Space there. They only work in Simulator mode, and not while you are typing in a box or in the serial console (those keys go to your program).
4.name: Keyboard shortcuts
4.sum: [color=#e5c07b][code]S[/code][/color] steps one instruction, [color=#e5c07b][code]B[/code][/color] steps back, [color=#e5c07b][code]Space[/code][/color] runs or pauses, [color=#e5c07b][code]O[/code][/color] steps over a call, [color=#e5c07b][code]C[/code][/color] steps one clock cycle, [color=#e5c07b][code]F2[/code][/color] opens the Performance window, [color=#e5c07b][code]F1[/code][/color] opens this guide, [color=#e5c07b][code]Ctrl/Cmd+O[/code][/color] opens a file and [color=#e5c07b][code]Ctrl/Cmd+R[/code][/color] reloads it. Holding a step key repeats it. The keys work only in Simulator mode, and not while you are typing in a box or in the serial console.

4.full:
[font_size=26][b]Troubleshooting[/b][/font_size]

[font_size=21][b]While it runs[/b][/font_size]

[color=#61afef][b]Nothing happens when I press Step or Run[/b][/color]
The program has halted (the status text says [i]halted[/i]) — press [color=#e5c07b][code]Reload[/code][/color]. Or no program is loaded, or you are in Pico mode — switch to Simulator.

[color=#61afef][b]I pressed Step and ended up in code I did not write[/b][/color]
That is the built-in OS, at addresses below [code]3000[/code]. The first three instructions of every run are the OS starting your [code]main[/code], and each [code]bl putchar[/code] goes into the OS for two instructions ([code]svc #2[/code], [code]bx lr[/code]) before coming back. Keep stepping, or use [color=#e5c07b][code]Step over[/code][/color] on the [code]bl[/code] line. See [url=running][color=#61afef][u]How a program runs[/u][/color][/url].

[color=#61afef][b]R0 suddenly holds 0x00002FFC or 0x00003001[/b][/color]
Those are from the OS's first two instructions, before your program starts. Your own code starts at [code]main[/code].

[color=#61afef][b]Run is very slow[/b][/color]
Move the [color=#e5c07b][code]Speed[/code][/color] slider to the right. At the starting speed (8 cyc/s) Run does about one instruction a second, so you can watch it. [b]Max[/b] finishes almost at once.

[color=#61afef][b]The program stops and waits[/b][/color]
It is in [code]getchar[/code], waiting for a key (the status text says [i]waiting for input[/i]). Click the serial console and type a key.

[color=#61afef][b]It prints a strange character instead of my number[/b][/color]
[code]putchar[/code] prints the character whose [i]code[/i] is in R0. Add [code]'0'[/code] to a number from 0 to 9 first; numbers of 10 or more need one digit at a time. See [url=numbers][color=#61afef][u]Hex, binary and ASCII[/u][/color][/url].

[color=#61afef][b]A value I saved in R0–R3 changed after bl putchar[/b][/color]
Functions are allowed to change R0–R3 (and LR). Keep values you need in R4–R7, and add those registers to [code]main[/code]'s [code]push[/code] and [code]pop[/code].

[color=#61afef][b]The program never halts, and ▶ is stuck on a bx lr[/b][/color]
A function called another function (even putchar) without saving LR first, so its [code]bx lr[/code] jumps back to itself forever. Add [code]push {lr}[/code] at its start and end it with [code]pop {pc}[/code]. See [url=stack][color=#61afef][u]The stack and functions[/u][/color][/url].

[color=#61afef][b]Go to in the Memory tab does nothing[/b][/color]
Type the label exactly as it is in your file (capital letters matter), or an address starting with [code]0x[/code], then press [color=#e5c07b][code]Enter[/code][/color]. Reload first if you have just added the label.

[color=#61afef][b]My data is not in the Disassembly[/b][/color]
Data after [code].data[/code] is not listed there: look at it in the Memory tab (Go to its label).

[color=#61afef][b]I can't find a button or panel from the guide[/b][/color]
Some appear only at higher levels. Raise the [color=#e5c07b][code]Level[/code][/color] menu in the toolbar; see [url=start][color=#61afef][u]Start here[/u][/color][/url].

[color=#61afef][b]The cycle inspector says no cycle has run yet[/b][/color]
Press [color=#e5c07b][code]Step cycle[/code][/color] ([color=#e5c07b][code]F11[/code][/color]). [color=#e5c07b][code]Step instruction[/code][/color] and [color=#e5c07b][code]Run[/code][/color] also run cycles, but they finish whole instructions; to see the cycles of one instruction, stop before it (a breakpoint) and use F11.

[color=#61afef][b]A value on the diagram is not the one in the Registers panel[/b][/color]
The diagram shows values [i]during[/i] the cycle; a register's new value appears as the yellow [code]old → new[/code] caption and moves into the box at the next cycle. The Registers panel shows the machine after the last clock edge. See [url=diagram][color=#61afef][u]Datapath diagram[/u][/color][/url].

[color=#61afef][b]The diagram shows the wrong machine[/b][/color]
The machine menu next to [color=#e5c07b][code]Show CPU Diagram[/code][/color] picks it: [color=#e5c07b][code]Multi-cycle[/code][/color] for the datapath with the cycle inspector, [color=#e5c07b][code]2-stage pipeline[/code][/color] for the Pico's pipeline.

[color=#61afef][b]The pipeline totals leave out some instructions[/b][/color]
SVC (putchar, getchar) and BKPT are not timed on the pipelines: the RP2040 datasheet gives no fixed count for them. The Performance window says how many were left out, and its CPI is over the rest.

[font_size=21][b]When it will not load[/b][/font_size]
The [b]Could not load program[/b] box shows the assembler's message. The number after the file name is the line, for example [code]add.s:12: Error: …[/code] is line 12. Fix the file, save it and press [color=#e5c07b][code]Reload[/code][/color].

[table=2][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]The message says[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]What is usually wrong[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]cannot honor width suffix[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]A missing S ([code]add[/code] instead of [code]adds[/code], [code]mov r0, #1[/code] instead of [code]movs[/code]), or a register from R8 to R12. Use R0–R7. See [url=instructions][color=#61afef][u]Instructions[/u][/color][/url].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]invalid immediate: 300 is out of range[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The constant is too big (or negative). [code]movs[/code], [code]cmp[/code] and two-register [code]adds[/code] / [code]subs[/code] take 0 to 255.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]immediate value out of range[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Three-register [code]adds r0, r1, #9[/code] takes only 0 to 7. Use [code]adds r0, #9[/code] on the same register, or put the constant in a register first.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]bad arguments to instruction[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]A missing comma or # (write [code]movs r0, #1[/code]), or a misspelt register.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]undefined reference to …[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]A branch or [code]bl[/code] to a label that does not exist. Check the spelling, and that the label line ends in a colon.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]The program has no main: label[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Put [code]main:[/code] on the line before your first instruction.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5][code]invalid offset, value too big[/code][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]A load or store offset that is too big, negative or not a multiple of the size; or, on an [code]ldr rX, =…[/code] line, a literal pool too far away (put [code].ltorg[/code] after a [code]b[/code] or [code]pop[/code]). See [url=loadstore][color=#61afef][u]Loads and stores[/u][/color][/url].[/cell][/table]

[color=#61afef][b]"Simulator backend disconnected"[/b][/color]
The Python backend stopped. Close picosim and start it again with [code]picosim --gui[/code].

[font_size=21][b]Pins[/b][/font_size]

[color=#61afef][b]A pin will not respond to clicks[/b][/color]
Only input pins can be driven. If your program configured the pin as an output (via [code]GPIO_OE[/code]), it controls the pin.

[color=#61afef][b]My program sets GPIO_OE and GPIO_OUT but the pin stays blank[/b][/color]
The pin is not connected to the SIO yet: write 5 (function SIO) to its IO_BANK0 CTRL register at [code]0x40014004 + 8 × pin[/code] first. The real RP2040 needs this too. Hover the pin for a reminder. See [url=gpio][color=#61afef][u]GPIO: controlling pins[/u][/color][/url].

[font_size=21][b]On a real Pico[/b][/font_size]

[color=#61afef][b]There is no Flash button[/b][/color]
Choose [b]Pico (USB serial)[/b] in the mode menu (it says [b]Simulator[/b]). Flash needs a loaded [code].s[/code] file.

[color=#61afef][b]Flash failed[/b][/color]
The console shows the reason; the table in [url=hardware][color=#61afef][u]Running on a real Pico[/u][/color][/url] says what to do. Most often the board is not in BOOTSEL mode: unplug it, hold BOOTSEL, plug it in, let go, and Flash again.

[color=#61afef][b]Nothing appears in the console after Flash[/b][/color]
Check that a port marked [i](Pico)[/i] is chosen and that the button says [b]Disconnect[/b] (it is connected); if not, press [color=#e5c07b][code]⟳[/code][/color] and [color=#e5c07b][code]Connect[/code][/color]. A board waits only 5 seconds for the console before it starts, so a short program may have finished before you connected: Flash again.

[font_size=21][b]"CPU fault: …" in the console[/b][/font_size]
Your program did something that would crash a real Pico, and the message says what and where. The most common ones:
[ul]​[b]Undefined instruction[/b] — not a Cortex-M0+ instruction (for example code written for a Cortex-M4), or the program ran into data.
​[b]Bus fault[/b] — the address is not RAM (0x0000–0xFFFF) or a simulated I/O register. The two most common causes at first: [code]main[/code] has no [code]pop {…, pc}[/code] at the end, so the CPU runs on through empty memory until it reaches [code]0x00010000[/code]; or [code]main[/code] pops without a matching [code]push {…, lr}[/code] at the start, so the pop reads past the top of RAM. Later on, a pointer that went wrong or a stack that grew too far (too many PUSHes without POPs) do the same.
​[b]… with bit 0 clear[/b] — BX, BLX or POP {PC} jumped to an even address. Put [code].thumb_func[/code] on the line before a label whose address you load with [code]ldr r0, =label[/code].
​[b]Unaligned access[/b] — LDR/STR need an address that is a multiple of 4, LDRH/STRH a multiple of 2. Use LDRB/STRB for single bytes, and put [code].align 2[/code] before word data.[/ul]
Press [color=#e5c07b][code]Reload[/code][/color] to start again.
4.name: Troubleshooting
4.sum:
Most problems have a quick fix. If Step does nothing, the program has finished: press [color=#e5c07b][code]Reload[/code][/color]. If it is waiting, type a key in the serial console. If Run is slow, move the [color=#e5c07b][code]Speed[/code][/color] slider to the right. If the program will not load, the [b]Could not load program[/b] box gives the line number and what is wrong: fix that line and save.

A [b]CPU fault[/b] message in the console means the program did something that would crash a real Pico. The most common cause is a [code]main[/code] without [code]pop {…, pc}[/code] at its end. The details list every message you may see, with what to do.

4.full:
[font_size=26][b]Ask picosim[/b][/font_size]

Click [color=#e5c07b][code]Ask[/code][/color] in the toolbar, or press [color=#e5c07b][code]?[/code][/color], and type a question in your own words. Typos are fine. Some good ones:

[table=2][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Ask about[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]For example[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Your program right now[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1][i]Why did it stop?[/i] · [i]What just happened?[/i] · [i]What happens next?[/i] · [i]Why is R0 72?[/i] · [i]Why is it waiting?[/i][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Errors and crashes[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1][i]What does this error mean?[/i] (or paste the error) · [i]Why did it crash?[/i][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]The buttons and panels[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1][i]What does Step over do?[/i] · [i]How do I set a breakpoint?[/i] · [i]How do I see decimal?[/i][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Assembly[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1][i]What does LDR do?[/i] · [i]movs vs mov?[/i] · [i]What is the Z flag?[/i] · [i]What is 0x2A in decimal?[/i][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Challenges[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1][i]What is the challenge?[/i] · [i]Did I pass?[/i] · [i]Give me a hint[/i][/cell][/table]

Follow-ups work too: [i]why?[/i], [i]tell me more[/i], [i]what about R1?[/i]. Chips under the conversation suggest questions that fit what is on screen, such as [i]Why did it crash?[/i] after a fault.

[color=#61afef][b]Hints, not answers[/b][/color]
It never writes your code or a challenge's solution, and nothing you type changes that. Ask for the answer and you get the next small hint: first the idea and the guide page, then where to look, then what kind of change to make. After three hints it stops: ask your teacher, or look the topic up online. Load errors and CPU faults are different: it tells you exactly what the assembler or the CPU complained about, because fixing those is not the exercise.

[color=#61afef][b]Where answers come from[/b][/color]
Each answer has a small tag. [b]built-in answer[/b] and [b]from the guide[/b] come from picosim itself: this guide and your program as it runs, so they match what you see. Above your Level it gives a short answer and says which Level covers it. 👍 and 👎 tell your teacher what helps; [b]Report[/b] saves the question and answer (without personal details) for them.
Please don't type personal details (phone numbers, addresses, passwords): the chat leaves them out. If something is really wrong, beyond picosim, talk to a teacher or another adult you trust.

[color=#61afef][b]For teachers: AI help[/b][/color]
By default everything works offline. A teacher can let questions the built-in answers cannot handle go to Claude, an AI made by Anthropic: run [code]picosim --chat-setup[/code] to see (and create) the config file, set [code]"ai": "on"[/code] there, install the extra with [code]pip install -e .[lb]ai][/code] (it needs Python 3.10 or newer) and set an Anthropic API key in [code]ANTHROPIC_API_KEY[/code]. The question, a summary of the machine and the student's program (personal data removed) are then sent to Anthropic, so check your school's rules first; the window shows a notice while AI is on. AI answers are tagged [b]AI answer[/b], follow the same hints-only rule, and are withdrawn if they show too much code. The config also sets the model, [code]max_ai_per_hour[/code] (20), a [code]helpline[/code] for the wellbeing reply and [code]log_unanswered[/code]. There is no setting for full answers.
Reports go to [code]chat_reports.jsonl[/code] and 👍 / 👎 counts to [code]chat_feedback.json[/code], next to the config. Write your own hints for a challenge with [code]@ Hint:[/code] lines (see [url=challenges][color=#61afef][u]Challenges[/u][/color][/url]).
4.name: Ask picosim
4.sum:
[color=#e5c07b][code]Ask[/code][/color] (top right, or the [color=#e5c07b][code]?[/code][/color] key) opens a chat where you can ask questions in your own words: [i]Why did my program stop?[/i], [i]Why is R0 72?[/i], [i]What does LDR do?[/i], [i]How do I set a breakpoint?[/i] It looks at your program as it runs and answers from this guide, with a link to the page and often a [b]Show me[/b] button that points at the control.

It gives [b]hints, never finished answers[/b]: ask it for the solution to a challenge and it gives the next small hint instead, up to three. If you need more help than that, ask your teacher, or look the topic up online. It only knows about picosim, ARM assembly and the Pico.

4.full:
[font_size=26][b]Glossary[/b][/font_size]

[table=2][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Word[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1f3048 padding=10,6,16,6][b]Meaning[/b][/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Address[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]A number that says where in memory something is, like a house number. Shown in hex, such as [code]3000[/code].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]AHB-Lite[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The RP2040's main bus between the processor and memory. A transfer takes an address cycle, then a data cycle.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Alignment[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]A word must be at an address that is a multiple of 4, a halfword at a multiple of 2. See [url=memmap][color=#61afef][u]Memory and addresses[/u][/color][/url].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]ALU[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Arithmetic Logic Unit: the part that adds, subtracts, ANDs and shifts. See [url=blocks][color=#61afef][u]Building blocks[/u][/color][/url].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]APB[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]A slower bus behind AHB-Lite for simple peripherals; IO_BANK0 and PADS_BANK0 are on it.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]ASCII[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The code that gives each character a number: 'A' is [code]0x41[/code]. See [url=numbers][color=#61afef][u]Hex, binary and ASCII[/u][/color][/url].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Assembler[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The program that turns your [code].s[/code] file into the bits the CPU runs. picosim runs it when you Open or Reload.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Assembly language[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Writing a program as the processor's own instructions, one per line, with names instead of bits.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Bit[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]One binary digit, 0 or 1. A register has 32.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]BOOTSEL[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The button on the Pico. Hold it while plugging the board in and it appears as a drive (RPI-RP2) you can copy a program to.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Branch[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]An instruction that jumps to another place in the program, always ([code]b[/code]) or only if a condition holds ([code]bne[/code], …).[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Breakpoint[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]A red ● on a Disassembly row: Run stops just before that instruction.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Built-in OS[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]picosim's tiny operating system at addresses [code]0000[/code]–[code]2FFF[/code]. It starts your [code]main[/code] and provides [code]putchar[/code] and [code]getchar[/code].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Bus[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Shared wires that carry one value at a time between the parts of the datapath.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Byte[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]8 bits: two hex digits, 0 to 255.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Calling convention[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The rules functions follow: arguments and result in R0–R3, R4–R7 kept, LR saved. See [url=stack][color=#61afef][u]The stack and functions[/u][/color][/url].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Clock cycle[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]One tick of the CPU's clock. An instruction takes several. See [url=cycles][color=#61afef][u]Cycle by cycle[/u][/color][/url].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Clock edge[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The tick that ends a clock cycle: the moment registers take their new values.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Clock frequency[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Clock cycles per second, in hertz. The RP2040 normally runs at 125 MHz.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Combinational logic[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Parts with no memory (muxes, adders, the ALU): their output follows their inputs straight away.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Comment[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Text after [code]@[/code] that the assembler ignores; it is for people.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Condition codes (LD.CC)[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Another name for the N Z C V flags. LD.CC is the control signal that loads them at the clock edge.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Control signal[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]An on/off (or select) line from the control unit that tells one part what to do this cycle. See [url=signals][color=#61afef][u]Control signals[/u][/color][/url].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Control unit (FSM)[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The finite-state machine that turns control signals on and off, one state per cycle.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Cortex-M0+[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The processor inside the Pico's RP2040 chip. picosim runs only its instructions.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]CPI[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Cycles per instruction: total clock cycles ÷ instructions. See [url=perfmath][color=#61afef][u]Performance formulas[/u][/color][/url].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]CPU fault[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]A mistake that would crash a real Pico, such as running something that is not an instruction. picosim stops and explains it in the console.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Datapath[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The parts that hold, move and compute data: registers, bus, ALU, adders, memory.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Directive[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]A line starting with a dot, such as [code].thumb[/code]: an instruction to the assembler, not to the CPU.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Disassembly[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Your program shown back from the bits in memory: see [url=memory][color=#61afef][u]Disassembly[/u][/color][/url].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Flags[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]N, Z, C and V: four bits describing the last result, used by conditional branches. See [url=branches][color=#61afef][u]Flags and branches[/u][/color][/url].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Flash[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]To copy a program into the Pico's flash memory, where it stays when the power is off. Also the name of that memory.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Floating[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]An input pin that nothing drives: it could read 0 or 1. A pull resistor prevents it.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Flush[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Throwing away an instruction a pipeline fetched from the wrong path, after a taken branch.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Function[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]A piece of code you call with [code]bl[/code] that returns with [code]bx lr[/code] or [code]pop {…, pc}[/code]. [code]putchar[/code] is one.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]GPIO[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]General-purpose input/output: a pin your program can drive high or low, or read. See [url=gpio][color=#61afef][u]GPIO: controlling pins[/u][/color][/url].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Halfword[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]2 bytes, 16 bits. Most Thumb instructions are one halfword.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Halted[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The program has finished (or faulted) and the CPU has stopped. Press Reload to start again.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Hazard[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Something that stops a pipeline finishing one instruction per cycle, such as a taken branch.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Hex[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Base 16, written with [code]0x[/code] in front: [code]0x2A[/code] = 42.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Immediate[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]A constant written inside the instruction after a [code]#[/code], as in [code]movs r0, #5[/code].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Instruction[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]One step for the CPU, such as [code]adds r2, r0, r1[/code].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]IOPORT[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The M0+'s private single-cycle port to the SIO block, so a GPIO access does not use AHB-Lite.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]IR / IR2[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Instruction registers: hold the instruction (and the second half of a 32-bit one) while it runs.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Label[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]A name followed by a colon, such as [code]loop:[/code]; it stands for the address of the next line.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Latch (ALU A / B)[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]A register that holds an input steady for the next cycle. The ALU's A and B latches (LD.ALUA, LD.ALUB) keep its inputs fixed while it computes.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Latency[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]How long one instruction (or job) takes from start to finish.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Leaf function[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]A function that calls no other function, so it need not save LR.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Literal pool[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Numbers the assembler stores after your code for [code]ldr rX, =value[/code]; listed as [code].word[/code] rows.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Little-endian[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Storing a word's lowest byte at the lowest address: [code]0x0000300D[/code] is stored as [code]0D 30 00 00[/code].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Load / store[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Copy a value from memory into a register ([code]ldr[/code]) or from a register into memory ([code]str[/code]).[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]LR[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Link register (R14): holds the address a function returns to.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]MAR / MDR[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Memory address register and memory data register: the address memory uses, and the data read or to be written.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Mask[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]A number with a 1 in the bits you care about, such as [code]1 << 15[/code] for GP15.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Memory-mapped I/O[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Controlling hardware by reading and writing special addresses with ordinary loads and stores.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Mnemonic[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The name of an instruction: [code]movs[/code], [code]adds[/code], [code]bne[/code].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Multiplexer (mux)[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Picks one of several inputs to pass on, chosen by a select signal.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Operand[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]What an instruction works on: the registers and constants after the mnemonic.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]PC[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Program counter (R15): the address of the next instruction.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Phase[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]One of the six parts of the instruction cycle: Fetch, Decode, Evaluate address, Fetch operands, Execute, Store result.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Pipeline[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Splitting instructions into stages that work on different instructions at the same time. See [url=pipeintro][color=#61afef][u]Pipelining: the big idea[/u][/color][/url].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Pipeline register[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The register between two stages (IF/EX) that hands an instruction on.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Pointer[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]A register (or word) holding an address: [code][lb]r1][/code] means the memory R1 points at.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Polling[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Reading an input over and over in a loop to see when it changes.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Pull-up / pull-down[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]A weak resistor inside the chip that holds an input at 1 (up) or 0 (down) while nothing else drives it.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Register[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]One of 16 storage boxes inside the CPU, each holding a 32-bit number.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Register file[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The block that holds R0–R12, SP and LR (the PC is a separate register), with ports to read two registers and write one.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Sequential logic[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Parts that remember (registers): they change only at the clock edge.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Serial console[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The text panel on the right: what your program prints, and where you type to it.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Sign-extend (SEXT)[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Widen a number by copying its top bit into the new bits, so a negative number stays negative: 8-bit 0xFE (−2) becomes 0xFFFFFFFE.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]SIO[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Single-cycle I/O: the block at 0xD0000000 whose registers set, clear and read the GPIO pins in one clock cycle.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]SP and the stack[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The stack is memory used to save registers ([code]push[/code] / [code]pop[/code]); SP (R13) points to its top. See [url=memory][color=#61afef][u]the Memory tab[/u][/color][/url].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Special registers[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Registers outside R0–R15 read with MRS and written with MSR: APSR (the flags), PRIMASK (turns interrupts off), CONTROL, and the two stack pointers MSP and PSP.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Speed-up[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Old time ÷ new time: how many times faster a change makes a program.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Stage[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]One step of a pipeline, such as Fetch or Execute.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]State[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]What the control unit is doing in one clock cycle, such as FETCH_ADDR. See [url=states][color=#61afef][u]FSM states[/u][/color][/url].[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Throughput[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]How many instructions finish per cycle (or per second).[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Thumb[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The 16-bit instruction set the Cortex-M0+ runs (a few instructions, like [code]bl[/code], are 32 bits).[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Thumb bit[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Bit 0 of an address you jump to with BX, BLX or POP {PC}. It must be 1, meaning "Thumb code"; the instruction itself is fetched from the even address.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Tri-state buffer[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]A switch between a part and the bus: on, the part drives the bus; off, it is disconnected.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]UF2[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]The file format the Pico loads programs from. Flash makes one from your [code].s[/code] file.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Wait state[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]An extra cycle a slow memory makes the processor wait.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Word[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]4 bytes, 32 bits: what one register holds.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]XIP[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Execute in place: the RP2040 runs code straight from external flash, through a cache.[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5]Zero-extend (ZEXT)[/cell][cell bg=#1d1d1d,#2a2a2a padding=10,5,16,5 expand=1]Widen a number by filling the new bits with 0: 8-bit 0xFE becomes 0x000000FE (254).[/cell][/table]
4.name: Glossary
4.sum: Short meanings of the words used in picosim and in this guide, in alphabetical order. More words appear as you raise the Level.
